additions.why: Part of breakfast (asa wa pan yaite taberu). Keeki o yaku (18) and kukkii o yaku (6) use the same verb for baking.
additions.gap: The yaku family has only niku o yaku (cut).

additions.trap: 'Do you take sugar?' is satou ireru?, not toru. Miruku ireru? works the same way.
additions.why: Comes with every offer of coffee or tea (satou to miruku iremasu ka?). 13% of sugar mentions go to ireru.
additions.gap: The ireru rows are coffee, tea, power, tattoo and pocket. Nothing for adding things to a drink.

additions.trap: 'Serve' or 'offer' suggests ageru. Guests are given tea with dasu (okyaku-san ni ocha dashite).
additions.why: Basic hospitality in Japanese homes and offices. It is the step after the kept ocha o ireru (making the tea).
additions.gap: The dasu rows are voice, rubbish, letters and car. Nothing for serving food or drink.

additions.trap: Rice balls and sushi are pressed by hand, so the verb is nigiru (squeeze). Onigiri o tsukuru is also heard.
additions.why: Home cooking, packed lunches and picnics (onigiri nigitte ageru). The noun itself comes from nigiru. Foreign films never show it.
additions.gap: The nigiru family has no row in the table.

additions.trap: Hurting yourself takes plain o + kiru with no word for 'myself' (yubi kitchatta).
additions.why: The standard kitchen accident (houchou de yubi kitta). 19 hits.
additions.gap: No yubi row. The kiru (cut) rows have no injuries.

additions.trap: 'Hold' is not motsu here. You stop (tomeru) the breath: iki o tomete kudasai at every X-ray.
additions.why: Heard at the doctor's and in swimming lessons, and in play. 56 hits.
additions.gap: The tomeru rows are car, water, button and alarm. The iki rows are suru, suu, dekiru, arai and kireru.

additions.trap: 'Relax' as rirakkusu suru is about mood. For muscles you pull the strength out (chikara nuite).
additions.why: Heard at massages, the doctor's, sport and yoga (motto chikara nuite). 52 pair hits and 75 phrase hits. The figurative kata no chikara o nuku is in the idiom pool; this entry is the literal body set.
additions.gap: The nuku rows are tooth, plug and breakfast only. No chikara row.

additions.english: a cough stops (mostly: can't stop coughing)
additions.trap: 'I can't stop coughing' is seki ga tomaranai (the cough won't stop), not seki o tomerarenai.
additions.why: The standard cold complaint (seki ga tomaranakute nerarenai). Shakkuri ga tomaranai and namida ga tomaranai (7) use the same frame. Films under-count everyday illness.
additions.gap: The tomaru rows are hotel and train. The cough row is seki ga deru only.

additions.trap: Healing uses the same naoru as getting over a cold. An injury is kega ga naoru.
additions.why: Said after any cut or graze (kizu mou naotta?). 23 hits.
additions.gap: naoru appears only with kaze (cut), and the kizu rows are tsuku and kizuato only.

additions.kana: たいじゅうけいにのる
additions.english: step on the scales, weigh oneself
additions.trap: 'Weigh myself' has no verb of its own. You get on (noru) the scale like a train: taijuukei ni noru no ga kowai.
additions.why: Comes up in diet talk and after holiday eating. Films rarely show it (1 phrase hit).
additions.gap: Every noru row is a vehicle. No 'step onto' sense.

additions.trap: Nutrition is taken (toru, also written 摂る), not eaten or got.
additions.why: Parents and doctors say it (chanto eiyou totte ne). 29% of nutrition mentions go to toru.
additions.gap: The toru body rows are suibun and suimin (both cut). No nutrition row.

additions.english: toss and turn, roll over in one's sleep
additions.trap: Rolling over is 'struck' (utsu), a verb no English speaker would guess, and fixed to this noun.
additions.why: Comes up in talk about sleep and babies (negaeri bakari utte nerarenakatta, akachan ga negaeri utta). Missing from film subtitles.
additions.gap: The utsu rows are head and injection only.

additions.trap: Lifting your eyes from a book, a phone or a bow is kao o ageru (kao agete), not just ue o miru.
additions.why: Heard from photographers and teachers, and when comforting someone (kao agete). 34 hits.
additions.gap: The ageru rows are hand, scream, speed and results. The kao rows are miru and iya na kao o suru.

additions.why: Said after every outing (ato de shashin okuru ne). 62 hits. It uses the same okuru as the kept meeru o okuru, but photos are what people send most.
additions.gap: The photo rows are toru, miru, miseru, ageru, kesu and utsuru. No sending.

additions.english: sound comes out (oto ga denai = no sound)
additions.trap: 'There's no sound' is oto ga denai (it doesn't come out), not oto ga nai.
additions.why: Used when TVs, speakers, phones or video calls go silent (oto denai yo). 32 hits.
additions.gap: The oto rows are suru, tateru, kikoeru and ookiku suru. No deru.

additions.trap: Volume goes up and down with ageru / sageru (boryuumu sagete).
additions.why: Half of all volume mentions go to ageru, and sageru adds 4 more. The table's oto o ookiku suru (a maybe) makes the same request with other words.
additions.gap: No volume row with ageru/sageru. Only oto o ookiku suru.

additions.english: press the shutter, take the picture
additions.trap: 'Press the shutter' is kiru (cut). Shattaa o osu is also heard.
additions.why: The request tourists make at every sight (sumimasen, shattaa kitte moraemasu ka?). Films rarely say it.
additions.gap: The kiru rows have no camera sense.

additions.trap: 'Write / type a message' is utsu (hit the keys), not kaku. Moji o utsu and LINE utsu work the same way.
additions.why: Phone life (ima meeru utteru kara chotto matte). It is the verb for tapping out text.
additions.gap: The utsu rows are head and injection. The meeru rows are okuru, kaesu, miru and kuru.

additions.trap: On screens 開く is read hiraku (fairu hiraite), while doors take akeru.
additions.why: Office and computer talk. 17 hits. Apuri o hiraku works the same way.
additions.gap: The hiraku rows are party and meeting only.

additions.trap: 'Become popular' is ninki ga deru (popularity comes out), not ninki ni naru.
additions.why: Said about shows, shops and products (ano mise kyuu ni ninki deta). It complements the kept ninki ga aru.
additions.gap: ninki appears only with aru.

additions.trap: Bikes take ni + noru like cars, not o (jitensha ni noreru? = can you ride a bike?).
additions.why: Bikes are everyday transport in Japan (jitensha ni noreru?, jitensha de iku). 48 phrase hits; the pair counter files 自転車 under kuruma. It shares its frame with the kept kuruma/basu/densha ni noru, so it may read as covered.
additions.gap: The noru rows cover car, bus, train, taxi, motorbike and boat, but not bicycles.

additions.trap: 'I'm flying to Osaka' is hikouki de iku / hikouki ni noru. Tobu is what the plane does.
additions.why: Travel talk (hikouki ni noru no ga kowai). 199 phrase hits, more than any kept vehicle set except kuruma. The tokenizer splits 飛行機, so it is counted as a phrase.
additions.gap: No hikouki row in the table.

additions.trap: Brakes are stepped on (fumu) or applied (kakeru, 18 hits), never 'hit' (utsu).
additions.why: Driving talk (bureeki funde!). Fumu takes 24% of brake mentions and kakeru 22%; the two are interchangeable.
additions.gap: No brake row. Found while checking kakeru's partners.

additions.trap: 'Collect / earn points' is tameru (save up), the same verb as okane o tameru.
additions.why: Point cards at every konbini, drugstore and app (pointo tamete kaimono shiteru). Films under-count it.
additions.gap: Only the intransitive pointo ga tamaru (cut) is in the table. tameru has only okane.

additions.kana: てすうりょうがかかる
additions.english: there's a fee, a charge applies
additions.trap: 'There's a fee' is tesuuryou ga kakaru, not aru. Souryou ga kakaru (shipping) works the same way.
additions.why: Comes up with ATM fees after hours and at konbini, bank transfers and online shopping (kono ATM tesuuryou kakaru?). Films ignore it. It is close to the kept okane ga kakaru.
additions.gap: The kakaru rows are time, money, cost, lock and phone. No fees.

additions.why: A constant topic in Japan lately (mata nedan agatta). Neagari / neage add 28 hits, and bukka ga agaru (6, 67% of bukka) covers the cost of living.
additions.gap: The agaru rows are stairs, stage, tension, salary and temperature. No prices.

additions.trap: 'Make plans' is tateru (stand up), not tsukuru.
additions.why: Used for trips and weekends (ryokou no yotei tateyou). 6 hits.
additions.gap: The table cut keikaku o tateru because 'everyday talk about plans uses yotei', but the yotei version is missing. The yotei rows are aru, nai, hairu, ireru and tsumaru.

additions.trap: Posting a card or letter is dasu (put out). Okuru also works but is less usual.
additions.why: December talk in Japan (nengajou mou dashita?). The cut tegami o dasu was noted as 'worth knowing for New Year's cards'.
additions.gap: No nengajou row. It is a seasonal set the corpus can't see.

additions.trap: Starting a school is hairu (formally nyuugaku suru), not hajimeru.
additions.why: Life-story talk (daigaku ni haitte kara hitorigurashi). 31 hits.
additions.gap: The table has daigaku ni iku/kayou, daigaku o deru and kaisha ni hairu, but not daigaku ni hairu.

additions.trap: Qualifications and licences are taken (toru), not received (morau).
additions.why: Qualifications are a big part of Japanese careers (shikaku toru tame ni benkyou shiteru). Same toru as menkyo o toru.
additions.gap: menkyo o toru (cut) is the only qualification row.

additions.trap: 'Get results' is kekka o dasu (put out), not morau.
additions.why: Work and sport talk (chanto kekka dasanai to). It is the transitive partner of the kept kekka ga deru. 63 hits.
additions.gap: kekka appears only with deru.

additions.trap: 'Meet a deadline' is mamoru (keep), not au.
additions.why: Office and school talk (shimekiri wa mamotte ne). 0 film hits, but it uses the same mamoru as rules, time and promises.
additions.gap: The mamoru rows are promise, rules, secret, time and self. No deadline.

additions.trap: 'Get permission' is usually toru. Morau is also heard.
additions.why: Comes up at work and school, and for photos and events (joushi ni kyoka totta?). 41 hits. Kyoka ga deru (67) is its partner.
additions.gap: No kyoka row in the table.

additions.why: Said in meetings, lessons and on phone calls (chotto memo toru ne). 16 hits. Nooto o toru (6) is the same set.
additions.gap: memo appears only with nokosu (cut).

additions.trap: 'Focus on / put effort into' is X ni chikara o ireru (put strength in), not shuuchuu suru for priorities.
additions.why: Used for priorities (ima eigo ni chikara irete iru) and for pushing harder (motto chikara irete). 47 hits. It is the opposite of chikara o nuku.
additions.gap: The ireru rows have no chikara.

additions.trap: 'Prepare materials' is tsukuru, not junbi suru. Shiryou covers slides, handouts and reports.
additions.why: Daily office work in Japan (kaigi no shiryou tsukutteru). Films under-count it (1 hit).
additions.gap: The tsukuru rows are list and dinner only.

additions.trap: 'Correct' is naosu (fix), the same verb as repairing things. Teisei suru is formal.
additions.why: Comes up with homework and documents, and when learning a language (nihongo no machigai naoshite kureru?).
additions.gap: The naosu rows are illness and cold only. The machigai row is okasu.

additions.trap: 'Draw' is kaku for pictures but hiku for lines.
additions.why: Used when studying and in the office (daiji na tokoro ni sen hiite), and also for drawing a limit. 17 pair hits, 31 phrase hits.
additions.gap: The hiku rows are cold, guitar, piano and dictionary.

additions.trap: 'Improve' is agaru (go up). Dropping grades are sagaru / ochiru.
additions.why: Talk between students and parents (seiseki agatta!). Seiseki ga ochiru adds 7. Films under-count school life.
additions.gap: seiseki appears only with ii (cut).

additions.why: Comes up with a new school, job or city (atarashii tomodachi tsukuritai). 69 hits. It is the active partner of the kept tomodachi ga dekiru.
additions.gap: The tomodachi rows are dekiru and naru. No tsukuru.

additions.trap: Polite language is used (tsukau), not spoken: keigo tsukawanakute ii yo.
additions.why: Every learner hears keigo tsukawanakute ii yo (no need to be formal). Keigo appears 18 times; in speech it nearly always comes with tsukau.
additions.gap: No keigo row in the table.

additions.trap: English has no matching set: a mood is 'repaired' (naosu). When it improves on its own it is kigen ga naoru (10).
additions.why: Between couples, kids and friends (mou kigen naoshite yo).
additions.gap: The kigen rows are ii, warui and kireru. Nothing for mending a mood.

additions.trap: Backchannelling has its own noun and verb in Japanese, aizuchi o utsu. English has no set phrase for it.
additions.why: A named part of Japanese conversation that learners get told about (motto aizuchi utte). 75% of aizuchi mentions go to utsu.
additions.gap: No aizuchi row. The utsu family is nearly empty.

additions.trap: A favour is treated as a debt that is returned (on o kaesu / ongaeshi suru).
additions.why: Ongaeshi gets 51 phrase hits and is a common value word. On o kaesu is its verb set.
additions.gap: The kaesu rows are money and mail. Only the figurative on o ada de kaesu is in the idiom pool.

additions.english: draw lots; draw a fortune slip
additions.trap: Drawing lots or a raffle ticket is hiku (pull). At shrines it is omikuji o hiku.
additions.why: Omikuji at New Year, kujibiki at shops and festivals, and deciding turns (kuji de kimeyou). 34% of kuji mentions go to hiku.
additions.gap: The hiku rows have no drawing of lots. takarakuji ga ataru covers winning only.

additions.trap: 'Take a lesson' is ukeru (receive), not toru.
additions.why: Piano, swimming, English conversation (shuu ichi de ressun ukete iru). 29% of lesson mentions go to ukeru. Close to the cut jugyou o ukeru, but this is the hobby version.
additions.gap: The ukeru rows cover classes and exams, but not private lessons.

additions.why: Games and skills (nihongo no reberu agatta ne). 13 hits. Reberu o ageru adds 9.
additions.gap: No reberu row in the table.

additions.trap: A rising wind 'comes out' (kaze ga dete kita). Fuku is only for blowing.
additions.why: Weather small talk (kaze dete kita ne, samuku naru ne).
additions.gap: The wind rows are fuku, tsuyoi and tsumetai kaze.

additions.why: Evening talk and moon-viewing (kyou tsuki dete nai ne). Hoshi ga deru (6) uses the same frame.
additions.gap: No moon row. Nature rows stop at sun, rainbow and lightning.

additions.trap: English 'shampoo' as a verb tempts shanpuu suru. The everyday wording is kami (o) arau.
additions.why: A daily bath-routine set that goes with the kept ofuro ni hairu (kami aratte kara neru).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 髪+洗う 21, log_dice 9.4. The table has eleven kami sets (kiru, kawakasu, someru...) but not this one.

additions.trap: 'Do the dishes' is osara (o) arau or araimono (o) suru, never a bare suru.
additions.why: A core household chore (osara arau ne / osara aratte oite). Film subtitles under-count chores. All written forms total 16.
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 皿+洗う 10, log_dice 9.1. No dishwashing set in the table, while other chores (sentakumono o hosu, heya o katazukeru) are there.

additions.english: have a stomach ache; feel sick with stress
additions.trap: For a stomach ache, onaka ga itai (kept) is the general form. I ga itai means the stomach itself, and people also say it about stress (kangaeru dake de i ga itai).
additions.why: A common body complaint at clinics and pharmacies, and also used about stress at work.
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 胃+痛い 18, share 0.21, log_dice 9.7. The table has atama, onaka, nodo, ashi and koshi ga itai, but not i.

additions.trap: 'Fart' is a noun + suru (onara shita?) or onara ga deru. He o kokeru is crude.
additions.why: An everyday family word with no polite alternative needed. Very typical for its noun (0.54). All written forms total 27.
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: おなら+為る 20, share 0.54. Not in the table in any form.

additions.trap: 'Sit up straight' uses neither suwaru nor 'straight': sesuji (o) nobashite. It also means 'brace yourself, be on your best behaviour'.
additions.why: Parents, teachers and coaches say it all the time. Very fixed (share 0.60, log_dice 10.5).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 背筋+伸ばす 15, share 0.60, log_dice 10.5. Not in the table.

additions.trap: 'I'm allergic to eggs' is tamago arerugii ga aru (noun + aru). Japanese has no adjective like 'allergic'.
additions.why: A must-say at restaurants and clinics. Typical for its noun (0.53), and written forms total 53.
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: アレルギー+有る 23, share 0.53. No allergy set in the table.

additions.trap: 'I'm so forgetful' is the forgetting is terrible (saikin monowasure ga hidokute). It isn't a wasureru adjective.
additions.why: A common self-deprecating remark among adults. Very fixed (0.56).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 物忘れ+酷い 10, share 0.56. Not in the table.

additions.english: go out (with friends), go and visit someone
additions.trap: Asobu covers far more than 'play'. Adults asobi ni iku to go out or visit, and kondo asobi ni kite means 'come over sometime'.
additions.why: Among the most frequent social sets. It's built like the kept kaimono ni iku. The partner asobi ni kuru counts 67 in written forms.
additions.gap: The table has no asobi set at all. The tokenizer tags 遊び as a verb stem, so pairs.tsv shows only 11 (share 0.10), but the written forms 遊びに行/い count 53 and 遊びに来 counts 67.

additions.english: put the lid on, cover (a pot)
additions.trap: 'Put the lid on' is futa (o) suru, not oku or noseru. Taking it off is futa o akeru/toru (futa o akeru: 19 hits).
additions.why: An everyday cooking and storage instruction (futa shite go-fun nikomu).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 蓋+為る 24, share 0.30. Only the idiom kusai mono ni futa o suru is on the idiom list. The literal set is in neither list.

additions.why: A standard small-talk remark (kamigata kaeta?) and salon request.
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 髪型+変える 21, share 0.19. Not in the table.

additions.trap: 'Wear perfume' takes tsukeru, not kiru. It's another 'wear' that isn't kiru.
additions.why: Common in getting-ready talk and compliments (kousui tsuketeru?). Typical for its noun (0.24).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 香水+付ける 19, share 0.24. The table has masuku o tsukeru and akusesarii o tsukeru (cut) but not perfume.

additions.trap: 'Wear a tie' uses suru (nekutai shiteru). Kiru is wrong, and shimeru describes the act of tying it.
additions.why: Office and dress-code talk. It's the suru-for-accessories pattern, like the kept masuku o suru.
additions.gap: nekutai-o-shimeru was cut with the note 'most people just say nekutai shiteru', but nekutai o suru is not in the table. pairs.tsv: ネクタイ+為る 16, share 0.17.

additions.trap: 'The battery died' is kireru (run out), not shinu.
additions.why: Remotes, clocks, toys, and phones in casual speech too. The log_dice is high (9.6), and written forms total 33.
additions.gap: Only juuden ga kireru (phones) is kept. pairs.tsv band: 電池+切れる 15, log_dice 9.6, and the dry-cell set is not in the table.

additions.trap: At the pump you say mantan de (onegaishimasu), not words like ippai.
additions.why: The fixed refuelling phrase. Very typical (0.70), and written forms with mantan ni/de total 45.
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 満タン+為る 23, share 0.70. The only refuelling set, gasorin o ireru, was cut.

additions.trap: 'The power went out' is teiden ni natta / teiden shita. Denki ga kieta (cut) is the lights going off.
additions.why: A seasonal-life set in Japan (typhoons, earthquakes). Written forms including teiden shita total 29.
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 停電+成る 11, share 0.15. Not in the table.

additions.trap: 'Talk to yourself' is one noun + iu (a, hitorigoto desu), not jibun to hanasu.
additions.why: Comes up often, including the stock line hitorigoto da yo when someone asks 'what?'. Very typical (0.57).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 独り言+言う 16, share 0.57. Not in the table.

additions.trap: No single English word fits. It covers digs and passive-aggressive comments (iyami iwanaide yo).
additions.why: Common in talk about coworkers and in-laws. Very fixed (0.68).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 嫌味+言う 17, share 0.68. Not in the table.

additions.trap: Wagamama is said of demands: wagamama iwanaide (stop being demanding). The polite wagamama o itte sumimasen apologises for a request.
additions.why: Parents say it to kids, and adults use it to apologise for a special request. It's a Japanese concept with no clean English match.
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 我が儘+言う 8, share 0.44. Not in the table.

additions.english: be picky, ask for too much
additions.trap: Literally 'say luxury'. Zeitaku wa iwanai means 'I won't be picky' (beggars can't be choosers).
additions.why: A frequent humble formula when choosing food or jobs (zeitaku iwanai kara). The meaning can't be guessed from English.
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 贅沢+言う 13, share 0.28. Not in the table.

additions.trap: 'Talk in your sleep' is one noun + iu. Negoto also means 'nonsense' (negoto wa nete ie).
additions.why: Household talk (yuube negoto itteta yo). Very fixed (0.82).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 寝言+言う 9, share 0.82. Not in the table.

additions.trap: A misunderstanding is untied (toku), not fixed with naosu.
additions.why: This is the set phrase for smoothing things over (gokai o tokitai). The log_dice is high (9.5).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 誤解+解く 22, log_dice 9.5. Not in the table.

additions.trap: 'Can't sit still' is a noun + nai, not a verb.
additions.why: Said about kids and nervous people (kyou ochitsuki nai ne). Very typical (0.51).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 落ち着き+無い 19, share 0.51. Not in the table.

additions.trap: 'Calm down' is ochitsuite or reisei ni natte. Shizuka ni means 'be quiet'.
additions.why: The usual way to urge clear thinking (chotto reisei ni natte). Typical (0.51).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 冷静+成る 23, share 0.51. Not in the table.

additions.trap: When thanking someone for support, Japanese says hagemi ni narimasu (it becomes encouragement), not an 'encourage' verb.
additions.why: A stock thank-you for support and comments. Very fixed (0.80).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 励み+成る 16, share 0.80. The table's naru sets (benkyou ni naru, sankou ni naru) don't include it.

additions.kana: くらべものにならない
additions.english: be in a different league, beyond comparison
additions.trap: Only the negative form is used. 'There's no comparison' is not kuraberarenai.
additions.why: Common in reviews and comparisons (mae no to kurabemono ni naranai). Every use of the noun goes to this set (share 1.0).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 比べ物+成る 17, share 1.00. Not in the table, and not on the idiom candidate list.

additions.english: still have feelings for, can't let go
additions.trap: There's no single English word. It means lingering attachment to an ex or a past choice (mada miren aru no?).
additions.why: A staple of relationship talk. Typical (0.59).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 未練+有る 17, share 0.59. Not in the table.

additions.trap: 'Rewarding' is a noun + aru (yarigai no aru shigoto), not an adjective.
additions.why: The standard way to talk about job satisfaction, in interviews and small talk. Very typical (0.69).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 遣り甲斐+有る 18, share 0.69. Not in the table.

additions.english: have a prior engagement, have other plans
additions.trap: Polite refusals cite sen'yaku ga atte rather than 'I'm busy'.
additions.why: The face-saving way to turn down invitations (sumimasen, sono hi wa sen'yaku ga atte). Very fixed (0.74).
additions.gap: pairs.tsv band: 先約+有る 17, share 0.74. Not in the table. The kept yotei ga aru is the plain cousin.

additions.english: give a return gift; pay someone back in kind
additions.trap: In Japanese gift etiquette you okaeshi suru for gifts you received (White Day, wedding and funeral gifts). It can also mean 'get back at someone'.

Hardest calls:

- tomodachi-o-tsukuru (69) = kept tomodachi-ga-dekiru.
- taichou-ga-warui (23) overlaps the kept guai-ga-warui and choushi-ga-warui. I took taichou-o-kuzusu instead.
- Also skipped as overlaps: okane-ga-tarinai (okane-ga-nai), kagi-o-shimeru (kagi-o-kakeru), ame-ga-agaru (ame-ga-yamu), denchi-ga-kireru (juuden-ga-kireru), onaka-ga-pekopeko (onaka-ga-suku), soudan-ga-aru (hanashi-ga-aru).

- I did keep hima-ga-nai (327) even though it is close to jikan-ga-nai. It uses a different, very common noun.

2. Counts inflated by films:
- Skipped: shigoto-ni-modoru (463), atama-o-utsu (231), mondai-ga-okiru (138), and hito-no-sei-ni-suru (180), which works more like a frame than a fixed set.
- Kept on count anyway: te-o-ageru (489), even though some hits are 'hands up!' lines, and koe-o-kiku (379), even though some are phone and romance lines.

3. Low or zero counts I added on daily-life judgement, against the data-first lens. The corpus is mostly foreign-film subtitles, so it misses Japanese daily life. Checking the written forms supports several:
- heya-ga-chirakaru: 散らか 104 hits
- soujiki-o-kakeru: 掃除機 66

4. Following your note, I chose sets because Japanese speakers say them often, whether or not English has a matching phrase. That brought in jikka ni kaeru, senyaku ga aru, guchi o iu, honne o iu, mendou o miru, hanko o osu, kibarashi ni naru, yarigai ga aru, jikkan ga waku, deai ga aru and kakkou o tsukeru. 5. Sets that repeat a pattern already on the list, kept because people say them so often:

So Japan-specific sets with no English twin came in on the same terms as the rest, as long as people say them often. Examples: kutsu o soroeru, kome o togu, bentou o atatameru, kotatsu ni hairu, futon o hosu, hatsumoude ni iku, omikuji o hiku, hanami ni iku, jikka ni kaeru, honne o iu, okaeshi o suru, otoshidama o morau, hanko o osu, tsurikawa ni tsukamaru, eki o norisugosu, shuuden ga nakunaru, kafun ga tobu, semi ga naku, pointo o tameru, senyaku ga aru. HARDEST CALLS:

Same meaning as a kept set, so left out despite strong counts. hima ga nai (327) repeats jikan ga nai. kagi o shimeru repeats kagi o kakeru (which counts 221 against 20). shigoto o yameru repeats kaisha o yameru. tomodachi o tsukuru repeats tomodachi ga dekiru. ame ga agaru repeats ame ga yamu. taichou ga warui repeats guai ga warui (216 against 20 as phrases) next to kibun ga warui and choushi ga warui. taichou ga warui is the calling-in-sick phrase, so it is the strongest of these to reconsider.
2. One exception to that rule: denwa ga aru overlaps the kept denwa ga kakaru. I added it anyway because 電話があった counts 240 against 20 for 電話がかかって, and it is the usual way to report 'X called'. Drop it if the one-entry rule must be strict.

   I added neither nengajou set, since young people now mostly send New Year greetings on LINE.
4. Covered by a kept set's verb, so left out: kutsushita o haku and sukaato o haku (zubon o haku and kutsu o haku), futa o akeru (doa o akeru), bentou o tsukuru (gohan o tsukuru, added), sukusho o toru (shashin o toru), kami o arau (te o arau and kao o arau, added).

6. Possible idioms. ki ga au is left out because it is already in idioms-build/candidates.json. I treated haji o kaku, baka ni suru, kakkou o tsukeru and honne o iu as literal enough to be collocations. Check them against the idiom list when it is finalised.
7. Guessable but very common sets came in on commonness alone: jitensha ni noru, hikouki ni noru, tomodachi ni au, eiga ni iku, shigoto ni iku.

2. **Which version to take when two say the same thing:**
   - kaado o tsukau (79 hits) over kaado de harau (3).
   - me o tojiru (353) over me o tsuburu (92).
   - memo o toru over nooto o toru.

4. **Several 'ni iku' and 'o suru' sets.** sanpo, asobi, karaoke, eiga, hanami, hatsumoude, kyanpu and tsuri ni iku all came in because each is common and typical. HOW I GOT THERE
The base list (every set with 2 or more votes) has 190 sets, and I kept all of them. I found no within-base pair that says the same thing. The pairs that look alike either use different verbs or are a matching pair of opposites or ga/o partners, so I kept both:

- jikan o toru, jikan o kakeru and jikan o tsukuru

I added 10 sets with only one vote, chosen on how often Japanese speakers say them:
- denwa ga aru: 電話があっ has 266 hits against 16 for 電話がかかって.
- doa ga shimaru: 62 hits. Every train announces it, and it pairs with the kept doa ga aku.
- taichou ga warui: judged 5. It is the stock phrase for calling in sick.

- kami o arau: completes te, kao and osara o arau.

USER'S NOTE
I read it as: choose sets because Japanese speakers say them, whether or not English has a matching phrase. Sets with no English twin came in on the same terms as the rest, for example jikka ni kaeru, sen'yaku ga aru, honne o iu, hanko o osu, kotatsu ni hairu, hatsumoude ni iku, bentou o atatameru, okaeshi o suru and shuuden ga nakunaru. Whether English misleads learners did not decide any pick.

NEAR-DUPLICATES WITH KEPT SETS: CALLS TO REVIEW
1. denwa ga aru repeats the kept denwa ga kakaru (c-denwa-ga-kakaru) but is said far more often. I recommend merging the two or making denwa ga aru the headword.
2. taichou ga warui sits next to the kept guai, choushi and kibun ga warui, and next to the added taichou o kuzusu. As with hima ga nai beside jikan ga nai, a different and very common noun is allowed in.
3. okane ga tarinai sits next to the kept okane ga nai. It stays because tarinai is the 'short of' verb, not 'have none'.

newEntries.verbSense: pile up, build up (snow, dust)
newEntries.trap: English 'the snow's sticking' points to tsuku, but snow building up on the ground is tsumoru; tsuku is snow stuck on things: kuruma ni yuki tsuiteru. Nokotteru is old snow that hasn't melted yet.

example.ja: 朝起きたら、雪積もってた。
example.english: When I got up, there was snow on the ground.

examplePolite.romaji: asa okitara, yuki ga tsumottemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 朝起きたら、雪が積もってました。
examplePolite.english: When I got up, there was snow on the ground.

newEntries.freqNote: 積もる #9027 also covers the figurative tsumoru hanashi (lots to catch up on). How often the set comes up depends on region and season, so commonness is a judgement.
newEntries.notes: Melting is tokeru: yuki mou toketa ne.

newEntries.use: Summer small talk, mostly semi naiteru (the cicadas are going) or semi nakihajimeta ne (the cicadas have started). Casual speech drops ga.
newEntries.verbSense: make its call (an animal, bird or insect)
newEntries.trap: English has a verb per creature (sing, chirp, buzz, meow), but Japanese uses naku (鳴く) for nearly all of them, and it sounds the same as naku 'cry' (泣く). Tori ga utau is poetic; in talk it's naku.

example.ja: セミ鳴き始めたね。
example.english: The cicadas have started up.

examplePolite.romaji: semi ga nakihajimemashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: セミが鳴き始めましたね。
examplePolite.english: The cicadas have started up.

newEntries.freqNote: セミ #14340 is the usual spelling (蝉 #48270). Kana なく is mostly 泣く 'cry' (#407), so the kanji 鳴く is used. Foreign films barely mention cicadas (2 hits for セミが鳴く, 7 more for セミの鳴き声), so commonness is a judgement.
newEntries.notes: Autumn nights have mushi ga naku (crickets and other insects); a barking dog is usually hoeru.

newEntries.use: Used when talking about a quake: jishin ga okita toki (when the earthquake hit), ookii jishin ga okitara (if a big one hits). In the moment people shout jishin da! or jishin kita!, and afterwards say kinou jishin atta ne.
newEntries.verbSense: happen, occur; also wake up, get up
newEntries.trap: English 'an earthquake hit' has no matching verb, and utsu or ataru don't work. It happens (okiru), or casually it comes or there is one (jishin kita!, jishin atta).

example.ja: 大きい地震起きたらどうする？
example.english: What would you do if a big earthquake hit?

examplePolite.romaji: ookii jishin ga okitara dou shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 大きい地震が起きたらどうしますか？
examplePolite.english: What would you do if a big earthquake hit?

newEntries.freqNote: Rank is for the kanji 地震, because kana じしん is dominated by 自信 (#839) and 自身 (#1355). 起きる #329 also covers waking and getting up. 揺れる (shake) is #3717.
newEntries.notes: The shaking is yureru: ima yureta? (did it just shake?), kekkou yureta ne.

newEntries.use: Said when you notice the moon: tsuki deteru (the moon's out), kyou tsuki detenai ne. Deteru means it's out now, not 'it's coming out'.
newEntries.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out

example.ja: 見て、月出てるよ。
example.english: Look, the moon's out.

examplePolite.romaji: hora, tsuki ga detemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ほら、月が出てますよ。
examplePolite.english: Look, the moon's out.

newEntries.freqNote: 月 #1720 is the 'moon' reading つき; read がつ (month) it is #8752. 出る #81 counts every sense. hoshi ga deru (6 corpus hits) uses the same frame.
newEntries.notes: A full moon is mangetsu: kyou mangetsu da tte (apparently it's a full moon tonight).

newEntries.use: Said about yourself or someone else in summer: atsusa ni yowai n da yo ne (I'm no good in the heat). The cold version, samusa ni yowai, is just as common. The ni stays.
newEntries.verbSense: weak, having little strength or tolerance
newEntries.trap: Atsusa takes ni: atsusa ga yowai isn't said (with osake, ga and ni both work). Atsui no nigate (I can't do heat) is just as everyday.

example.romaji: atsusa ni yowai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 暑さに弱いんだよね。
example.english: I'm no good in the heat.

examplePolite.romaji: atsusa ni yowai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 暑さに弱いんですよね。
examplePolite.english: I'm no good in the heat.

newEntries.freqNote: 暑さ #11178; 寒さ is #7547. 弱い #970 counts every sense of weak. No corpus hits for the pair, so commonness is a judgement.
newEntries.notes: The opposite is atsusa ni tsuyoi; atsusa is atsui + -sa (the heat), like samusa from samui.

newEntries.kana: てんきよほうがはずれる
newEntries.use: A grumble, almost always in the past: tenki yohou hazureta (the forecast got it wrong), usually without ga, or just yohou hazureta once the weather is already the topic. When it gets it right: yohou atatta.
newEntries.verbSense: miss, come off; turn out wrong (a forecast, guess, lottery ticket)
newEntries.trap: A forecast misses (hazureru) or hits (ataru), like a guess or a lottery ticket. Machigaeru is a person's slip, so yohou ga machigaeta doesn't work; yohou machigatteta (it was wrong) is also fine, but hazureta is the usual word.

example.ja: 天気予報、また外れたね。
example.english: The forecast got it wrong again.

examplePolite.romaji: tenki yohou, mata hazuremashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 天気予報、また外れましたね。
examplePolite.english: The forecast got it wrong again.

newEntries.freqNote: Rank is for the compound 天気予報; 予報 alone is #13931. 外れる #1999 counts every sense (come off, miss). Its partner 当たる is #719. No corpus hits for the pair, so commonness is a judgement.
alsoIn: vocab-trainer utility-vocab: weather-terms (tenki, inside tenki yohou)
newEntries.notes: What it says: yohou de wa ame da tte (the forecast says rain).

newEntries.use: Mostly heard as a request, me tojite: at the dentist under the lamp, with eye drops, or before a surprise. Photos are the opposite: me tsubutchatta (I blinked). Casual speech uses me tsubutte just as much, and o often drops in both.
newEntries.verbSense: close, shut (eyes, a book, an app); doors and windows take shimeru instead
newEntries.trap: Doors and windows take shimeru, so learners say me o shimeru. Eyes take tojiru, or the casual tsuburu: me tsubutte.

example.romaji: ii tte iu made, me tojitete ne.
example.ja: いいって言うまで、目閉じててね。
example.english: Keep your eyes shut till I say so.

examplePolite.romaji: ii to iu made, me o tojite ite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: いいと言うまで、目を閉じていてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please keep your eyes closed until I say so.

newEntries.freqNote: 目 #216; 閉じる #3880, with the casual つぶる #8069 not far behind. Phrase entries 目を閉じる #6910 and 目をつぶる #7140 are almost level.
newEntries.notes: Opening them again is me o akeru. Me o tsuburu also means 'let it slide' (overlook a fault).

newEntries.use: Heard in class, at meetings and at events as a request: shitsumon aru hito, te agete. With ni and a person it means raising a hand against them: kodomo ni te o ageru (hit a child).
newEntries.verbSense: raise, lift up; the same-sounding ageru also means give

example.ja: 質問ある人、手挙げて。
example.english: Anyone with a question, put your hand up.

examplePolite.romaji: shitsumon ga aru kata wa, te o agete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 質問がある方は、手を挙げてください。
examplePolite.english: If you have a question, please raise your hand.

newEntries.freqNote: 手 #259; 挙げる #2605 is the spelling for raising a hand (挙手 kyoshu #13383 is the formal word). 上げる #837 is also written, and is the usual spelling for 'hands up!' and for hitting someone; kana あげる #668 is mostly 'give'. Phrase entries 手を上げる #8267 and 手を挙げる #11089.
newEntries.notes: Films inflate the count with police shouting te o agero (hands up!). Putting it down is te o orosu.

newEntries.use: Said when you spot a cut: chi deteru yo (you're bleeding), or chi deta (it bled). Ga often drops in casual talk, and when it stops the blood tomaru (chi tomatta?).
newEntries.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out
newEntries.trap: 'Bleed' is one verb in English; Japanese says blood comes out, chi ga deru (chi deteru yo). Shukketsu suru is the medical word.

example.romaji: are, yubi kara chi deteru yo.
example.ja: あれ、指から血出てるよ。
example.english: Hey, your finger's bleeding.

examplePolite.romaji: are, yubi kara chi ga dete imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、指から血が出ていますよ。
examplePolite.english: Oh, your finger is bleeding.

newEntries.freqNote: 血 #1261; 出る #81. No phrase entry; 出血 shukketsu #4944 is the medical and news word.
newEntries.notes: A nosebleed has its own word: hanaji ga deru (hanaji deteru yo).

newEntries.english: be in good shape, going well
newEntries.use: The opposite of choushi ga warui, for your body, your form or a device: kyou choushi ii (I'm on form today), and choushi dou? asks how things are going. Ga often drops.
newEntries.verbSense: good, fine, OK
partners: guai (condition: guai ga ii = feel well; of a thing, work properly)
kaoiro (complexion: kaoiro ga ii = look well)
kigen (mood: kigen ga ii = be in a good mood)

example.romaji: saikin, karada no choushi ii n da.
example.ja: 最近、体の調子いいんだ。
example.english: I've been feeling good lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, karada no choushi ga ii n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近、体の調子がいいんです。
examplePolite.english: I've been in good shape lately.

newEntries.freqNote: 調子 #1124; いい #24; phrase entry 調子がいい #16780 (調子が良い #43063), well below 調子が悪い #8863.
newEntries.notes: About someone's words it means glib: choushi ii koto bakari iu (always says whatever suits them).

newEntries.use: A caring remark to someone who looks ill, kaoiro warui yo, usually followed by daijoubu? Ga often drops, and when they look better it's kaoiro yoku natta ne.
newEntries.verbSense: bad, in poor condition
newEntries.trap: Not kao ga shiroi, which sounds like fair skin: 'you look pale' is kaoiro ga warui (kaoiro warui yo). Kao ga aoi also works and sounds stronger; kao ga massao is white as a sheet, from shock, fear or feeling very sick.
partners: guai (condition: guai ga warui = feel unwell)

example.ja: 顔色悪いよ。大丈夫？
example.english: You look pale. Are you OK?

examplePolite.romaji: kaoiro ga warui desu yo. daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 顔色が悪いですよ。大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: You look pale. Are you all right?

newEntries.freqNote: 顔色 #2897; 悪い #139; phrase entry 顔色が悪い #13422.
newEntries.notes: Kaoiro o ukagau (read someone's face) is a separate idiom: checking their mood before you act.

newEntries.use: Said every day, before meals and on coming in: te aratte kite (go wash your hands), te aratta? O often drops in these reminders.
newEntries.verbSense: wash with water (hands, dishes, a car)

example.romaji: gohan da yo. te aratte kite.
example.ja: ごはんだよ。手洗ってきて。
example.english: Dinner's ready. Go wash your hands.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan desu yo. te o aratte kite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ごはんですよ。手を洗ってきてください。
examplePolite.english: The meal's ready. Please go and wash your hands.

newEntries.freqNote: 手 #259; 洗う #1246. No phrase entry; お手洗い otearai (toilet) #5898 is built from the same two words.
newEntries.notes: Only literal. Ashi o arau (wash your feet) is the idiom for quitting a shady line of work; pulling out of a deal or matter is te o hiku.

newEntries.use: Part of the morning routine, and the way to wake yourself up: kao aratte kuru (I'll go wash my face). O often drops in casual talk.
newEntries.verbSense: wash with water (hands, dishes, a car)

example.ja: 眠いから、顔洗ってくる。
example.english: I'm sleepy, so I'll go wash my face.

examplePolite.romaji: nemui node, kao o aratte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 眠いので、顔を洗ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm sleepy, so I'll go and wash my face.

newEntries.freqNote: 顔 #174; 洗う #1246. No phrase entry; 洗顔 sengan #29643 is the word on face-wash labels.
newEntries.notes: Kao aratte denaoshite koi (go wash your face and come back) is a rough, stock brush-off for someone not ready.

newEntries.use: Asked after a pill as kusuri kiita? and said as it kicks in, kusuri kiite kita. Ga often drops; when the effect wears off, the medicine kireru (kusuri ga kireta).
newEntries.verbSense: take effect, work (medicine, air con, a remedy); sounds the same as kiku 'listen, ask'
newEntries.trap: Not kusuri ga hataraku: medicine 'takes effect', kusuri ga kiku, which sounds just like kiku 'listen'.
partners: eakon (air con: eakon kiitenai = the AC isn't doing anything)

example.ja: 薬効いてきた。だいぶ楽。
example.english: The medicine's kicking in. I feel much better.

examplePolite.romaji: kusuri ga kiite kimashita. daibu raku ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 薬が効いてきました。だいぶ楽になりました。
examplePolite.english: The medicine is starting to work. I feel much better.

newEntries.freqNote: 薬 #1283; 効く #1822 (its homophone 聞く 'listen' is #67); phrase entry 薬が効く #19852.
newEntries.notes: Kiku~! is also what people say when wasabi or a strong drink hits.

newEntries.use: Heard as news, tabako yameta (I've quit), or advice, tabako yameta hou ga ii yo. Wa is common for contrast (tabako wa yameta), and osake o yameru works the same way.
newEntries.verbSense: stop, give up (a habit, an activity); quitting a job is the same-sounding yameru (辞める), as in kaisha o yameru
newEntries.trap: English 'stop smoking' pulls toward tomeru, which is stopping a machine or a person (kuruma o tomeru). A habit you give up is yameru: tabako yameta.

example.ja: タバコ、去年やめたんだ。
example.english: I quit smoking last year.

examplePolite.romaji: tabako wa kyonen yamemashita.
examplePolite.ja: タバコは去年やめました。
examplePolite.english: I gave up smoking last year.

newEntries.freqNote: タバコ #4158 (たばこ #7069); kana やめる #117 counts every 'stop, quit' use (辞める 'quit a job' #604). Phrase entry タバコをやめる #84839; 禁煙 kin'en #10367.
newEntries.notes: Kin'en chuu (I'm off cigarettes for now) is the other everyday phrase; kin'en on a sign means no smoking.

newEntries.use: The standard way to explain a minor illness, mostly in the past: taichou kuzushichatte (I came down with something). It fills excuses for missing work or school, and the send-off taichou kuzusanai you ni ne (look after yourself). O often drops.
newEntries.verbSense: knock down, break up (a wall, a pose); upset, throw off (balance, health, pace); also break a note into change
newEntries.trap: Byouki ni naru isn't wrong but sounds like a proper illness; for a passing bug or being run down, people say taichou (o) kuzushita.
partners: choushi (form: choushi o kuzusu = go off form)

example.ja: ちょっと体調崩して、昨日休んだ。
example.english: I got a bit run down and took yesterday off.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto taichou o kuzushite, kinou wa yasumimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと体調を崩して、昨日は休みました。
examplePolite.english: I was a bit under the weather, so I took yesterday off.

newEntries.freqNote: 体調 #1944; 崩す #3822; phrase entry 体調を崩す #9388, high for a phrase.
newEntries.notes: Taichou ga warui is the state; taichou o kuzusu is falling into it.

newEntries.politeJa: アレルギーがあります
newEntries.use: Put the cause in front: tamago arerugii ga aru, or ebi no arerugii ga aru. Restaurants and clinics ask about it (arerugii wa arimasu ka?), and casual talk drops ga.
newEntries.verbSense: there is, exist (for things); here, have
newEntries.trap: Said the German way, arerugii (a-re-ru-gii), not like English 'allergy'. The cause goes in front: tamago arerugii, or tamago ni arerugii ga aru.

example.ja: エビアレルギーあるから、食べられない。
example.english: I'm allergic to shrimp, so I can't eat it.

examplePolite.romaji: ebi no arerugii ga aru node, taberaremasen.
examplePolite.ja: エビのアレルギーがあるので、食べられません。
examplePolite.english: I have a shrimp allergy, so I can't eat it.

newEntries.freqNote: アレルギー #6251; ある #21. No phrase entry.
newEntries.notes: Hay fever is kafunshou (kafunshou nan desu), the allergy nearly everyone in Japan talks about each spring.

newEntries.use: The follow-up to any fever: netsu sagatta? answered with sagatta or mada sagaranai. Ga often drops; a fever going up is netsu ga agaru.
newEntries.verbSense: go down, drop (temperature, prices); also step back
newEntries.trap: Not netsu ga oriru or heru: a fever 'drops', netsu ga sagaru (netsu sagatta?).

example.ja: 薬飲んだら、熱下がった。
example.english: I took some medicine and my fever went down.

examplePolite.romaji: kusuri o nondara, netsu ga sagarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 薬を飲んだら、熱が下がりました。
examplePolite.english: After I took the medicine, my fever came down.

newEntries.freqNote: 熱 #1641; 下がる #1064 (上がる #503, for a fever going up). No phrase entry.
newEntries.notes: Bringing a fever down is netsu o sageru; the medicine for it is genetsuzai. Netsu ga hiku (the fever subsides) is also fine.

newEntries.use: Often the first sign of a cold: nanka nodo itai, with ga dropped. Add n da or n desu when it explains a rough voice or skipping karaoke.
newEntries.verbSense: painful, it hurts

example.ja: なんか喉痛い。風邪かも。
example.english: My throat's kind of sore. Might be a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka nodo ga itai n desu. kaze kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: なんか喉が痛いんです。風邪かもしれません。
examplePolite.english: My throat is a bit sore. It might be a cold.

newEntries.freqNote: 喉 #3552 (kana のど #7553); 痛い #336. No phrase entry.
newEntries.notes: The same nodo is in nodo ga kawaku (thirsty); a scratchy throat is nodo ga igaiga suru.

newEntries.use: The discreet everyday way to mention diarrhoea or a bad stomach, mostly past: onaka kowashita. Also a warning: sonna ni tabetara onaka kowasu yo. O often drops.
newEntries.verbSense: break, damage (a thing); with the body, harm it
newEntries.trap: English 'have an upset stomach' gives no usable verb. Japanese 'breaks' the stomach with kowasu, transitive, with the speaker as subject: onaka kowashita.
partners: karada (health: karada o kowasu = ruin your health)

example.ja: 冷たいもの飲みすぎて、お腹壊した。
example.english: I drank too much cold stuff and upset my stomach.

examplePolite.romaji: tsumetai mono o nomisugite, onaka o kowashimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 冷たいものを飲みすぎて、お腹を壊しました。
examplePolite.english: I had too many cold drinks and upset my stomach.

newEntries.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 壊す #1284. Phrase entries お腹を壊す #76983 and the rougher 腹を壊す #50251.
newEntries.notes: Onaka no choushi ga warui is the vaguer, more discreet version; geri (diarrhoea) is the clinic word.

newEntries.use: Asked after someone's cold as kaze naotta? and answered mou naotta or mada naoranai. Ga drops, and kaze itself is often left out once the topic is clear.
newEntries.verbSense: heal, get better (an illness, an injury); the same-sounding naoru also means a thing gets fixed

example.ja: 風邪、もう治った？
example.english: Are you over your cold yet?

examplePolite.romaji: kaze wa mou naorimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 風邪はもう治りましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you got over your cold?

newEntries.freqNote: 風邪 #2666; 治る #1604 (transitive 治す #2761; 直る 'be fixed' #4537 is a homophone). No phrase entry.
newEntries.notes: Hayaku naoshite ne (get well soon) uses the transitive naosu; odaiji ni is the stock polite wish.

newEntries.use: For a cough you've had a while, said to friends or at the doctor's: seki ga deru n desu, or seki ga tomaranai (I can't stop coughing). For coughing right now, seki shiteru is just as natural.
newEntries.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out

example.romaji: netsu wa nai kedo, seki ga deru.
example.ja: 熱はないけど、咳が出る。
example.english: No fever, but I've got a cough.

examplePolite.romaji: netsu wa nai n desu kedo, seki ga demasu.
examplePolite.ja: 熱はないんですけど、咳が出ます。
examplePolite.english: I don't have a fever, but I have a cough.

newEntries.freqNote: 咳 #21022 is the kanji only. Kana せき #11682 probably holds most spoken uses but can't be told apart from kana 席/関, so it is not used. 出る #81; phrase entry 咳が出る #70272.
newEntries.notes: Seki (o) suru, coughing as an action, is more frequent in films (31 hits to 4). Clinics ask netsu ya seki wa arimasu ka? too.

newEntries.use: Heard as an instruction at massages, the doctor's, sport and yoga: chikara nuite, or motto kata no chikara nuite. O often drops in the request.
newEntries.verbSense: pull out, take out (a tooth, a plug); let out (air, tension); also skip (a meal)
partners: kuuki (air: let air out of a tyre)
ki (attention: ki o nuku = let your guard down)

example.romaji: motto chikara nuite. sou, sono kanji.
example.ja: もっと力抜いて。そう、その感じ。
example.english: Relax more. Yes, like that.

examplePolite.romaji: motto chikara o nuite kudasai. hai, sono kanji desu.
examplePolite.ja: もっと力を抜いてください。はい、その感じです。
examplePolite.english: Please relax a bit more. Yes, that's it.

newEntries.freqNote: 力 #456; 抜く #1432; phrase entry 力を抜く #17281.
newEntries.notes: The opposite is chikara o ireru (put strength in). Rirakkusu shite is the other everyday instruction; chikara nuite targets a tense part (kata no chikara nuite), and kata no chikara o nuku also means 'stop trying so hard'.

newEntries.use: The heavy, achy feeling of a cold coming on or a bad night: nanka karada darui, with ga dropped. Darui alone is just as common, and about a task it's a casual, youthful 'what a drag' (gakkou darui), not for use with superiors.
newEntries.verbSense: heavy, sluggish, listless; casually, 'what a drag'
newEntries.trap: Tsukareta isn't wrong, but it points to effort; the heavy, achy feeling with no clear cause, as when a cold is coming, is karada ga darui.

example.ja: 朝からなんか体だるい。
example.english: I've felt heavy and sluggish since this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: asa kara nanka karada ga darui n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝からなんか体がだるいんです。
examplePolite.english: I've been feeling sluggish since this morning.

newEntries.freqNote: 体 #371; だるい #10091 (怠い #97383). No phrase entry; しんどい #3271 is the near-synonym.
newEntries.notes: Shindoi (rough, worn out) overlaps; it comes from western Japan but is heard everywhere.

newEntries.use: Most often heard in the negative: nete mo tsukare ga torenai (I sleep and still feel tired). After a bath, a massage or a holiday it's tsukare toreta, and ga often drops.
newEntries.verbSense: come off, come out (a button, a stain); also can get (potential of toru)
newEntries.trap: Not tsukare ga naoru: tiredness isn't cured, it 'comes off' (toreru).

example.ja: 寝ても、全然疲れ取れない。
example.english: Even after sleeping, I can't shake the tiredness.

examplePolite.romaji: nete mo, zenzen tsukare ga toremasen.
examplePolite.ja: 寝ても、全然疲れが取れません。
examplePolite.english: Even after sleeping, I still feel tired.

newEntries.freqNote: 疲れ #3920; 取れる #631 counts all its senses (come off, can get, be taken). No phrase entry; transitive 疲れを取る #62068.
newEntries.notes: Tsukare o toru is doing something about it: onsen de tsukare o toru (soak it away at a hot spring). Tsukare ga nukenai (the tiredness won't leave) is also common.

newEntries.use: Said of a cold or hay fever, often as hanamizu ga tomaranai (my nose won't stop running). Hanamizu deteru yo, ga dropped, tells someone their nose is running.
newEntries.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out
newEntries.trap: 'Runny' has nothing to copy: the noun is hanamizu (nose water), and it comes out, hanamizu ga deru (hanamizu deteru yo).

example.ja: 鼻水出てるよ。はい、ティッシュ。
example.english: Your nose is running. Here, a tissue.

examplePolite.romaji: hanamizu ga dete imasu yo. tisshu, douzo.
examplePolite.ja: 鼻水が出ていますよ。ティッシュ、どうぞ。
examplePolite.english: Your nose is running. Here's a tissue.

newEntries.freqNote: 鼻水 #12653; 出る #81. No phrase entry; 鼻 hana #2627.
newEntries.notes: A blocked nose is hana ga tsumaru (hana tsumatteru); blowing it is hana o kamu.

newEntries.use: The everyday back-pain complaint after lifting, sitting all day or sleeping badly: koshi itai, with ga dropped. Older people say it constantly.
newEntries.verbSense: painful, it hurts
newEntries.trap: 'My back hurts' usually means the lower back, which is koshi. Senaka is the upper and middle back, so senaka ga itai points higher.

example.romaji: omoi mono motte, koshi itaku natta.
example.ja: 重いもの持って、腰痛くなった。
example.english: I lifted something heavy and now my back hurts.

examplePolite.romaji: omoi mono o motte, koshi ga itaku narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 重いものを持って、腰が痛くなりました。
examplePolite.english: I lifted something heavy and hurt my back.

newEntries.freqNote: 腰 #2126; 痛い #336. No phrase entry; 腰痛 youtsuu #15563 is the clinic word, and ぎっくり腰 gikkurigoshi (a sudden back spasm) is #17355.
newEntries.notes: Koshi covers the lower back and hips together.

newEntries.use: Said as a reminder or a chore: tsume kitte (cut your nails), tsume kiranakya. O often drops; the clippers are tsumekiri.
newEntries.verbSense: cut (with a blade or scissors)

example.ja: そろそろ爪切らなきゃ。
example.english: It's about time I cut my nails.

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro tsume o kiranai to ikemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: そろそろ爪を切らないといけませんね。
examplePolite.english: It's about time I cut my nails.

newEntries.freqNote: 爪 #4532; 切る #546; 爪切り tsumekiri (nail clippers) #36115.
newEntries.notes: Many people still know the superstition against cutting your nails at night (yoru tsume o kiru to...).

newEntries.english: not feel well, be under the weather (the safe phrase at work)
newEntries.use: The stock phrase for calling in sick or cancelling: taichou ga warui node, kyou wa yasumasete kudasai. Casual talk drops ga (chotto taichou warui), and others ask taichou dou? or taichou daijoubu?
newEntries.verbSense: bad, in poor condition

example.romaji: gomen, taichou warui kara kyou yasumu.
example.ja: ごめん、体調悪いから今日休む。
example.english: Sorry, I'm not feeling well, so I'm taking today off.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, taichou ga warui node, kyou wa yasumasete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、体調が悪いので、今日は休ませてください。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I'm not feeling well. Could I have today off?

newEntries.freqNote: 体調 #1944; 悪い #139. No phrase entry (体調を崩す is #9388).
newEntries.notes: A little more neutral than guai ga warui, so it's the safe choice at work; the opposite is taichou ga ii.

newEntries.use: Talk of the bath or shower routine: kami aratte kara neru, or kami arau no mendokusai (washing my hair is a pain). At home people say atama arau just as often (atama aratta?, especially to kids). O drops in casual speech.
newEntries.verbSense: wash with water (hands, dishes, a car)

example.ja: 髪洗ってから寝る。
example.english: I'll wash my hair, then go to bed.

examplePolite.romaji: kami o aratte kara nemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 髪を洗ってから寝ます。
examplePolite.english: I'll wash my hair before I go to bed.

newEntries.freqNote: 髪 #1752 (髪の毛 #3658); 洗う #1246; シャンプー #7199 is the product and the salon word.
newEntries.notes: Drying it afterwards is kami o kawakasu (kami kawakashite). Shanpuu suru is also everyday (shanpuu shite kara neru).

newEntries.use: Said to someone flushed from drink, a fever or embarrassment, often teasing: kao akai yo. Ga usually drops; going red as it happens is kao ga akaku naru (kao akaku natteru).
newEntries.verbSense: red
newEntries.trap: 'Blush' has no single everyday verb: the face goes red, kao ga akaku naru, or you tereru (get bashful); sekimen suru is bookish.
partners: me (eyes: me ga akai = red eyes)

example.ja: 顔赤いよ。酔った？
example.english: Your face is red. Are you drunk?

examplePolite.romaji: kao ga akai desu yo. yotta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 顔が赤いですよ。酔ったんですか？
examplePolite.english: Your face is red. Have you been drinking?

newEntries.freqNote: 顔 #174; 赤い #1711; 真っ赤 makka #5350 (kao ga makka = bright red).
newEntries.notes: Tereru (get bashful) is the verb behind most blushing: tereteru no?

newEntries.use: Mostly heard as a check or a complaint when trying things on or ordering online: saizu atteru? (does it fit?), saizu awanai (it's not my size). Casual speech drops ga.
newEntries.verbSense: match, fit together
newEntries.trap: English 'it fits' makes the clothes the subject. Japanese usually makes the size the subject: saizu ga au, mostly heard as saizu awanai. Don't reach for niau, which is about looks (it suits you). fitto suru exists but means snug, close to the body.
partners: kutsu (shoes: kono kutsu, ashi ni awanai)
megane no do (glasses' prescription: do ga awanai = wrong prescription)
makura (pillow: makura ga awanai = it isn't right for me)

example.ja: これ、ちょっとサイズ合わないかも。
example.english: I don't think this is quite my size.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa chotto saizu ga awanai kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: これはちょっとサイズが合わないかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: This might not be quite the right size.

newEntries.freqNote: Ranks are for サイズ #3308 and 合う #563; kana あう is mostly 会う 'meet' (#110). Shop and online-order talk is under-counted in film subtitles, so pairing commonness is judged.
newEntries.notes: If you can't get it on at all, say hairanai (kono zubon hairanai). Too tight is kitsui, too loose yurui, and a perfect fit pittari. This au sounds exactly like au 'meet' (same pitch); saizu, or the thing being tried on, tells you which.

newEntries.use: Mostly heard as yubiwa shiteru (has a ring on) or shitenai, very often about a wedding ring: kekkon yubiwa shiteru. Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: do; with small worn items, have on
newEntries.trap: Not yubiwa o kiru: a ring, like a watch, mask or tie, takes suru (yubiwa shiteru).

example.romaji: ano hito, kekkon yubiwa shiteru ne.
example.ja: あの人、結婚指輪してるね。
example.english: Oh, he's wearing a wedding ring.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa kekkon yubiwa o shitemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は結婚指輪をしてますね。
examplePolite.english: He's wearing a wedding ring.

newEntries.freqNote: Ranks are for 指輪 #3345 and する #15; 結婚指輪 kekkon yubiwa is #12423. Pairing commonness is judged.
newEntries.notes: Slipping one on is often yubiwa o hameru, the same verb as for gloves (tebukuro o hameru), and hameteru also means has one on; yubiwa o tsukeru is fine too, a little more formal. The finger takes ni: kusuriyubi ni yubiwa shiteru (has a ring on the ring finger). It comes off with hazusu.

newEntries.use: kigaeru already means 'change clothes', so fuku is often dropped: chotto kigaete kuru (I'll just go and get changed). What you change into takes ni: pajama ni kigaeru.
newEntries.verbSense: change clothes (kiru 'wear' + kaeru 'change')
newEntries.trap: fuku o kaeru isn't wrong, but it's about switching to a different outfit (are, fuku kaeta? = oh, you've changed your outfit?). The everyday verb for getting changed is kigaeru, and English 'change into' becomes ni (seifuku ni kigaeru).

example.ja: ちょっと服着替えてくる。
example.english: I'm just going to go and get changed.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto fuku o kigaete kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと服を着替えてきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll just go and get changed.

newEntries.freqNote: Ranks are for 服 #1051 and 着替える #1536. The verb usually comes without fuku (着替えて alone has 158 corpus hits, against 27 for the pair); the noun 着替え kigae is #5293.
newEntries.notes: The noun kigae is a change of clothes: kigae motteku (I'll bring a change of clothes). Some speakers say kikaeru; it's the same word.

newEntries.english: suit someone, look good on someone
newEntries.use: Mostly said as a compliment: sono fuku niau ne, or yoku niatteru (it really suits you). ga is dropped, and so is the noun once it's clear. The person it looks good on takes ni: watashi ni niau kana? (would it suit me?). Politely, and from every shop assistant, it's (yoku) oniai desu ne.
newEntries.verbSense: suit, look good on someone
newEntries.trap: Suit and fit are different verbs: niau is about looks, saizu ga au is about size (niau ne vs saizu atteru?). What looks good takes ga, and the person takes ni (watashi ni niau kana?) or comes first as the topic (kanojo wa aka ga niau ne = red suits her).

example.ja: その服、よく似合ってるね。
example.english: That outfit really suits you.

examplePolite.romaji: sono fuku, yoku oniai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: その服、よくお似合いですね。
examplePolite.english: That outfit really suits you.

newEntries.freqNote: Ranks are for 服 #1051 and 似合う #941. The pair count is low (8) because the noun is usually dropped or replaced by sore; 似合ってる alone has 178 corpus hits. お似合い oniai is #2476 (181 corpus hits).
newEntries.notes: It works for any look, not just clothes: kami mijikai no mo niau ne (short hair suits you too). oniai also describes a well-matched couple (oniai no futari), and said with a sneer it means 'it's what you deserve' (omae ni wa oniai da).

newEntries.use: Heard as kousui tsuketeru? (are you wearing perfume?) or as a complaint, tsukesugi (too much). Casual speech drops o. tsuketeru means it's on, not that someone is putting it on now.
newEntries.verbSense: attach, apply; put on (jewellery, perfume, cream)
newEntries.trap: Not kousui o kiru: perfume takes tsukeru, the verb for anything applied or attached (earrings, a necklace, cream). kiru is only for clothes on the torso or whole body.

example.ja: いい匂い、香水つけてる？
example.english: You smell nice, are you wearing perfume?

examplePolite.romaji: ii kaori desu ne. kousui o tsuketeru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: いい香りですね。香水をつけてるんですか？
examplePolite.english: What a lovely scent. Are you wearing perfume?

newEntries.freqNote: Ranks are for 香水 #6814 and kana つける #393, which pools every tsukeru sense (付ける #1452, 着ける #3726). Pairing commonness is judged.
newEntries.notes: For spraying it on, kousui o kakeru is also common (12 corpus hits against 19 for tsukeru).

newEntries.use: Mostly heard as nekutai shiteru (has a tie on) or, in dress-code talk, nekutai shinakute ii (no tie needed). Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: do; with small worn items, have on
newEntries.trap: Not nekutai o kiru: a tie takes suru, like a mask or a watch (nekutai shiteru). nekutai o shimeru is tying it, and shimeteru is also a slightly more formal 'has one on'. It comes off with hazusu or toru.

example.romaji: kyou wa nekutai shinakute ii yo.
example.ja: 今日はネクタイしなくていいよ。
example.english: You don't need a tie today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nekutai o shinakute mo ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はネクタイをしなくてもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to wear a tie today.

newEntries.freqNote: Ranks are for ネクタイ #5375 and する #15. Office talk is under-counted in film subtitles, so pairing commonness is judged.
newEntries.notes: Loosening it is nekutai o yurumeru; the summer kuuru bizu dress code means noo nekutai (no tie).

newEntries.use: For stepping out of a building or room, often just for a moment: chotto soto deyou (let's go out for a bit, get some air). Casual speech drops ni (soto deta); setting off for the day is uchi o deru or dekakeru.
newEntries.verbSense: go out, leave; also come out, appear

example.ja: 寒いから外出たくない。
example.english: It's cold, I don't want to go out.

examplePolite.romaji: samui node, soto ni detakunai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 寒いので、外に出たくないです。
examplePolite.english: It's cold, so I don't want to go outside.

newEntries.freqNote: 外 #437 is the そと reading; 出る #81 counts every sense of deru.
newEntries.notes: Going inside is naka ni hairu (back in: naka ni modoru). soto also means away from home: soto de taberu (eat out).

newEntries.use: For putting something back where it was or how it was: tsukattara moto ni modoshite ne. It also covers undoing a change (a setting, an edit); things going back to normal by themselves is moto ni modoru.
newEntries.verbSense: return something to where or how it was
newEntries.trap: Not moto ni modoru when you do the putting: modoru is the thing (or you) going back. Putting something back yourself is modosu: moto ni modoshite.

example.ja: 使ったら元に戻してね。
example.english: Put it back when you're done with it.

examplePolite.romaji: tsukattara moto ni modoshite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 使ったら元に戻してくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please put it back after you use it.

newEntries.freqNote: 元 #642 counts every sense of moto (origin, former); the intransitive 戻る modoru is #166.
newEntries.notes: Giving a borrowed thing back to its owner is kaesu (hon o kaesu), not modosu.

newEntries.use: For getting rid of anything, at home or out: kono gomi doko ni suteru? (where does this go?). Casual speech drops o, and the thing itself often replaces gomi: kore sutete ii? (can I throw this out?).
newEntries.verbSense: throw away, discard; also abandon
newEntries.trap: 'Throw' points to nageru, which is throwing through the air (a ball). Throwing away is suteru; only in Hokkaido and Tohoku dialect does gomi o nageru mean this.

example.romaji: kono gomi, doko ni sutetara ii?
example.ja: このゴミ、どこに捨てたらいい？
example.english: Where should I throw this away?

examplePolite.romaji: kono gomi wa doko ni sutetara ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: このゴミはどこに捨てたらいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Where should I throw this rubbish away?

newEntries.freqNote: ゴミ #2709 (ごみ #8915); 捨てる #436 also covers abandoning people and plans.
newEntries.notes: Putting the bags out on collection day is gomi o dasu; the bin is gomibako.

newEntries.use: The after-meal chore, often an offer: osara arau ne (I'll do the dishes). Casual speech drops o; the chore nouns sara-arai and araimono (washing-up) are just as common: araimono shitoku ne.
newEntries.verbSense: wash with water (hands, face, dishes, a car)
newEntries.trap: 'Do the dishes' has no do-verb with osara itself: say osara (o) arau, or put suru on a chore noun: sara-arai (o) suru or araimono (o) suru.

example.romaji: osara wa watashi ga arau ne.
example.ja: お皿は私が洗うね。
example.english: I'll do the dishes.

examplePolite.romaji: osara wa watashi ga araimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: お皿は私が洗いますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll wash the dishes.

newEntries.freqNote: お皿 #5119 (plain 皿 #5569). In films the chore nouns win: 皿洗い sara-arai 40 hits and 洗い物 araimono (#10157) 23, against 15 for (o)sara o arau.
newEntries.notes: Clearing the table first is osara o sageru or katazukeru; shokki o arau (wash the tableware) is the same chore, and a dishwasher is shokusenki.

newEntries.english: (a room) gets messy, is a mess
newEntries.use: Nearly always the state chirakatteru: heya chirakatteru (my room's a mess), or the host's apology chirakatteru kedo gomen ne as a guest comes in. Casual speech drops ga; making the mess is chirakasu.
newEntries.verbSense: get scattered, become cluttered

example.ja: ごめん、部屋散らかってるけど。
example.english: Sorry, the place is a mess.

examplePolite.romaji: heya ga chirakatte ite, sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋が散らかっていて、すみません。
examplePolite.english: Sorry the room is such a mess.

newEntries.freqNote: 散らかる #5946; the transitive 散らかす chirakasu (make a mess) is #9673.
newEntries.notes: heya kitanai is also said of a messy room (kitanai covers dirty and messy, and is blunter); chirakatteru is stuff lying everywhere. The fix is heya o katazukeru; a tidy room is katazuiteru or kirei.

newEntries.use: The everyday way to say 'vacuum': soujiki kakeru kara chotto doite (I'm vacuuming, move a sec). Casual speech drops o; souji suru (clean) covers it along with the rest of the cleaning.
newEntries.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set a device going
newEntries.trap: English 'vacuum' is a verb, but Japanese runs the machine with kakeru: soujiki (o) kakeru. Casual soujiki suru is also heard, and soujiki o tsukau (use the vacuum) is fine but less usual.

example.ja: あとで掃除機かけとくね。
example.english: I'll vacuum later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de soujiki o kakete okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あとで掃除機をかけておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll do the vacuuming later.

newEntries.freqNote: かける #244 counts every sense of kakeru (掛ける #2742); 掃除 souji is #1393.
newEntries.notes: The same kakeru irons a shirt (airon o kakeru) and sets an alarm (mezamashi o kakeru).

newEntries.use: Said about family, worried or annoyed: otousan kaeri osoi ne. Your own heads-up is kyou kaeri osoku naru (I'll be home late today), with ga usually dropped.
newEntries.verbSense: late; also slow
newEntries.trap: Not okureru for 'I'll be late tonight': okureru is being late for something with a set time (a train, a meeting). Getting home late is kaeri ga osoku naru, or just osoku naru.

example.ja: 今日帰り遅くなるから。
example.english: I'll be home late today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kaeri ga osoku narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は帰りが遅くなります。
examplePolite.english: I'll be home late today.

newEntries.freqNote: 帰り #1209 also counts 'on the way home' (kaeri ni); 遅い #328 covers both late and slow.
newEntries.notes: The opposite is kaeri ga hayai; the same noun gives kaeri ni (on the way home): kaeri ni konbini yoru.

newEntries.use: Said in the evening or when the sun is in your eyes: kaaten shimete (close the curtains). Casual speech drops o; opening them in the morning is kaaten o akeru.
newEntries.verbSense: shut something (a door, a window, a lid); with kagi, lock

example.ja: まぶしいから、カーテン閉めて。
example.english: It's too bright, close the curtains.

examplePolite.romaji: mabushii node, kaaten o shimete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: まぶしいので、カーテンを閉めてください。
examplePolite.english: It's bright, so please close the curtains.

newEntries.freqNote: 閉める #1764; the sound-alike 締める (tighten, fasten) is #4630.
newEntries.notes: The state is kaaten shimatteru (the curtains are shut) or kaaten aiteru (open).

newEntries.use: For renting a place to live as the tenant: hitorigurashi de heya karita (I rented a place of my own). Casual speech drops o, and heya here usually means the whole flat.
newEntries.verbSense: borrow; use something that is someone else's, free or paid
newEntries.trap: There's no separate 'rent' verb: the tenant kariru (borrows) and the landlord kasu (lends), so heya o kasu means letting it out. rentaru suru is for cars and kimono, not flats.

example.romaji: eki no chikaku ni heya karita n da.
example.ja: 駅の近くに部屋借りたんだ。
example.english: I've rented a place near the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki no chikaku ni heya o karita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 駅の近くに部屋を借りたんです。
examplePolite.english: I've rented a place near the station.

newEntries.freqNote: 借りる #673 counts every kind of borrowing; 貸す kasu (lend, let out) is #658.
newEntries.notes: The monthly rent is yachin (yachin takai = the rent's high).

newEntries.use: A small chore before and after meals, usually a request: teeburu fuite (give the table a wipe). Casual speech drops o; the cloth is a daifukin (table-wiping cloth) or a damp towel.
newEntries.verbSense: wipe (with a cloth or towel)

example.ja: ちょっとテーブル拭いてくれる？
example.english: Can you give the table a wipe?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto teeburu o fuite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとテーブルを拭いてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you wipe the table, please?

newEntries.freqNote: 拭く #2732; kana ふく is shared with 服 (clothes) and 吹く (blow).
newEntries.notes: souji suru is for a room or the whole house; a table just gets a wipe.

newEntries.use: For putting the kettle on, for tea, coffee or instant noodles: oyu wakasu kedo, nanka nomu? Casual speech drops o; when it's ready, oyu waita (the water's boiled).
newEntries.verbSense: bring to the boil, heat (water, a bath)
newEntries.trap: 'Boil' points to niru or yuderu, which are for cooking food (yuderu for eggs and pasta). Water is heated with wakasu, and it's usually called oyu (hot water) already; mizu o wakasu is also fine.

example.ja: お湯沸かすけど、なんか飲む？
example.english: I'm putting the kettle on, want anything?

examplePolite.romaji: oyu o wakashimasu kedo, nanika nomimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お湯を沸かしますけど、何か飲みますか？
examplePolite.english: I'm boiling some water. Would you like something to drink?

newEntries.freqNote: 沸く waku #6780 is the intransitive (oyu ga waku = the water boils).
newEntries.notes: The kettle is a yakan or a denki ketoru (electric kettle); the same verb heats the bath (ofuro o wakasu).

newEntries.use: For deliveries and online orders, mostly in the past: nimotsu todoita (my parcel came), or still waiting: mada todokanai. Casual speech drops ga.
newEntries.verbSense: reach, get to (someone); also reach with a hand
newEntries.trap: 'Arrive' points to tsuku, which is people and trains arriving (eki ni tsuku). Things sent to you mostly todoku, 'reach you', the same verb as for letters and messages; nimotsu ga tsuku is heard but less usual.

example.ja: 昨日頼んだ荷物、もう届いた。
example.english: The parcel I ordered yesterday already came.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou tanonda nimotsu ga mou todokimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日頼んだ荷物がもう届きました。
examplePolite.english: The package I ordered yesterday has already arrived.

newEntries.freqNote: 届く #738 also counts reaching (te ga todokanai = can't reach); 届ける todokeru (deliver, hand in) is #1208.
newEntries.notes: A missed delivery means asking for saihaitatsu (redelivery).

newEntries.use: Rooms and flats are usually judged semai (cramped) or hiroi (roomy): semai heya da kedo, douzo. As a comment it's heya ga semai, usually without ga: kono heya semai ne.
newEntries.verbSense: narrow, cramped; small in floor space
newEntries.trap: 'Small' points to chiisai, but a room that feels cramped is semai, and a roomy one is hiroi: kono heya semai ne. chiisai heya is fine for a room's size (chiisai heya ga futatsu aru), just not as the complaint.

example.ja: 狭い部屋だけど、どうぞ。
example.english: It's a tiny place, but come in.

examplePolite.romaji: semai heya desu kedo, douzo.
examplePolite.ja: 狭い部屋ですけど、どうぞ。
examplePolite.english: It's a small room, but please come in.

newEntries.freqNote: 狭い #1805; its opposite 広い hiroi is #1347.
newEntries.notes: The host's set line is semai tokoro da kedo, douzo (politely semai tokoro desu ga); the visitor's compliment is hiroi ne! semai also covers narrow roads.

newEntries.use: The daily shave, mostly heard as hige sotta? or hige soranakya; o is often dropped. Stubble is hige ga nobiteru (your beard's grown).
newEntries.verbSense: shave off (hair)
newEntries.trap: Not hige o kiru, which sounds like trimming it with scissors; shaving it off is soru. soru takes the hair (hige, ke, mayu) or the place (atama o soru).

example.ja: 今日ひげ剃るの忘れた。
example.english: I forgot to shave today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hige o soru no o wasuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はひげを剃るのを忘れました。
examplePolite.english: I forgot to shave today.

newEntries.freqNote: ひげ #10683; the katakana spelling ヒゲ is #9045 and 髭 #35748. 剃る #18134.
newEntries.notes: Growing one is hige o hayasu; hige hayashiteru = he has a beard.

newEntries.english: get into bed, get under the covers
newEntries.use: For getting under the covers, not necessarily asleep yet: mou futon haitta (I'm in bed now). Casual speech drops ni. futon also means the covers on a bed, so it's said with any bed; beddo ni hairu is also common.
newEntries.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)

example.ja: もう布団入ったけど、眠れない。
example.english: I'm in bed, but I can't sleep.

examplePolite.romaji: futon ni haitte mo, nakanaka nemurenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 布団に入っても、なかなか眠れないんです。
examplePolite.english: Even after I get into bed, I can't get to sleep.

newEntries.freqNote: 入る #115 counts every sense of hairu; ベッド beddo is #2222.
newEntries.notes: Laying the futon out is futon o shiku; folding it away in the morning is futon o tatamu.

newEntries.use: Winter at home: sitting with your legs under the heated table's quilt, often with mikan. Mostly heard as kotatsu haitte (get in) or kotatsu kara derarenai (I can't get out of the kotatsu).
newEntries.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)

example.ja: 寒い！早くこたつ入ろう。
example.english: It's freezing! Let's get under the kotatsu.

examplePolite.romaji: samui desu ne. hayaku kotatsu ni hairimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 寒いですね。早くこたつに入りましょう。
examplePolite.english: It's cold. Let's get under the kotatsu.

newEntries.freqNote: こたつ #18598 (コタツ #37599); no film hits, since foreign films have no kotatsu.
newEntries.notes: Same hairu as futon ni hairu and ofuro ni hairu. Dozing off in it (kotatsu de neru) is the classic way to catch a cold.

newEntries.kana: せんたくものがかわく
newEntries.use: Comes up with the weather: sentakumono kawaita? (is the washing dry?), and in the rainy season the complaint sentakumono ga kawakanai. Casual speech drops ga.
newEntries.verbSense: become dry (laundry, paint, hair)
newEntries.trap: Not sentakumono o kawaku: kawaku is the laundry drying by itself. Hanging it out to dry is sentakumono o hosu; drying something yourself with heat is kawakasu (kami o kawakasu, dry your hair).

example.ja: 今日は洗濯物乾かないね。
example.english: The washing won't dry today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa sentakumono ga kawakimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は洗濯物が乾きませんね。
examplePolite.english: The laundry won't dry today, will it?

newEntries.freqNote: 乾く #6556; its homophone 渇く (nodo ga kawaku, thirsty) is #6159.
newEntries.notes: Washing hung indoors on a rainy day is heyaboshi; a tumble dryer is kansouki.

newEntries.use: Usually once the dry washing has been brought in (sentakumono o torikomu): fuku tatande (fold your clothes), with sentakumono as the object just as often (sentakumono tatanda?). Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: fold up; also close (an umbrella), shut down (a shop)
newEntries.trap: Not oru: oru is folding paper (origami) or snapping something (hone o oru). Clothes, futons and umbrellas are tatamu.

example.ja: 服、ちゃんと畳んでよ。
example.english: Fold your clothes properly.

examplePolite.romaji: fuku wa chanto tatande kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 服はちゃんと畳んでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please fold your clothes properly.

newEntries.freqNote: 畳む #6592 (kana たたむ #20410); kana ふく also matches 拭く (wipe).
newEntries.notes: Folded clothes then go away with shimau: tatande shimatte (fold them and put them away).

newEntries.use: Heard in every train and lift announcement: doa ga shimarimasu (the doors are closing). At home it's mostly the state, doa shimatteru (the door's shut), or doa shimatchatta when it swings shut by itself.
newEntries.verbSense: of a door, window or lid: close by itself, or be shut
newEntries.trap: Not doa ga shimeru: with ga the verb is shimaru (doa shimatteru). shimeru needs someone doing the shutting, as in doa shimete.

example.ja: 玄関のドア、ちゃんと閉まってる？
example.english: Is the front door properly shut?

examplePolite.romaji: genkan no doa wa chanto shimatte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 玄関のドアはちゃんと閉まっていますか？
examplePolite.english: Is the front door properly closed?

newEntries.freqNote: 閉まる #3722; 締まる (tighten) #14106 is another kanji for the same sound.
newEntries.notes: A door that won't shut is doa ga shimaranai; the opening half is doa ga aku.

newEntries.use: Housework as a whole (cooking, cleaning, laundry), mostly in talk about who does what at home: kaji wa futari de yatteru (we both do the housework). Casual speech drops o, and yaru often replaces suru.
newEntries.verbSense: do; the general verb for tasks and chores

example.ja: 今日は一日家事してた。
