example.english: I spent all day on housework.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ichinichi kaji o shite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は一日家事をしていました。
examplePolite.english: I spent the whole day doing housework.

newEntries.freqNote: 家事 #3945; kana かじ is also 火事 'fire' (#3576).
newEntries.notes: Helping with it is kaji o tetsudau; splitting it is kaji o buntan suru.

newEntries.use: The standard invitation and plan for a night out: kondo nomi ni ikou (let's go for a drink sometime), kyou nomi ni ikanai? Bare nomi already means alcohol. Naming the drink is fine too (osake nomi ni iku, koohii nomi ni iku), and a café break is ocha shi ni iku. Casual speech sometimes drops ni (nomi iku).
newEntries.verbSense: go; with a verb stem or activity noun + ni, go (out) to do it (tabe ni iku, kaimono ni iku)

example.romaji: kondo, issho ni nomi ni ikou yo.
example.ja: 今度、一緒に飲みに行こうよ。
example.english: Let's go for a drink together sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo, issho ni nomi ni ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 今度、一緒に飲みに行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's go for a drink together sometime.

newEntries.freqNote: The noun 飲み is #15171 (kana のみ #1942 is mostly the particle 'only'); 飲み会 (nomikai) is #4920. 行く #40 counts all going. The phrase 飲みに行 occurs 141 times in the subtitles, and only 7 times without ni.
newEntries.notes: A drinking party with colleagues or a club is a nomikai, and moving on to a second place afterwards is the nijikai (second round).

newEntries.use: The everyday way to say who's cooking: kyou wa watashi ga gohan tsukuru, or gohan tsukutte kureta (they made me dinner). Casual speech drops o, and the meal is named only when it matters (bangohan, obentou). ryouri suru also works for tonight's cooking (kyou wa boku ga ryouri suru), but it leans toward cooking as an activity (ryouri suru no ga suki).
newEntries.verbSense: make; with food, prepare or cook

example.romaji: kyou wa watashi ga gohan tsukuru ne.
example.ja: 今日は私がご飯作るね。
example.english: I'll make dinner tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa watashi ga gohan o tsukurimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は私がご飯を作りますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll make dinner tonight.

newEntries.freqNote: ご飯 #1225 (kana ごはん #2244 counted separately); 作る #146 counts all making. 料理 (ryouri) is #856. In the subtitles o is dropped in 11 of 14 hits.
newEntries.notes: Cooking the rice itself is gohan o taku (in a rice cooker).

newEntries.use: Said about leftovers and shopping, usually with -toku: reizouko ni iretoku ne (I'll put it in the fridge), or as a request, reizouko iretoite. ni is often kept, but casual speech drops it too, and reizouko ni shimau (put away in the fridge) is also common.
newEntries.verbSense: put in, put inside
newEntries.trap: English 'put' leads to oku, which is mainly setting something down on a surface. Into the fridge, a bag or a box, the usual verb is ireru; reizouko ni oite aru (it's been left in the fridge) is also heard.

example.romaji: amatta no, reizouko ni iretoku ne.
example.ja: 余ったの、冷蔵庫に入れとくね。
example.english: I'll put what's left in the fridge.

examplePolite.romaji: amatta no wa, reizouko ni irete okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 余ったのは、冷蔵庫に入れておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll put what's left in the fridge.

newEntries.freqNote: 冷蔵庫 #2894; 入れる #222 counts every sense of ireru (put in, include, switch on, make tea). The phrase 冷蔵庫に入れ occurs 12 times in the subtitles and 冷蔵庫に置 once; subtitles keep particles more than speech does.
newEntries.notes: Taking it out is reizouko kara dasu; chilling a drink is hiyasu (biiru hiyashitoku).

newEntries.use: Said about servings in restaurants and when sharing food: koko ryou ooi ne (the portions here are big), ryou ooi kara hanbunko shiyou (it's a lot, let's share). Casual speech drops ga, and the opposite is ryou ga sukunai.
newEntries.verbSense: many, much, a lot (number or amount)
newEntries.trap: English 'a big portion' leads to ookii, which is the size of a thing (ookii sara, a big plate). An amount of food is ooi or sukunai: ryou ga ooi.
partners: shigoto (work: shigoto no ryou ga ooi)

example.romaji: koko no raamen, ryou ooi ne.
example.ja: ここのラーメン、量多いね。
example.english: The ramen here comes in big portions.

examplePolite.romaji: koko no raamen wa, ryou ga ooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここのラーメンは、量が多いですね。
examplePolite.english: The ramen here comes in big portions.

newEntries.freqNote: 量 #1956; 多い #360 counts every sense of many and much. All 17 subtitle hits keep ga. Most are compounds such as koutsuuryou (traffic volume), and only a few are about food, which the films under-count.
newEntries.notes: When ordering, ask for oomori (a large serving) or sukuname (a smaller one): gohan sukuname de onegai shimasu.

newEntries.use: Said at breakfast about toast (pan yaku? = want some toast?) and about baking at home. Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: cook with dry heat: grill, roast, bake, toast; also burn

example.romaji: asa wa itsumo pan yaite taberu.
example.ja: 朝はいつもパン焼いて食べる。
example.english: I always have toast in the morning.

examplePolite.romaji: asa wa itsumo pan o yaite tabemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝はいつもパンを焼いて食べます。
examplePolite.english: I always have toast in the morning.

newEntries.freqNote: パン #2129; 焼く #1576 counts all grilling, baking and burning. パン + 焼く occurs 15 times in the subtitles (with o in 14), against 4 for トーストし (toosuto suru). The noun トースト (toast) is #14928.
newEntries.notes: When it's done, the intransitive yakeru: pan yaketa yo (the toast is ready). yaku covers toast, bake and grill alike (keeki o yaku, niku o yaku, sakana o yaku). toosuto suru exists but is mostly recipe and packaging language; at home people say pan yaku.

newEntries.use: Asked when making someone coffee or tea (satou ireru? = sugar?), and also said about adding sugar when cooking. Casual speech drops o, and polite speech says osatou.
newEntries.verbSense: put in; add (to a drink or dish)
newEntries.trap: English 'do you take sugar?' has no 'take' in Japanese: sugar or milk going into a drink is ireru (satou ireru?). Say irete for yes and daijoubu for no; a bare iranai is only for friends.

example.ja: 紅茶に砂糖入れないでね。
example.english: Don't put sugar in my tea, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: koucha ni wa, osatou o irenaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 紅茶には、お砂糖を入れないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't put sugar in my tea.

newEntries.freqNote: 砂糖 #4869 (kana さとう #22633); 入れる #222 counts every sense of ireru. Only 9 subtitle hits, because offering sugar is daily-life talk the films miss.
newEntries.notes: Black coffee is burakku: burakku de ii yo (black's fine).

newEntries.kana: おべんとうをあたためる
newEntries.use: Heard at every konbini checkout as a question, obentou atatamemasu ka? (shall I heat it up?), answered with onegai shimasu or daijoubu desu. At home renji de chin suru (zap it) is the casual alternative.
newEntries.verbSense: warm up, heat (food, a room, hands)
newEntries.trap: English 'heat up' leads to atsuku suru; warming food is atatameru. At the till, daijoubu desu means 'no, thanks', so say onegai shimasu if you want it heated.

example.romaji: obentou, renji de atatamete kuru ne.
example.ja: お弁当、レンジで温めてくるね。
example.english: I'll go heat up my lunch in the microwave.

examplePolite.romaji: obentou, renji de atatamete kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: お弁当、レンジで温めてきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll go heat up my lunch in the microwave.

newEntries.freqNote: お弁当 #2384; the plain 弁当 (bentou) is #3091 and counted separately. 温める #4658. No subtitle hits, because the konbini question is daily life the films miss.
newEntries.notes: At the same till you'll hear ohashi otsuke shimasu ka? (want chopsticks?).

newEntries.use: Said while cooking and storing food: futa shite gofun (lid on for five minutes), futa shitoite (keep it covered). Casual speech drops o, and taking the lid off is futa o toru or futa o akeru.
newEntries.verbSense: do; with a lid, plug or wrap, put it on (as with worn items: masuku o suru)
newEntries.trap: English 'put the lid on' leads to futa o oku, which means setting the lid down somewhere. Covering a pot is futa (o) suru, the same suru as masuku o suru.
partners: raappu (cling film: raappu shite reizouko ni ireru)
sen (a plug or stopper: ofuro no sen o suru)

example.ja: 蓋して、五分ぐらい煮込んで。
example.english: Put the lid on and let it simmer about five minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: futa o shite, gofun gurai nikonde kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 蓋をして、五分ぐらい煮込んでください。
examplePolite.english: Put the lid on and let it simmer for about five minutes.

newEntries.freqNote: 蓋 #11198 (ふた #18330 and フタ #14988 counted separately); する #15 counts every use of suru. The 24 subtitle hits are almost all figurative (kusai mono ni futa o suru, covering things up); cooking talk is daily life the films miss.
newEntries.notes: futa o shimeru (close the lid) works for pots and boxes too, and is the only choice for a screw-top bottle or jar; opening is futa o akeru.

newEntries.use: Said about busy mornings and diets: asagohan nuita (I skipped breakfast), with o dropped and asagohan often cut to asa (asa nuichatta). For a habit you hear asa wa itsumo nuiteru.
newEntries.verbSense: pull out, take out, leave out
newEntries.trap: English 'skip' leads to tobasu, which is for pages or steps, not meals. Leaving out a meal is nuku; asagohan tabenakatta (didn't eat breakfast) is also fine.

example.ja: 今日朝ご飯抜いちゃった。
example.english: I skipped breakfast today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa asagohan o nuichaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は朝ご飯を抜いちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I skipped breakfast today.

newEntries.freqNote: 朝ご飯 #5780; the kana spelling 朝ごはん (#6629), the rough 朝飯 (asameshi, #9447) and the stiff 朝食 (choushoku, #4784) are counted separately. Only 7 subtitle hits, mostly choushoku o nuku in translated dialogue.
newEntries.notes: When ordering, X nuki de means 'without X': sabi nuki de (no wasabi), koori nuki de (no ice).

newEntries.use: Said when offering to pay and when telling who paid: kyou wa ogoru yo (it's on me), senpai ni gohan ogotte moratta (my senpai bought me dinner). The meal is often left out, and casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: pay for someone else, treat
newEntries.trap: ogoru is the payer's verb, like 'treat'. When you are the one treated, add kureta or moratta (senpai ga ogotte kureta, senpai ni ogotte moratta); ogotta with no subject named is heard as 'I paid'.

example.romaji: tetsudatte kureta kara, kondo gohan ogoru ne.
example.ja: 手伝ってくれたから、今度ご飯おごるね。
example.english: You helped me out, so I'll buy you dinner sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: tetsudatte moratta node, kondo gohan o ogorimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 手伝ってもらったので、今度ご飯をおごりますね。
examplePolite.english: You helped me out, so I'll buy you dinner sometime.

newEntries.freqNote: ご飯 #1225; the kana おごる (#2743) is far more common than 奢る (#15720). Forms of the verb ogoru occur about 340 times in the subtitles (about 490 counting the noun ogori), ogoru yo 52 of them, mostly with the object left out.
newEntries.notes: In polite speech the usual offer is gochisou shimasu (kondo gochisou shimasu ne). To a senior, ogorasete kudasai (let me treat you) also works; the noun is ogori: kyou wa watashi no ogori.

newEntries.use: Said to get people to the table (hayaku, samechau yo) or about a drink left too long (koohii sameta). Hosts say samenai uchi ni douzo (eat it while it's hot).
newEntries.verbSense: lose heat and cool down (food, drinks, bath water)
newEntries.trap: Not samuku naru: samui is for weather and how you feel, and hot food or drink cooling off is sameru. tsumetaku naru is for something that has gone fully cold.

example.ja: 早く食べよう、ご飯冷めちゃうよ。
example.english: Come on, let's eat, the food'll get cold.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku tabemashou, gohan ga samechaimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 早く食べましょう、ご飯が冷めちゃいますよ。
examplePolite.english: Come on, let's eat, the food'll get cold.

newEntries.freqNote: 冷める #2747 also counts feelings cooling. The verb goes with any hot food or drink, so gohan is only the headword noun. ご飯 + 冷める has no subtitle hits; お茶 + 冷める (5) and スープ + 冷める (3) show the pattern, and most bare 冷めた hits are about feelings cooling.
newEntries.notes: samasu (let it cool) is the transitive partner. The sameru of me ga sameru (wake up) is a different word.

newEntries.use: Said about food in the fridge and about cards, passports and coupons, mostly as kireteru or kireta: kore, kigen kireteru (this is past its date). For food the full noun is common: shoumi kigen kireteru.
newEntries.verbSense: snap, run out; for a time limit, lapse
newEntries.trap: Dictionaries give shikkou suru or manryou for 'expire', which are legal and formal words. Food, passports and coupons just run out: kigen ga kireta.

example.ja: この牛乳、期限切れてるよ。
example.english: This milk is past its date.

examplePolite.romaji: kono gyuunyuu, kigen ga kiretemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この牛乳、期限が切れてますよ。
examplePolite.english: This milk is past its date.

newEntries.freqNote: 期限 #4825; 賞味期限 (shoumi kigen, best-before) #12993 and the noun 期限切れ (kigengire, expired) #36600 are counted separately. 切れる #1147 counts every sense; 期限が切れ / 期限切れ occur 45 times in the subtitles.
newEntries.notes: Don't mix it up with kigen ga warui (in a bad mood), which is a different kigen (機嫌).

newEntries.use: Said about food with a lot of salt, soy sauce or sauce, often as a mild complaint (chotto aji koi ne) and sometimes as praise for food that goes with rice. Casual speech drops ga, and before a noun it is koi aji.
newEntries.verbSense: dense, strong in concentration (taste, colour, coffee)
newEntries.trap: English 'strong flavour' leads to aji ga tsuyoi, which is said of a pungent, distinctive taste. Heavy seasoning is koi (dense), the same word as strong coffee and dark colour. 'Too salty' on its own is shoppai.

example.romaji: aji koi kara, gohan susumu ne.
example.ja: 味濃いから、ご飯進むね。
example.english: It's richly seasoned, so it goes great with rice.

examplePolite.romaji: aji ga koi node, gohan ga susumimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 味が濃いので、ご飯が進みますね。
examplePolite.english: It's richly seasoned, so it goes great with rice.

newEntries.freqNote: The rank is for the kanji 濃い (#3669); kana こい also matches 来い and 恋. Only 3 subtitle hits, because food talk is daily life the films miss.
newEntries.notes: aji ga usui is the opposite; aji koisugiru (way too strong) is a clear complaint.

newEntries.use: Said about people at drinking parties, often as surprised praise: osake tsuyoi ne! (you can really drink!), or as a question, osake tsuyoi n desu ka? Casual speech drops ga, and osake ni tsuyoi is equally common.
newEntries.verbSense: strong; with something you take or face, able to handle it
partners: kikai (machines: kikai ni tsuyoi, good with tech)

example.romaji: osake tsuyoi ne. zenzen kao ni denai.
example.ja: お酒強いね。全然顔に出ない。
example.english: You can really drink. It doesn't even show on your face.

examplePolite.romaji: osake ga tsuyoi desu ne. zenzen kao ni demasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: お酒が強いですね。全然顔に出ませんね。
examplePolite.english: You can really drink. It doesn't show on your face at all.

newEntries.freqNote: お酒 #1229 (bare 酒 #1131 counted separately); 強い #310 counts every sense of strong. In the subtitles 酒 + 強い is mostly tsuyoi sake (strong liquor), and the drinker sense shows up only about five times, so its commonness is judged.
newEntries.notes: osake ga yowai is the opposite. With the drink as the subject, kono osake tsuyoi means the drink is high-proof. Someone who never seems to get drunk is jokingly called a zaru (a sieve).

newEntries.use: Said when people share photos, mostly as kono shashin mite (look at this photo) while holding out a phone, or shashin mita? (did you see the photo I sent?). Casual speech drops o. Something you've only seen in pictures is shashin de mita.
newEntries.verbSense: see, look at, watch

example.ja: ちょっとこの写真見て。
example.english: Take a look at this photo.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kono shashin o mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとこの写真を見てください。
examplePolite.english: Please take a look at this photo.

newEntries.freqNote: verbRank is 見る pooling every sense (see, look, watch).
newEntries.notes: Asking to see someone's photos uses miseru: shashin misete (show me).

newEntries.use: Said about keeping up with the news, often in the past as a conversation opener: nyuusu mita? (did you see the news?). Something you learned from it is nyuusu de mita (I saw it on the news) or nyuusu de yatteta (it was on the news). It covers news apps on a phone too. Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: see, look at, watch

example.ja: 今朝のニュース見た？
example.english: Did you see the news this morning?

examplePolite.romaji: kesa no nyuusu o mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今朝のニュースを見ましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you see the news this morning?

newEntries.freqNote: verbRank is 見る pooling every sense (see, look, watch).
newEntries.notes: nyuusu ni naru = make the news: ano jiko, nyuusu ni natteta.

newEntries.use: Said as a heads-up when a phone rings, in the -teru form: denwa natteru yo (your phone's ringing), often just natteru yo. Casual speech drops ga. The past natta is for a ring that already happened: sakki denwa natta yo.
newEntries.verbSense: ring, sound (a phone, bell or alarm)
newEntries.trap: Spelled like naru 'become' and conjugated alike (natteru, natta), but the pitch differs: naru 'ring' is flat (na-RU), while naru 'become' falls after na (NA-ru). So keitai natteru yo means 'your phone's ringing'. Ringing something yourself is the transitive narasu (chaimu o narasu).

example.ja: ねえ、電話鳴ってるよ。
example.english: Hey, your phone's ringing.

examplePolite.romaji: denwa ga nattemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 電話が鳴ってますよ。
examplePolite.english: Your phone's ringing.

newEntries.freqNote: verbRank is 鳴る only; kana なる (#29) is almost all 'become'.
newEntries.notes: Alarms and stomachs use it too: mezamashi naranakatta (my alarm didn't go off), onaka natta (my stomach rumbled).

newEntries.use: Said about switching on a phone, computer or machine, often while troubleshooting: dengen ireta? (did you turn it on?). A device that won't start is dengen ga hairanai (or tsukanai), with intransitive hairu. Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: put in; switch on (the power, a switch)
newEntries.trap: English 'turn on' pulls toward tsukeru, the verb for the appliance itself (denki, terebi, eakon). The power or a switch usually takes ireru ('put in'); dengen tsukeru is heard, but much less. Join the device with no: sumaho no dengen irete.
partners: eakon (air conditioner; tsukeru is more usual)

example.ja: ちゃんと電源入れた？
example.english: Did you actually turn it on?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, purojekutaa no dengen o irete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、プロジェクターの電源を入れてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you turn on the projector?

newEntries.freqNote: Phrase entry 電源を入れる is #32795 (the tokenizer merges only some uses); 電源を切る is #16226.
newEntries.notes: Off is dengen o kiru. For a computer, pasokon tsukeru and kidou suru (boot up) are heard too.

newEntries.use: Said when calls break up or pages won't load, usually without ga: koko denpa warui ne (the signal's bad here). On a call it comes as an apology: gomen, denpa warukute kikoenai (sorry, bad signal, I can't hear you).
newEntries.verbSense: bad; poor (quality, condition)
newEntries.trap: Not shingou: phone signal is denpa ('radio waves'); shingou is a traffic light.

example.ja: ここ、電波悪いね。
example.english: The signal's bad here, huh?

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa denpa ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここは電波が悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: The signal's bad here, isn't it?

newEntries.freqNote: 圏外 (kengai, out of range) is #16111; verbRank 悪い pools every sense of bad.
newEntries.notes: A weak signal is denpa ga yowai; no signal at all is usually denpa hairanai, also denpa nai or kengai (out of range).

newEntries.use: Said about checking facts, words and places online, often as an offer or a report: netto de shirabete miru (I'll look it up online), netto de shirabeta kedo wakannakatta (I looked it up but couldn't work it out). The de stays even in casual speech.
newEntries.verbSense: look into, check, look up

example.ja: ちょっとネットで調べてみる。
example.english: Let me look it up online.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto netto de shirabete mimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとネットで調べてみます。
examplePolite.english: Let me look it up online.

newEntries.freqNote: ググる (guguru, google it) is #24884 and 検索 (kensaku, search) #4276.
newEntries.notes: o marks what you look up (netto de imi o shiraberu), and netto o shiraberu (search the net) is fine too. To find something like a shop or a flat, the verb is sagasu: netto de sagasu. guguru (google it) is the casual verb: gugutte mita.

newEntries.english: sound comes out (of a TV, speaker, phone)
newEntries.use: Said about TVs, speakers, laptops and video calls, most often in the negative or as a check: oto denai (there's no sound), oto deteru? (is there sound?). ga is usually dropped, and on a call oto dete nai yo means your sound isn't coming through.
newEntries.verbSense: come out, go out; appear
newEntries.trap: Not oto ga ugokanai: when a TV, speaker or call goes silent, the sound 'doesn't come out', oto ga denai. oto nai is heard too, and it is the plain way to say a clip has no sound at all: kono douga, oto nai yo.

example.romaji: are, oto denai n da kedo.
example.ja: あれ、音出ないんだけど。
example.english: Huh, there's no sound.

examplePolite.romaji: are, oto ga denai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、音が出ないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Huh, there's no sound.

newEntries.freqNote: nounRank is 音 read oto; verbRank 出る pools every sense (leave, appear, answer the phone).
newEntries.notes: Different from oto ga suru (you hear a noise). Muting is oto o kesu; turning it down is oto o sageru.

newEntries.politeJa: チャンネルを変えます
newEntries.use: Said in front of the TV, mostly as a request: channeru kaete ii? (mind if I change the channel?). Casual speech drops o, and the show you switch to takes ni: nyuusu ni kaete.
newEntries.verbSense: change, switch (one thing for another)

example.ja: チャンネル変えてもいい？
example.english: Mind if I change the channel?

examplePolite.romaji: channeru o kaete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: チャンネルを変えてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Do you mind if I change the channel?

newEntries.freqNote: verbRank is the 変える spelling; 替える (#2801) is the same verb and is also written for channels.
newEntries.notes: kaete (change it) and kaette (go home) differ by one t. A YouTube channel is channeru too: channeru touroku shita (I subscribed).

newEntries.use: Said when swapping numbers, mostly as the request bangou oshiete (give me your number), softened to bangou oshiete kurenai? Here bangou means denwa bangou (phone number). Casual speech drops o, and asking someone for theirs is bangou o kiku.
newEntries.verbSense: teach; tell, let someone know
newEntries.trap: English 'give' pulls toward ageru or kudasai, but the everyday set is oshieru ('tell'): 'give me your number' is bangou oshiete and 'I gave him my number' is bangou oshieta. bangou ageru is heard, bangou choudai works among close friends, and bangou o kudasai sounds stiff.

example.ja: よかったら、番号教えてくれない？
example.english: Could I get your number?

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, bangou o oshiete kuremasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、番号を教えてくれませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you mind giving me your number?

newEntries.freqNote: 電話番号 (denwa bangou) is #4138 and 連絡先 (renrakusaki, contact details) #2550.
newEntries.notes: Among friends, contacts now go over LINE: rain koukan shiyou (let's swap LINE).

newEntries.english: install an app, get an app
newEntries.use: Said when recommending or setting up apps: kono apuri irete (get this app), mada irete nai (I haven't got it yet). Casual speech drops o. daunroodo suru is just as everyday (shop staff and signs use it), and younger speakers also say otosu (apuri otoshita). insutooru suru sounds more technical.
newEntries.verbSense: put in; install (an app, software)
newEntries.trap: Not apuri o morau: English 'get the app' pulls toward morau, which sounds like someone handed it to you. Putting it on your phone is ireru ('put in').

example.romaji: kono apuri irete mite, benri da yo.
example.ja: このアプリ入れてみて、便利だよ。
example.english: Try getting this app, it's handy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono apuri, benri desu yo. yokattara irete mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: このアプリ、便利ですよ。よかったら入れてみてください。
examplePolite.english: This app is handy. Give it a try if you like.

newEntries.freqNote: No count: the films have no アプリを入れ. インストール (insutooru) is #23611.
newEntries.notes: Deleting an app is apuri o kesu; updating it is appudeeto suru.

newEntries.english: (someone) called, there was a call from X
newEntries.use: Said when passing on who called, in the past with the caller marked by kara: obaachan kara denwa atta yo (Grandma called). At work, passing on a call takes the polite odenwa: tanaka-san kara odenwa ga arimashita. Casual speech often drops ga.
newEntries.verbSense: there is, exist; have; happen
newEntries.trap: 'Your mom called' is okaasan kara denwa atta yo, with the caller marked by kara; okaasan ni denwa atta means a call came for her. okaasan ga denwa shita sounds like she called someone else.

example.romaji: tanaka-san kara denwa atta yo. orikaeshite hoshii tte.
example.ja: 田中さんから電話あったよ。折り返してほしいって。
example.english: Tanaka called. He wants you to call him back.

examplePolite.romaji: sakihodo tanaka-san kara odenwa ga arimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 先ほど田中さんからお電話がありました。
examplePolite.english: Mr. Tanaka called earlier.

newEntries.freqNote: verbRank pools every use of ある (there is, have, happen). The count also holds 'there's a phone' uses; the call forms 電話(が)あった and 電話がありました alone are 233.
newEntries.notes: denwa kakatte kita tells the call coming in to you; denwa atta reports that a call happened, often to pass it on. denwa kita is the casual short form, and renraku atta covers word by any channel.

newEntries.use: Said after outings and when sharing on LINE, mostly as a promise or a request: ato de shashin okuru ne (I'll send you the photos later), shashin okutte. The person takes ni and the app takes de. Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: send; see someone off

example.romaji: kinou no shashin, rain de okutte.
example.ja: 昨日の写真、LINEで送って。
example.english: Send me yesterday's photos on LINE.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no shashin, rain de okutte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の写真、LINEで送ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please send me yesterday's photos on LINE.

newEntries.freqNote: verbRank 送る also counts seeing someone off and sending parcels.
newEntries.notes: Photos arriving take kuru, like meeru ga kuru: shashin kita yo (got the photos).

newEntries.use: Used for the flight itself: hikouki notta koto aru? (have you ever flown?), hikouki notteru aida (during the flight). To say how you get somewhere, use de: hikouki de iku. Casual speech drops ni.
newEntries.verbSense: ride; get onto (a vehicle, a bike, a ride)
newEntries.trap: Not hikouki o toru for 'take a plane': hikouki totta? means 'have you booked your flight?'. Being on board is ni noru, like every vehicle, and how you get there takes de: hikouki de iku. oosaka ni tobu (fly off to Osaka) is real too, but casual, with a sudden, business-trip feel.

example.ja: 飛行機乗ってる間、ずっと寝てた。
example.english: I slept the whole flight.

examplePolite.romaji: hikouki ni notteru aida, zutto netemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 飛行機に乗ってる間、ずっと寝てました。
examplePolite.english: I slept the whole flight.

newEntries.freqNote: The tokenizer splits 飛行機, so the pair isn't counted. 飛行機に乗 has 197 literal film hits, more than バスに乗 (160).
newEntries.notes: A flight is a bin: nanji no bin? (what time's your flight?).

newEntries.use: Used for being able to ride (jitensha noreru? = can you ride a bike?) and for riding one now (jitensha notteru). To say how you get somewhere, use de: jitensha de iku. Casual speech drops ni, and the slangy chari (charinko) often replaces jitensha.
newEntries.verbSense: ride; get onto (a vehicle, a bike, a ride)
newEntries.trap: Not jitensha o noru: English 'ride a bike' takes an object, but a bike takes ni noru like every other vehicle.

example.ja: 自転車乗って、コンビニ行ってくる。
example.english: I'm going to bike over to the convenience store.

examplePolite.romaji: jitensha ni notte, konbini ni itte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 自転車に乗って、コンビニに行ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to ride my bike to the convenience store.

newEntries.freqNote: The tokenizer splits 自転車 into 自転 + 車, so its ~42 hits (自転車に乗) are counted inside kuruma ni noru's 458. The casual chari is #15668.
newEntries.notes: Pedalling is kogu (jitensha o kogu), and the everyday shopping bike with a basket is a mamachari.

newEntries.use: Mostly a request or an offer: nosete kureru? (can you give me a lift?), eki made nosete tte (give me a lift to the station), nosete ku yo (I'll give you a lift), nosete moratta (I got a lift). Once the car is clear the noun often drops.
newEntries.verbSense: put on board; give someone a ride (the transitive of noru)
newEntries.trap: Not raido o ageru or kuruma o ageru (that gives the car away): giving a lift is noseru (put on board), the transitive of noru, with kureru or iku only as helpers after it (nosete kureru?, nosete ku yo). norasete means 'let me ride it', as with a friend's new bike, not 'give me a lift'.

example.ja: 帰り、車乗せてくれる？
example.english: Can you give me a lift back?

examplePolite.romaji: kaeri, kuruma ni nosete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 帰り、車に乗せてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you give me a lift back?

newEntries.freqNote: 乗せる is ranked apart from 載せる (#3380, put on top or publish). okuru (#324) also covers sending mail and messages.
newEntries.notes: Driving someone all the way somewhere is often okuru: ie made okuru yo (I'll take you home).

newEntries.use: Mostly in the past, michi machigaeta (I went the wrong way), often as the reason you're late. Casual speech drops o, and the same frame covers the wrong train or exit: densha machigaeta, deguchi machigaeta.
newEntries.verbSense: get wrong; mistake one thing for another
newEntries.trap: A word-for-word machigatta michi ni itta is understood but stiff, and machigatta michi mostly means the wrong path in life. For a route, the road is the object: michi machigaeta (casually also michi machigatteru). michi ni mayou is different: being lost, with no idea where you are.

example.ja: あ、道間違えたかも。
example.english: Oh, I think we went the wrong way.

examplePolite.romaji: a, michi o machigaeta kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: あ、道を間違えたかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: Oh, I think we may have gone the wrong way.

newEntries.freqNote: machigaeru's rank covers every kind of mistake, not just routes.
newEntries.notes: Getting on the train going the other way is hantai no densha ni notchatta.

newEntries.use: Heard in directions. The corner takes o because you go round it, and the side takes ni: futatsume no kado o migi ni magatte (turn right at the second corner). With no side named, kado magattara (once you turn the corner) says a place is just round it.
newEntries.verbSense: bend; turn (when moving along a road)
newEntries.trap: Not kado ni magaru: ni marks the side (migi ni), so the corner takes o (de also works: kado de migi ni magatte). kado o mawatta tokoro (just round the corner) is also fine, but a turn with a side named is magaru.

example.romaji: ano kado magattara, sugu da yo.
example.ja: あの角曲がったら、すぐだよ。
example.english: It's just round that corner.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kado o magattara, sugu desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの角を曲がったら、すぐですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's just around that corner.

newEntries.freqNote: Both parts rank mid-list because drama talk rarely gives directions, but a quarter of kado's film uses are with magaru.
newEntries.notes: A street corner is kado; the inside corner of a room is sumi (heya no sumi).

newEntries.use: Mostly asked and planned: doko tomaru? (where are you staying?), kyou wa hoteru ni tomaru. Casual speech can drop ni, and the same verb covers a sleepover: tomodachi no uchi ni tomaru.
newEntries.verbSense: stay the night (away from home)
newEntries.trap: Not hoteru ni nokoru, which is staying in rather than going out. hoteru ni iru says where you are or are based, not where you sleep: 'where are you staying?' is doko ni tomatteru?, and taizai suru is the formal word.

example.romaji: ekimae no hoteru ni tomaru yo.
example.ja: 駅前のホテルに泊まるよ。
example.english: I'm staying at a hotel by the station.

examplePolite.romaji: ekimae no hoteru ni tomarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 駅前のホテルに泊まります。
examplePolite.english: I'm staying at a hotel by the station.

newEntries.freqNote: 泊まる is ranked apart from 止まる (#776, stop).
newEntries.notes: Booking a room is hoteru o toru; putting someone up is tomeru: hitoban tomete kureru? (can you put me up for the night?).

newEntries.use: Mostly an offer: nimotsu motsu yo, or motou ka? (shall I take that?). Casual speech drops o, and nimotsu motteru means you have bags with you.
newEntries.verbSense: hold, carry (in your hands); have with you
newEntries.trap: English 'carry' points to hakobu, which is moving things to a place (a porter, a removal van). Taking a bag off someone's hands, or carrying your own, is motsu.

example.ja: 重いでしょ、荷物持つよ。
example.english: That must be heavy, let me take your bag.

examplePolite.romaji: omoi desu yo ne, nimotsu mochimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 重いですよね、荷物持ちますよ。
examplePolite.english: That looks heavy, let me carry your bag.

newEntries.freqNote: motsu's rank covers holding, owning and lasting.
newEntries.notes: nimotsu is also a parcel: nimotsu todoita (my package came).

newEntries.use: Nearly always in the past, norisugoshita or norisugoshichatta, and usually without eki: nechatte norisugoshita (I fell asleep and missed my stop). How far you went is counted in stops: hitoeki norisugoshita. When the noun is said, it's oriru eki: oriru eki norisugoshita (I went past my stop).
newEntries.verbSense: ride past (noru 'ride' + sugosu 'let go by')
newEntries.trap: Not eki o nogasu or eki o misu shita: staying on past your stop is norisugosu (ride past), and nogasu is for a train that left without you. orisokoneta (didn't manage to get off) also works, say on a packed train.

example.ja: 寝ちゃって、一駅乗り過ごした。
example.english: I fell asleep and went one stop too far.

examplePolite.romaji: nete shimatte, hitoeki norisugoshimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 寝てしまって、一駅乗り過ごしました。
examplePolite.english: I fell asleep and went one stop too far.

newEntries.freqNote: No film hits, and norisugosu ranks #51053 in drama, yet it is everyday commuter talk. nesugosu (sleep past) is #25205.
newEntries.notes: Sleeping through the stop is also nesugoshita; oversleeping in the morning is nebou shita.

newEntries.use: Heard on trips and at an inn: onsen haitta? (been in the hot spring yet?), onsen haitte kuru, mostly without ni. Going to a hot-spring town or bathhouse is onsen ni iku: onsen ikitai na.
newEntries.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)
newEntries.trap: Not onsen o abiru: abiru is for showers. You get into a hot spring the way you get into a bath, with ni hairu (ofuro ni hairu).

example.romaji: gohan no mae ni, onsen haitte kuru.
example.ja: ご飯の前に、温泉入ってくる。
example.english: I'm going to soak in the hot spring before dinner.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan no mae ni, onsen ni haitte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯の前に、温泉に入ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to have a dip in the hot spring before dinner.

newEntries.freqNote: Only 3 film hits (onsen ni iku has 6 of the noun's 16), but hairu is the verb for the bathing itself. 入る #115 counts every sense of hairu.
newEntries.notes: A long soak is tsukaru: yukkuri onsen ni tsukaritai (I want a good long soak).

newEntries.use: Comes up on every trip: omiyage kawanakya (I need to get gifts to take back), omiyage nani ga ii? Casual speech drops o. A small gift you bring when visiting someone's home is also omiyage.
newEntries.verbSense: buy
newEntries.trap: English 'souvenir' is often something for yourself, but omiyage are mainly gifts for others, family and coworkers above all, often boxed local sweets and close to expected. One for yourself is jibun-you (or jokingly jibun e no omiyage), and a keepsake is kinenhin.

example.romaji: kaisha no hito ni, omiyage kawanakya.
example.ja: 会社の人に、お土産買わなきゃ。
example.english: I need to get gifts for the people at work.

examplePolite.romaji: kaisha no hito ni, omiyage o kawanai to ikenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 会社の人に、お土産を買わないといけないんです。
examplePolite.english: I need to buy gifts for the people at work.

newEntries.freqNote: Films under-count it (6 pair hits), yet kau takes a sixth of omiyage's verbs there. Plain 土産 is #6311.
newEntries.notes: Handing one over: kore, omiyage (here, a little something from my trip).

newEntries.use: Mostly a timetable question: tsugi no densha nanji ni deru? As it pulls away, densha itchatta or densha dechatta (the train's just gone). Casual speech drops ga.
newEntries.verbSense: go out; leave (a place)
newEntries.trap: For 'what time does it leave?', not densha ga hanareru or densha ga saru: those describe it pulling away (densha ga hoomu o hanareru). The departure itself is deru, the same verb as leaving the house. shuppatsu suru also works, and hassha is the announcement word.

example.romaji: tsugi no densha, nanji ni deru?
example.ja: 次の電車、何時に出る？
example.english: What time does the next train leave?

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi no densha wa nanji ni demasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 次の電車は何時に出ますか？
examplePolite.english: What time does the next train leave?

newEntries.freqNote: No film hits. deru's rank covers every sense of going out or appearing; the formal shuppatsu is #2505 and hassha #14705.
newEntries.notes: The first train of the day is shihatsu: shihatsu made nomu (drink until the first train).

newEntries.kana: しゅうでんがなくなる
newEntries.english: the last train is gone (no way home)
newEntries.use: Said as a warning or an excuse near midnight: shuuden nakunatchau (I'll miss the last train), shuuden nakunatta (the trains have stopped for the night). Casual speech drops ga. shuuden nogashita (I missed the last train) is just as common and makes it your miss.
newEntries.verbSense: run out; be gone (nai 'none' + naru 'become')
newEntries.trap: Not shuuden o misu suru (misu is a mistake): Japanese says the last train 'is gone', with the train as the subject. shuuden nogashita and shuuden ni maniawanakatta also work.

example.romaji: shuuden nakunatchau kara, mou kaeru ne.
example.ja: 終電なくなっちゃうから、もう帰るね。
example.english: I'll miss the last train, so I'm heading home.

examplePolite.romaji: shuuden ga nakunaru node, mou kaerimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 終電がなくなるので、もう帰りますね。
examplePolite.english: The last train will be gone soon, so I'll head home now.

newEntries.freqNote: Rare in films (10 hits for 終電 alone). 397 is the kana spelling なくなる, which covers running out of anything (無くなる #8961).
newEntries.notes: shuuden nanji? (when's your last train?) is the usual question as a night out winds down.

newEntries.use: Said about being too busy, with a verb in front naming what you have no time for: ...teru hima wa nai is the commonest shape (nonbiri shiteru hima wa nai), and a plain verb usually takes mo (asobu hima mo nai, neru hima mo nai). As a brush-off it's sonna hima (wa) nai (I've got no time for that); plain ga is heard less than wa.
newEntries.verbSense: there isn't; not have (negative of aru)

example.romaji: saikin isogashikute, asobu hima mo nai.
example.ja: 最近忙しくて、遊ぶ暇もない。
example.english: I've been so busy lately I don't even have time to go out.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin isogashikute, asobu hima mo nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近忙しくて、遊ぶ暇もないんです。
examplePolite.english: I've been so busy lately I don't even have time to go out.

newEntries.freqNote: 暇 #909 also counts the adjective hima (free, bored). ない #43 is the kana form (無い #6807). Phrase entry 暇がない #16117. Pair count 327 (wa 198, ga 47, mo 41, none 40); films inflate it with 'we don't have time for this' lines (...teru hima wa nai).
newEntries.notes: hima is also an adjective: hima? (are you free?), hima da naa (I'm bored). Unlike jikan ga nai, it never means you're running late: in a hurry it's mou jikan nai!, not mou hima nai!

newEntries.use: Said when you hold off acting to see how things go: a cold, a noise in the car, a plan (toriaezu yousu miyou). Doctors say nisannichi yousu o mimashou. It also means going to check on someone: chotto yousu mite kuru.
newEntries.verbSense: see, look, watch
newEntries.trap: English 'wait and see' leads to plain matsu, which says nothing about watching how things go. For holding off on a problem (a cold, a noise in the car, a plan) the set phrase is yousu o miru, 'look at how things are'. mou sukoshi matte miyou also works when you're waiting for something to happen.
partners: keika (progress: keika o mimashou = let's see how it goes, a doctor's line)
joukyou (how things stand: joukyou mite kimeyou = let's decide once we see how things are)
hannou (a reaction: aite no hannou o miru = see how they react)

example.ja: とりあえず様子見ようか。
example.english: Shall we just wait and see for now?

examplePolite.romaji: toriaezu yousu o mimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: とりあえず様子を見ましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we just wait and see for now?

newEntries.freqNote: Phrase entry 様子を見る #3061. 見る #55 covers every sense. Pair count 314 (o 282); the noun 様子見 adds 27.
newEntries.notes: The same noun describes how someone seems: yousu ga hen (he's acting strange). The noun yousumi is everyday too: shibaraku yousumi da ne (let's wait and see for a while).

newEntries.use: Said as a reminder (yakusoku mamotte ne), a reproach (yakusoku mamoranakatta ja nai) or, with wa, a pledge: daijoubu, yakusoku wa mamoru yo (don't worry, I'll keep my word). Being on time works the same way: jikan o mamoru.
newEntries.verbSense: protect, defend; keep to (a promise, a rule, a deadline)
newEntries.trap: English 'keep' leads to motsu or tamotsu, but promises, rules and deadlines are 'protected': yakusoku o mamoru, ruuru o mamoru, shimekiri o mamoru.
partners: jikan (time: jikan o mamoru = be on time)

example.romaji: kondo wa chanto yakusoku mamotte ne.
example.ja: 今度はちゃんと約束守ってね。
example.english: Make sure you keep your promise this time.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo wa chanto yakusoku o mamotte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今度はちゃんと約束を守ってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please make sure you keep your promise this time.

newEntries.freqNote: 守る #303 also counts its 'protect' sense, inflated by drama plots. Phrase entry 約束を守る #7216. Pair count 247 (o 159, wa 73), with film pledges inflating the wa share.
newEntries.notes: Breaking one is yakusoku o yaburu (yakusoku yabutta!). yakusoku also covers plans with friends: kyou wa tomodachi to yakusoku shiteru (I'm meeting a friend today).

newEntries.use: For working out a plan ahead: a trip, savings, a study schedule. You mostly hear tateta or tateteru: ryokou no keikaku tateteru. The same verb goes with yotei: natsuyasumi no yotei o tateru.
newEntries.verbSense: stand something up; set up (a plan, a goal)
newEntries.trap: English 'make a plan' leads to keikaku o tsukuru, which is heard but far less often (17 against 128 in the subtitles). Plans and goals are 'stood up': keikaku o tateru, mokuhyou o tateru.

example.romaji: ima ryokou no keikaku tateteru n da.
example.ja: 今旅行の計画立ててるんだ。
example.english: I'm planning a trip right now.

examplePolite.romaji: ima ryokou no keikaku o tateteru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今旅行の計画を立ててるんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm planning a trip right now.

newEntries.freqNote: 計画 #1502 covers every sense of 'plan', including projects. 立てる #1187. Phrase entry 計画を立てる #10041.
newEntries.notes: 'Got plans?' is yotei aru?, not keikaku aru?; keikaku is a worked-out scheme.

newEntries.use: Mostly as the question at a till or before going in: kaado tsukaemasu ka? (or kaado daijoubu desu ka?), answered hai, daijoubu desu or hai, otsukai itadakemasu, or genkin nomi desu (cash only). The particle often drops, or becomes ga with the potential: kaado ga tsukaeru.
newEntries.verbSense: use
newEntries.trap: 'Do you take cards?' is kaado tsukaemasu ka? (can I use a card?), not kaado torimasu ka?.

example.ja: ここ、カード使える？
example.english: Do they take cards here?

examplePolite.romaji: koko, kaado tsukaemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ここ、カード使えますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you take cards here?

newEntries.freqNote: カード #2450 counts every card (ID cards, game cards). 使う #171. Pair count 79 (o 48, ga 14); films undercount till talk.
newEntries.notes: When paying, you say kaado de onegai shimasu. For a credit card, staff may ask oshiharai kaisuu wa?; the answer is ikkatsu de or ikkai de (in one payment).

newEntries.use: The standard reason to leave or go to bed early: ashita asa hayai kara, mou neru ne. ga is nearly always dropped, and ashita hayai kara alone is common too. Said about someone's routine, asa hayai ne means they're up early.
newEntries.verbSense: early; also fast, quick
partners: kaeri (getting home: kyou kaeri hayai ne)

example.romaji: ashita asa hayai kara, mou neru ne.
example.ja: 明日朝早いから、もう寝るね。
example.english: I've got an early start tomorrow, so I'm off to bed.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa asa ga hayai node, mou nemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は朝が早いので、もう寝ますね。
examplePolite.english: I've got an early start tomorrow, so I'll go to bed now.

newEntries.freqNote: 朝 #453; 早い #396 (速い 'fast' is #2346). Phrase entry 朝が早い #41988.
newEntries.notes: The opposite is asa ga osoi (a late start), and asa yowai means you're not a morning person. ashita hayaku okinakya (I have to get up early) works just as well.

newEntries.use: Mostly about spending too much, or on what: kongetsu okane tsukaisugita, nani ni sonna ni tsukatta no?. Once an amount is said, okane drops: ichiman en tsukatchatta.
newEntries.verbSense: use; spend (money, effort)
newEntries.trap: Dictionaries give tsuiyasu for 'spend', which is formal, and sugosu, which is only for time. Everyday spending is tsukau, 'use': ryokou de ichiman en tsukatta.

example.ja: 今月、お金使いすぎちゃった。
example.english: I've spent too much this month.

examplePolite.romaji: kongetsu wa okane o tsukaisugichaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今月はお金を使いすぎちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I've spent too much this month.

newEntries.freqNote: お金 #422; 使う #171 covers every sense of 'use'.
newEntries.notes: Wasting money is mudazukai: mudazukai shichatta.

newEntries.use: Said when you're early or waiting for someone: kafe de jikan tsubushiteru ne. The noun himatsubushi (something to pass the time) is just as common: himatsubushi ni sumaho miteta.
newEntries.verbSense: crush, squash; use up (time); ruin
newEntries.trap: Not jikan o korosu: killing time is tsubusu, 'crush'.

example.romaji: hayaku tsuita kara, kafe de jikan tsubushiteru.
example.ja: 早く着いたから、カフェで時間潰してる。
example.english: I got here early, so I'm killing time in a café.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku tsuita node, kafe de jikan o tsubushitemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 早く着いたので、カフェで時間を潰してます。
examplePolite.english: I got here early, so I'm killing time in a café.

newEntries.freqNote: 潰す #2027 also covers 'crush' and 'ruin'; the kana つぶす is #4184. Phrase entry 時間を潰す #32831; 暇つぶし #12575. Pair count 35.
newEntries.notes: tsubusu also means flatten (akikan o tsubusu). A day off that gets eaten up is yasumi ga tsubureta.

newEntries.use: How events get cancelled, mostly in the past: ame de shiai chuushi ni natta. Put off to a later date is enki ni naru, in the same frame.
newEntries.verbSense: become; X ni naru = end up as X
newEntries.trap: English 'cancelled' leads to kyanseru, which fits bookings, orders and your own plans (yoyaku kyanseru shita, kyou no yakusoku kyanseru shite ii?). An event that gets called off, such as a match, a festival, a concert or a school trip, is usually chuushi ni natta, and a cancelled flight is kekkou ni natta.

example.romaji: ame de shiai chuushi ni natta.
example.ja: 雨で試合中止になった。
example.english: The game got rained off.

examplePolite.romaji: ame de shiai ga chuushi ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 雨で試合が中止になりました。
examplePolite.english: The game was rained off.

newEntries.freqNote: 中止 #2024; なる #29 is the kana form. 延期 enki #6376; phrase entry 延期になる #20128.
newEntries.notes: Among friends, a plan that's off is often just nakunatta: kyou no nomikai nakunatta.

newEntries.english: set aside time, take up time
newEntries.use: Mostly in thanks and apologies: jikan totte kurete arigatou (thanks for making time), ojikan torasete sumimasen (sorry to take up your time). It also means setting time aside: kondo chanto jikan toru ne.
newEntries.verbSense: take; get (here: take or set aside time)
newEntries.trap: English 'it takes an hour' leads to toru, but how long something takes is kakaru: ichijikan kakaru. toru is someone setting time aside, or taking up yours: jikan totte kurete arigatou, ojikan torasete sumimasen.

example.romaji: kyou wa jikan totte kurete arigatou.
example.ja: 今日は時間取ってくれてありがとう。
example.english: Thanks for making time today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ojikan totte itadaite, arigatou gozaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はお時間取っていただいて、ありがとうございました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for making time today.

newEntries.freqNote: 取る #228 (撮る, take a photo, is #649). Phrase entry 時間を取る #24464. Pair count 89.
newEntries.notes: jikan toreru? asks if someone can spare time. A short polite thank-you, (kichou na) ojikan o arigatou gozaimashita, is also fine, and formal thanks use saku: ojikan o saite itadaite.

newEntries.use: Said when comparing shops or weighing up a buy: koko, nedan chotto takai ne. Day to day people just say takai! about a thing; nedan comes in when the price itself is the point, often with mo: oishii kedo nedan mo takai.
newEntries.verbSense: high; expensive
newEntries.trap: A low price isn't hikui in speech: cheap is yasui (nedan ga yasui). hikui turns up only in written kakaku ga hikui.

example.romaji: koko, oishii kedo nedan chotto takai ne.
example.ja: ここ、おいしいけど値段ちょっと高いね。
example.english: This place is good, but it's a bit pricey.

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa oishii kedo, nedan ga chotto takai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここはおいしいけど、値段がちょっと高いですね。
examplePolite.english: This place is good, but it's a bit pricey.

newEntries.freqNote: 値段 #2953; 高い #421 also covers 'high' and 'tall'. Pair count 16 (mo 6, ga 6).
newEntries.notes: nedan no wari ni = for the price: nedan no wari ni oishii. kakaku is the written word on signs and sites.

newEntries.use: The polite way to turn down an invitation for a particular day: sumimasen, sono hi wa senyaku ga atte..., left trailing, since a flat ...kara sounds like an excuse. Friends say it too (gomen, senyaku aru n da) when the plan is with someone else; yotei aru is vaguer.
newEntries.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)

example.romaji: gomen, sono hi wa senyaku ga atte...
example.ja: ごめん、その日は先約があって…
example.english: Sorry, I've already got plans that day...

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sono hi wa senyaku ga aru n desu ga...
examplePolite.ja: すみません、その日は先約があるんですが…
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I already have plans that day...

newEntries.freqNote: 先約 #13651 is rare as a word because it lives almost only in this set (74% of its uses). ある #21. Pair count 17.
newEntries.notes: Same trailing shape as youji ga atte...: the 'so I can't' is left unsaid.

newEntries.english: put time into, take time over
newEntries.use: For spending time on something on purpose, mostly as kakete before another verb: jikan kakete tsukutta (I put real time into making it). With an amount, jikan drops: sanjikan kaketa. 'Take your time' is usually yukkuri de ii yo; jikan kakete ii yo is for a task: jikkuri jikan kakete ii yo.
newEntries.verbSense: hang; put on; spend (time or money on something)
newEntries.trap: 'I spent three hours on it' is sanjikan kaketa (or kakatta), not sugoshita: sugosu is for spending time somewhere or with someone.
partners: tema (effort: tema o kakeru = go to the trouble)

example.romaji: kore, kekkou jikan kakete tsukutta n da.
example.ja: これ、けっこう時間かけて作ったんだ。
example.english: I put quite a lot of time into making this.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa kekkou jikan o kakete tsukutta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: これはけっこう時間をかけて作ったんです。
examplePolite.english: I put quite a lot of time into making this.

newEntries.freqNote: かける #244 is the kana form across every sense (call, sit, put on glasses); 掛ける #2742. Phrase entry 時間をかける #5443. Pair count 191.
newEntries.notes: Its intransitive partner jikan ga kakaru is how long something takes; kakeru is you choosing to spend it.

newEntries.use: Said at the till or when you're short for something: are, gohyaku en tarinai (oh, I'm 500 yen short). The amount often takes the place of okane. As a general state, okane tarinai means money's tight.
newEntries.verbSense: not be enough (negative of tariru, be enough)
newEntries.trap: Not okane ga sukunai, which is having little money in general. Being short for something is tarinai (not enough): gohyaku en tarinai.
partners: ninzuu (headcount: ninzuu tarinai = we're a person short)

example.ja: ごめん、お金足りないから貸して。
example.english: Sorry, I'm short. Can you lend me some?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, okane ga tarinai node kashite moraemasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、お金が足りないので貸してもらえませんか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm short. Could you lend me some?

newEntries.freqNote: 足りる #764 pools its forms; 足りない also has its own entry at #3974. お金 #422.
newEntries.notes: okane nai is being broke; tarinai is being short for something. Enough is tariru: kore de tariru? (will this cover it?).

newEntries.use: Said about cooking, chores and paperwork that eat up effort: kore, kekkou tema kakaru n da yo. Before a noun, ga becomes no: tema no kakaru ryouri (a fiddly dish).
newEntries.verbSense: be hung on or applied; of time, money or effort: be needed, be used up
newEntries.trap: English 'it takes a lot of effort' leads to doryoku, which is effort as in trying hard. A chore that's fiddly or slow is tema ga kakaru, with the same kakaru as jikan ga kakaru.

example.romaji: kono ryouri, kekkou tema kakaru n da.
example.ja: この料理、けっこう手間かかるんだ。
example.english: This dish takes quite a bit of work.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ryouri wa kekkou tema ga kakaru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: この料理はけっこう手間がかかるんです。
examplePolite.english: This dish takes quite a bit of work.

newEntries.freqNote: 手間 #4541; かかる #385 is the kana form across all senses. Phrase entry 手間をかける #19815; no entry for 手間がかかる. Pair counts: ga kakaru 18, o kakeru 40 (films over-count kakesaseru plot lines); kakaru leads here because daily talk about chores and cooking uses it.
newEntries.notes: tema o kakeru is going to the trouble on purpose: tema kakete tsukutta. Apologising for someone's trouble: otesuu o okake shimashita.

newEntries.use: Said to kids (chanto junban matte ne) and as a pointed remark to someone pushing in: minna junban matteru n desu kedo. The noun junban machi is common too (ima sanjuppun junban machi da tte), and when your turn comes it's junban ga kita, or just ban: tsugi, dare no ban?
newEntries.verbSense: wait

example.ja: ちゃんと順番待ってね。
example.english: Wait your turn, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: chanto junban o matte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちゃんと順番を待ってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please wait your turn.

newEntries.freqNote: 順番 #3213; 待つ #71; 番 ban #1055. Pair count 15; the noun 順番待ち adds 8.
newEntries.notes: Pushing in is warikomi: warikomi shinaide.

newEntries.use: Said about the point cards and apps at konbini, drugstores and supermarkets: itsumo koko de pointo tameteru. At the till staff ask pointo kaado omochi desu ka? (do you have a points card?).
newEntries.verbSense: let something build up; store up

example.romaji: itsumo koko de pointo tameteru n da.
example.ja: いつもここでポイント貯めてるんだ。
example.english: I always collect points here.

examplePolite.romaji: itsumo koko de pointo o tameteru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: いつもここでポイントを貯めてるんです。
examplePolite.english: I always collect points here.

newEntries.freqNote: ポイント #2464 counts every 'point' (score, main point). 貯める #10930 is the saving spelling; the kana ためる #3410 covers every sense. No count in the subtitles; commonness is judged from how often point cards come up at Japanese tills.
newEntries.notes: Same verb as okane o tameru; kasegu is for racking points up fast (poikatsu de pointo kasegu). pointo ga tsuku = points get added; to spend them, staff ask pointo otsukai ni narimasu ka? (hai, tsukaimasu).

newEntries.use: Said when promising to fit someone in, often in the potential: raishuu nara jikan tsukureru yo. In thanks it's jikan tsukutte kurete arigatou.
newEntries.verbSense: make; create

example.ja: 来週なら時間作れるよ。
example.english: I can make time next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu nara jikan o tsukuremasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 来週なら時間を作れますよ。
examplePolite.english: I can make time next week.

newEntries.freqNote: 作る #146 covers every sense of make and cook. Phrase entry 時間を作る #16575. Pair count 52.
newEntries.notes: Close to jikan o toru: tsukuru stresses squeezing time out of a busy schedule. Both work in thanks (jikan tsukutte kurete arigatou / jikan totte kurete arigatou).

newEntries.use: Said in class, interviews and arguments, often as a demand (chanto shitsumon ni kotaete) or a refusal (sono shitsumon ni wa kotaerarenai). The ni almost always stays.
newEntries.verbSense: answer, reply
newEntries.trap: English 'answer the question' has a direct object, which tempts shitsumon o kotaeru. In Japanese you answer to a question: shitsumon ni kotaeru. Answering the phone is a different verb: denwa ni deru.

example.ja: その質問には答えられない。
example.english: I can't answer that question.

examplePolite.romaji: sono shitsumon ni wa kotaeraremasen.
examplePolite.ja: その質問には答えられません。
examplePolite.english: I can't answer that question.

newEntries.freqNote: The whole phrase 質問に答える has its own entry in the drama list at #6167 (質問 #1058, 答える #646). In the subtitles 362 of 367 hits keep ni.
newEntries.notes: Asking is shitsumon suru or just kiku; the answer itself is kotae (kotae wa?).

newEntries.use: Said in job talk and about life, usually with what kind before it: baito no keiken aru? Casual speech drops ga, and the negative keiken nai (I've never done it) is common too.
newEntries.verbSense: there is; have (things, a background)
newEntries.trap: 'Have experience' tempts keiken o motteru, which sounds like a CV. Experience exists: keiken aru? For one thing you've done once, -ta koto aru is more natural: itta koto aru?
partners: buranku (a gap in your work history: buranku ga aru)

example.romaji: kou iu shigoto no keiken aru?
example.ja: こういう仕事の経験ある？
example.english: Have you done this kind of work before?

examplePolite.romaji: kou iu shigoto no keiken wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: こういう仕事の経験はありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have experience with this kind of work?

newEntries.freqNote: 経験 #1077, ある #21. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 経験 + ある has 231 hits (133 with ga, 39 with no particle); 経験 + ない has 117; 経験 + 持つ only 16.
newEntries.notes: After a trip or a hard time: ii keiken ni natta (it was a good experience).

newEntries.use: Said when explaining your schedule or why you can't talk: kore kara kaigi aru kara. Casual speech drops ga, and smaller team or client meetings are uchiawase, with the same verb.
newEntries.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)
newEntries.trap: 'Have a meeting' tempts kaigi o motsu, which only works as stiff 'hold a meeting' (the everyday 'hold' is kaigi o hiraku). A meeting on your calendar just exists: kaigi ga aru. Attending is kaigi ni deru; kaigi o deru is leaving the room.

example.romaji: gomen, kore kara kaigi aru n da.
example.ja: ごめん、これから会議あるんだ。
example.english: Sorry, I've got a meeting now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kore kara kaigi ga aru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、これから会議があるんです。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I've got a meeting now.

newEntries.freqNote: 会議 #1612, ある #21, 打ち合わせ uchiawase #2320. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 80 of 81 hits keep ga; 会議 + 開く has 23.
newEntries.notes: Someone in one right now is kaigi-chuu: ima kaigi-chuu desu.

newEntries.english: have good grades, do well at school
newEntries.use: Said about kids, classmates and students, often as praise: seiseki ii ne, usually without ga. About yourself it sounds like bragging, so people say seiseki agatta (my grades went up) or play it down: seiseki yokunai.
newEntries.verbSense: ii: good
newEntries.trap: 'Get good grades' pushes toward a verb (ii seiseki o morau). Japanese describes the grades: seiseki ga ii. ii seiseki o toru also works for one term or exam.

example.romaji: otouto, seiseki ii n da yo.
example.ja: 弟、成績いいんだよ。
example.english: My little brother gets good grades.

examplePolite.romaji: otouto wa seiseki ga ii n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 弟は成績がいいんですよ。
examplePolite.english: My little brother gets good grades.

newEntries.freqNote: 成績 #3011, いい #24. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 30% of everything said with 成績 goes to いい/良い (32 hits: 15 of them ii seiseki before the noun, 10 with ga); 成績 + 悪い has 6.
newEntries.notes: ii conjugates from yoi: seiseki yokatta (past), yokunai (not good). The opposite is seiseki ga warui; falling grades are seiseki ga sagaru.

newEntries.use: The standard reason for cancelling: kyuu ni shigoto haitchatta (work came up suddenly). Mostly in the past, or as haitteru (I've got work booked); ga is usually dropped.
newEntries.verbSense: go in, enter; get put into something

example.ja: ごめん、急に仕事入っちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, something came up at work.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kyuu ni shigoto ga haitchaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、急に仕事が入っちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, something came up at work.

newEntries.freqNote: 仕事 #134, 入る #115. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 18 of 30 hits keep ga.
newEntries.notes: Same frame as yotei ga hairu (see there for why not okiru). Freelancers and shops also use it for work coming in: atarashii shigoto ga haitta, yoyaku ga haitta.

newEntries.use: Said about test results, almost always with the number fused to ten: hyakuten totta, ii ten toreta (I managed a good score). Casual speech often drops o, and in sport it means scoring.

newEntries.trap: 'Get a hundred' tempts morau, which only fits a mark someone awards you (sensei ni hyakuten moratta). A score you earn on a test is taken: hyakuten totta. This is the toru that English 'take an exam' wrongly points to; the exam itself is shiken o ukeru.

newEntries.use: Said about breaks at work or while studying, especially the ones you're owed: chanto kyuukei totte ne, juppun kyuukei torou. Casual speech drops o, and for calling a break on the spot kyuukei shiyou or chotto yasumou is more common.

newEntries.trap: 'Take a break' tempts yasumi o toru, which means time off or proper rest (chanto yasumi totte ne). A few minutes' break is kyuukei: kyuukei torou.

newEntries.verbSense: busy (a person, their work or schedule)
newEntries.trap: English 'busy' also covers crowds and phone lines. A shop packed with customers, from the customer's side, is konderu (mise ga komu); mise ga isogashii is how the staff put it. A busy phone line is hanashi-chuu.

newEntries.use: Said about performance at work, in sport or in study, often as a must: kekka dasanai to (I need to show results). Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: put out, take out, send out; here: produce
newEntries.trap: 'Get results' tempts kekka o morau. Results you achieve are put out: kekka o dasu. Results being announced is kekka ga deru, and kekka o morau only fits being handed a results sheet.

newEntries.use: Heard at the bank, the city office, at work and for deliveries: koko ni hanko oshite kudasai. Casual speech drops o; for deliveries a signature usually works too: sain de ii desu ka?
newEntries.verbSense: push, press

newEntries.use: Said when explaining plans or turning things down: raishuu shiken aru kara muri. Casual speech drops ga, and for school tests students say tesuto more than shiken.
newEntries.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)
newEntries.trap: 'Have an exam' tempts shiken o motsu. An exam on your calendar exists: shiken ga aru. Sitting it is shiken o ukeru.

newEntries.use: The usual way to share or ask job news, almost always in the past: atarashii shigoto mitsukatta? Casual speech drops ga, and mada mitsukaranai means you're still looking.

nimotsu (bags: nimotsu mitete = watch my bags)
mise (the shop: mise mitete = mind the shop)

newEntries.use: Mostly the request namae oshiete (what's your name?), a friendly alternative to onamae wa? or namae nante iu no?. The same oshieru asks for any personal details: bangou oshiete (give me your number).
