examplePolite.english: We had a baby last week.

newEntries.freqNote: 子供 #589 (子ども #2264 separate); 生まれる #534 (産まれる #6622 separate). 赤ちゃん #2204.
newEntries.notes: Your own birth takes the same verb: toukyou de umareta (I was born in Tokyo).

newEntries.use: A stock grumble about bosses, principals and relatives: buchou no hanashi nagai n da yo (my boss goes on forever), with ga dropped. Before a noun it becomes nagai hanashi (a long talk), and 'it's a long story' is hanaseba nagaku naru.
newEntries.verbSense: long (length or time)
partners: denwa (phone calls: denwa nagai = always on the phone for ages)
ofuro (baths: ofuro nagai ne = you take long baths)

example.romaji: buchou no hanashi, honto nagai yo ne.
example.ja: 部長の話、ほんと長いよね。
example.english: The boss's talks go on forever, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: buchou no hanashi wa hontou ni nagai desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 部長の話は本当に長いですよね。
examplePolite.english: The manager's talks really do go on, don't they.

newEntries.freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; 長い #467. Only about 10 of the 73 pair hits are the predicate hanashi ga nagai (63 are nagai hanashi); an everyday grumble that films under-count. 長話 (nagabanashi) #29859.
newEntries.notes: nagabanashi = a long chat: nagabanashi shichatte gomen (sorry for keeping you). Someone who just talks a lot is oshaberi, or yoku shaberu.

newEntries.use: The everyday way to ask or report whether someone got in touch: renraku kita? (did they get in touch?), mada renraku konai (still nothing from them), with ga dropped. The sender takes kara: kare kara renraku kita.
newEntries.verbSense: come, arrive
newEntries.trap: English 'hear from him' leads to kare kara kiku, which means being told something by him. Getting a message or call from him is kare kara renraku ga kita. renraku o morau also works, but kita is what you hear most.

example.ja: 彼からまだ連絡来ない。
example.english: I still haven't heard from him.

examplePolite.romaji: kare kara mada renraku ga kimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 彼からまだ連絡が来ません。
examplePolite.english: I still haven't heard from him.

newEntries.freqNote: 連絡 #326; 来る #52 counts all coming (kana くる #429 is mostly -te kuru). No phrase entry. Written 連絡が来 37, 連絡がき 6, 連絡来 2.
newEntries.notes: renraku kitara oshiete = let me know if you hear from them.

newEntries.use: Said by the one giving support, as an offer (nanka attara soudan ni noru yo) or a request (chotto soudan notte kurenai? = can I run something by you?). It means listening and helping think it through, not just telling someone what to do.
newEntries.verbSense: ride, get on; here, get on board with someone's problem
newEntries.trap: English 'give advice' leads to adobaisu suru, which is fine for passing on tips. Offering to hear someone out and help them think it through is soudan ni noru, and asking for that is soudan suru.

example.ja: いつでも相談に乗るよ。
example.english: I'm always here if you need to talk.

examplePolite.romaji: itsudemo soudan ni norimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いつでも相談に乗りますよ。
examplePolite.english: I'm happy to help anytime.

newEntries.freqNote: 相談 #560; 乗る #439 (載る #2368 is a different verb). Phrase entry 相談に乗る #3754, high for a phrase.
newEntries.notes: The asker opens with soudan ga aru n da kedo, or says senpai ni soudan shita (I went to my senpai for advice). noru also means go along with: sono hanashi noru (I'm in), sasoi ni noru (take someone up on an offer).

newEntries.use: The everyday way to say what you're doing on a day off: kyou wa tomodachi ni au (I'm seeing a friend today). tomodachi to au is also heard and stresses a meet-up you both arranged; asobu (hang out) is the other weekend verb.
newEntries.verbSense: meet, see (a person)
newEntries.trap: English 'meet a friend' or 'see a friend' leads to tomodachi o au or tomodachi o miru. People you meet take ni or to (tomodachi ni au, tomodachi to au), and miru with a person means watching or minding them (kodomo mitete = keep an eye on the kids).

example.romaji: ashita tomodachi ni au n da.
example.ja: 明日友達に会うんだ。
example.english: I'm seeing a friend tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa tomodachi ni au n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は友達に会うんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm meeting a friend tomorrow.

newEntries.freqNote: 友達 #405; 会う #110 (合う #563 is 'fit, match'). Written 友達に会 37 vs 友達と会 6.
newEntries.notes: Bumping into a friend by chance is also au: eki de guuzen atta.

newEntries.english: make fun of, look down on
newEntries.use: Heard most in protest: baka ni shinaide (don't make fun of me), baka ni shiteru no? (are you mocking me?), and in the passive, baka ni sareta (they made fun of me). It covers both mocking and treating someone as stupid.
newEntries.verbSense: do; with X ni, treat as or make into X
newEntries.trap: English 'make fun of' leads to karakau, which is right for playful teasing but too light for contempt. Mocking someone or treating them as stupid is baka ni suru.
partners: nakamahazure (leaving someone out: nakamahazure ni sareta)

example.ja: バカにしないでよ。
example.english: Don't make fun of me.

examplePolite.romaji: baka ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: バカにしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't make fun of me.

newEntries.freqNote: nounRank is katakana バカ #433 (ばか #2695, 馬鹿 #6994). Phrase entry バカにする #1657, high for a phrase (馬鹿にする #14581). The pair count (39, mostly を) is baka o suru 'do something stupid', not this set; written バカに/馬鹿に/ばかに + する forms (incl. sareta): about 524 hits.
newEntries.notes: baka ni dekinai = not to be underestimated: konbini no bentou, baka ni dekinai yo.

newEntries.use: Two everyday uses: honne o iu to... opens a frank admission (to be honest...), and honne itte yo asks someone to drop the politeness and tell you straight. honne is the real feeling behind tatemae, the polite surface.
newEntries.verbSense: say

example.romaji: honne o iu to, chotto iya da na.
example.ja: 本音を言うと、ちょっと嫌だな。
example.english: To be honest, I'm not too keen.

examplePolite.romaji: honne o iu to, chotto iya na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 本音を言うと、ちょっと嫌なんです。
examplePolite.english: To be honest, I'd rather not.

newEntries.freqNote: 本音 #3070; 言う #28. Phrase entry 本音を言う #14580; 建前 (tatemae) #19759. Written 本音を言 31.
newEntries.notes: honne to tatemae (real feelings vs the polite front) is a pair every Japanese person knows; shoujiki ni iu to also means 'to be honest'.

newEntries.use: Used about parenting as a whole: hitori de kodomo o sodateta (she raised her kids alone), kodomo sodateru no tte taihen da yo. Everyday talk often uses the noun kosodate (parenting) instead: ima kosodate chuu (I'm busy raising kids).
newEntries.verbSense: raise, bring up, grow (children, plants, juniors)
partners: buka (subordinates: buka o sodateru = bring your team on)

example.romaji: kodomo sodateru no tte taihen da yo ne.
example.ja: 子供育てるのって大変だよね。
example.english: Raising kids is tough, isn't it.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo o sodateru no wa taihen desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 子供を育てるのは大変ですよね。
examplePolite.english: Raising children is hard work, isn't it.

newEntries.freqNote: 子供 #589; 育てる #894. 子育て (kosodate) #4148; 育つ #1371.
newEntries.notes: sodatsu is the intransitive side: inaka de sodatta (I grew up in the countryside). Having a dog is inu o kau; inu o sodateru is only raising one from a puppy.

newEntries.use: Mostly heard as the caring question nanka nayami aru no? (is something bothering you?) or the offer nayami ga aru nara kiku yo (if something's on your mind, I'll listen). nayamigoto means the same, and koi no nayami is love trouble.
newEntries.verbSense: there is; have (things, problems, something to bring up)

example.ja: なんか悩みあるの？
example.english: Is something bothering you?

examplePolite.romaji: nanika nayami demo aru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何か悩みでもあるんですか？
examplePolite.english: Is something on your mind?

newEntries.freqNote: 悩み #2043; ある #21. 悩み事 (nayamigoto) #9993. Written 悩みがあ 16.
newEntries.notes: The verb nayamu means to agonise or be torn: dotchi ni suru ka nayanderu (I can't decide which). shinpai is worrying about what might happen; nayami is a problem you keep turning over. nayami o motsu and nayami o kakaeru (be carrying worries) say the same in a more written style.

newEntries.use: Venting about work, family or your lot, usually to a friend over a drink: guchi itte gomen (sorry for moaning), guchi bakkari (always moaning). The listener's side is guchi o kiku (guchi nara kiku yo), and guchiru is the one-word casual verb. monku o iu is objecting to someone or something; guchi is letting off steam about your situation.
newEntries.verbSense: say

example.ja: ごめん、愚痴ばっかり言って。
example.english: Sorry, all I do is moan.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, guchi bakari itte shimatte.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、愚痴ばかり言ってしまって。
examplePolite.english: Sorry for complaining so much.

newEntries.freqNote: 愚痴 #4194; 言う #28. The verb 愚痴る (guchiru) #10411. 愚痴 appears 68 times in the subtitles, 愚痴を言 7.
newEntries.notes: guchi o kobosu means the same and sounds a little more literary.

newEntries.use: The holiday question and answer: oshougatsu wa jikka ni kaeru? (going home for New Year?), obon wa jikka kaeru yo. It takes kaeru because it's a return, even after years of living away.
newEntries.verbSense: go back to where you belong (home, your country)
newEntries.trap: English 'go to my parents' place' leads to oya no uchi ni iku, which sounds like a visit. The home you grew up in is jikka, and you kaeru to it. Your spouse's family home takes iku: tsuma no jikka ni iku.
partners: inaka (your home region in the country)

example.romaji: oshougatsu wa jikka ni kaeru no?
example.ja: お正月は実家に帰るの？
example.english: Are you going home for New Year?

examplePolite.romaji: oshougatsu wa jikka ni kaerimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お正月は実家に帰りますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you going back to your family's for New Year?

newEntries.freqNote: 実家 #1109; 帰る #101 (変える #450 is 'change'). 里帰り (satogaeri) #15496. Written 実家に帰 17.
newEntries.notes: satogaeri = a trip back to your family home, also a mother-to-be going home to give birth.

newEntries.use: The offer at the end of an evening is okutteku yo (I'll walk or drive you home), often without naming the place, and the thanks is okutte kurete arigatou. made marks how far you go: eki made okuru (see someone to the station). The one taken home says uchi, their own home: uchi made okutte kureta (they saw me home).
newEntries.verbSense: send; also see someone off or take them somewhere
newEntries.trap: English 'take you home' leads to tsurete iku, which sounds like leading someone who can't go alone (a child, a drunk friend). Seeing someone home as a courtesy, on foot or by car, is okuru: okutteku yo.
partners: genkan (the front door: genkan made okuru = see someone to the door)

example.romaji: osoi kara, ie made okutteku yo.
example.ja: 遅いから、家まで送ってくよ。
example.english: It's late, I'll see you home.

examplePolite.romaji: osoi node, ie made okurimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 遅いので、家まで送りますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's late, so I'll take you home.

newEntries.freqNote: Noun is 家 (ie) #152. 送る #324 also counts sending things; 見送る (miokuru) #3407. Written 家まで送 109, うちまで送 1; 送ってく 384 vs 送っていく 29. The pair counter does not see made, so there is no measured count.
newEntries.notes: miokuru is seeing someone off at the door, station or airport.

newEntries.use: Mostly in the negative, the stock complaint deai ga nai (I never meet anyone), and in good wishes: ii deai ga arimasu you ni (hope you meet someone great). Often about romance, but it also covers new friends at a new job or school.
newEntries.verbSense: there is; have (events, chances)
newEntries.trap: English 'I never meet anyone' leads to dare ni mo awanai, which sounds like you never see people at all. Meeting someone new is talked about as a deai (an encounter): deai ga nai.

example.romaji: shokuba ni zenzen deai nai n da yo.
example.ja: 職場に全然出会いないんだよ。
example.english: I never meet anyone at work.

examplePolite.romaji: shokuba ni wa zenzen deai ga nai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 職場には全然出会いがないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I never get to meet anyone at work.

newEntries.freqNote: 出会い #1993; ある #21. The verb 出会う (deau) #608. Written 出会いがあ 15, 出会い(が)な 11.
newEntries.notes: deau is the verb, for meeting for the first time or by chance: daigaku de deatta (we met at uni).

newEntries.use: Said about two people or groups (ano futari, naka warui no?), or with to for you and someone: oya to naka warui n da (I don't get on with my parents). Falling out is naka ga waruku naru, and plain 'not close' is often softened to amari naka yokunai.
newEntries.verbSense: bad (adjective; past warukatta)
partners: aishou (compatibility: aishou ga warui = we just don't click)

example.ja: あの二人、仲悪いの？
example.english: Do those two not get along?

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari wa naka ga warui n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの二人は仲が悪いんですか？
examplePolite.english: Are those two on bad terms?

newEntries.freqNote: 仲 #1305; 悪い #139. Phrase entry 仲が悪い #13246; 仲良く #1816. Written 仲が悪 18, 仲悪 7.
newEntries.notes: The opposite of naka ga ii. kenka shiteru (they've fallen out) is a current fight; naka ga warui is the lasting state.

newEntries.use: Opens a talk about something you need help deciding, and usually trails off: chotto soudan ga aru n da kedo... ga is usually kept, as with hanashi ga aru and onegai ga aru, though soudan aru n da kedo is heard too.
newEntries.verbSense: there is; have (things, plans, something to bring up)
newEntries.trap: soudan sounds like a formal 'consultation', but it's the everyday word for running something by a friend. 'Can I ask your advice?' is chotto soudan ga aru n da kedo; adobaisu kudasai sounds abrupt.

example.romaji: chotto soudan ga aru n da kedo, ii?
example.ja: ちょっと相談があるんだけど、いい？
example.english: Can I ask your advice about something?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto soudan ga aru n desu kedo, ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと相談があるんですけど、いいですか？
examplePolite.english: Could I ask your advice about something?

newEntries.freqNote: 相談 #560 counts every soudan use (soudan suru, soudan ni noru); ある #21. No phrase entry. Written 相談があ 18.
newEntries.notes: The listener answers un, nani? or ii yo, soudan noru yo (sure, I'm listening).

newEntries.kana: たんじょうびをいわう
newEntries.use: Mostly about others doing it for or with you: minna ga tanjoubi iwatte kureta (everyone celebrated my birthday), or planning: kanojo no tanjoubi, dou iwaou? The greeting itself is tanjoubi omedetou.
newEntries.verbSense: celebrate, mark a happy occasion

example.romaji: minna ga tanjoubi iwatte kureta n da.
example.ja: みんなが誕生日祝ってくれたんだ。
example.english: Everyone celebrated my birthday for me.

examplePolite.romaji: minna ga tanjoubi o iwatte kureta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: みんなが誕生日を祝ってくれたんです。
examplePolite.english: Everyone celebrated my birthday.

newEntries.freqNote: 誕生日 #1370; 祝う #3023. お祝い (oiwai) #1674 is more frequent than the verb. Written 誕生日(を)祝 18 hits; the pair counter misses it.
newEntries.notes: oiwai suru is the softer noun form: tanjoubi no oiwai shiyou (let's do something for the birthday).

newEntries.use: Mostly heard as the offer to drop it: keigo tsukawanakute ii yo (no need to be formal with me), often followed by tameguchi de ii yo (talk to me casually). Also for describing relationships: senpai ni wa keigo tsukau (I speak politely to my seniors).
newEntries.verbSense: use
newEntries.trap: English 'speak keigo' leads to keigo o hanasu, on the model of nihongo o hanasu. It is heard (keigo ga hanasenai), but the everyday verb is tsukau (keigo tsukau), or keigo de hanasu.
partners: kotoba (words: warui kotoba o tsukau = use bad language)
eigo (English: eigo o tsukau shigoto = a job using English)

example.ja: 敬語使わなくていいよ。
example.english: No need to be formal with me.

examplePolite.romaji: keigo wa tsukawanakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 敬語は使わなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to speak formally with me.

newEntries.freqNote: 敬語 #6169 (警護 'guard' is listed separately, #8020); 使う #171. タメ口 (tameguchi) #10671. 敬語 appears only 18 times in the subtitles (敬語(を)使 once), so commonness is judged.
newEntries.notes: Sounds like ki tsukawanakute ii yo (don't go to any trouble), the other host line; drill them together.

newEntries.use: Said about hiking up a mountain as much as real climbing, often in the past or as an experience: fujisan nobotta koto aru? The mountain usually takes ni (o is also heard), and casual speech sometimes drops it. The hobby itself is yama nobori (mountain climbing).
newEntries.verbSense: climb, go up (mountains, trees, stairs)
newEntries.trap: English 'climb' takes a direct object, so learners default to yama o noboru. That is fine too, mostly when the way up is the point (kewashii yama o nobotta, climbed a steep mountain), but for having climbed a mountain ni is about three times as common: fujisan ni nobotta.

example.romaji: shuumatsu, tomodachi to yama ni nobotta.
example.ja: 週末、友達と山に登った。
example.english: I climbed a mountain with friends at the weekend.

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu, tomodachi to yama ni noborimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 週末、友達と山に登りました。
examplePolite.english: I climbed a mountain with friends at the weekend.

newEntries.freqNote: 登る #3936. The subtitle count files 山に登る under the other spelling 上る (#3537, used for stairs and slopes): 43 hits, ni 26 and o 9. The hobby nouns are 山登り #17609 (26 in the subtitles) and 登山 #14277.
newEntries.notes: An easy walk in the hills is haikingu; climbing as a hobby is yama nobori or tozan (shumi wa tozan desu).

newEntries.english: get some exercise, move your body
newEntries.use: The everyday way to talk about getting exercise, often as something you should do: tama ni wa karada ugokasanakya. Casual speech usually drops o, and karada ugokasu no ga suki means you like being active.
newEntries.verbSense: move something, set it in motion (the transitive of ugoku)
newEntries.trap: Not karada o ugoku. ugoku is the intransitive 'move' (karada ga ugokanai = I can't move), and only ugokasu takes o.

example.ja: たまには体動かさなきゃ。
example.english: I need to get some exercise now and then.

examplePolite.romaji: tama ni wa karada o ugokasanakya ikemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: たまには体を動かさなきゃいけませんね。
examplePolite.english: I really should get some exercise now and then.

newEntries.freqNote: The whole phrase 体を動かす has its own entry at #13082. 運動 (undou, exercise) is #3290.
newEntries.notes: undou suru is the general word for exercise, from sport to the gym (undou busoku = not enough exercise); karada o ugokasu covers any getting moving, from a walk to cleaning.

newEntries.use: Said about fishing trips, as plans or as a habit. Casual speech often drops ni (tsuri iku?), and tsuri itteru means someone is out fishing now, not on their way.
newEntries.verbSense: go (tsuri is the noun of tsuru, catch on a line)

example.romaji: yasumi no hi wa, yoku tsuri ni iku.
example.ja: 休みの日は、よく釣りに行く。
example.english: I often go fishing on my days off.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumi no hi wa, yoku tsuri ni ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 休みの日は、よく釣りに行きます。
examplePolite.english: I often go fishing on my days off.

newEntries.freqNote: The whole phrase 釣りに行く has its own entry at #18346. The verb 釣る (catch on a line) is #3657.
newEntries.notes: A fish on the line is tsureru: nanka tsureta? (catch anything?). tsukamaeru is catching something that could get away, like a bug or a thief, so it fits a fish caught by hand or net, not on a rod.

newEntries.use: Said about lessons with a teacher, now or as a child: piano naratteru (I take lessons), naratteta (I used to). Casual speech drops o. Childhood lessons like this are a standard getting-to-know-you topic.
newEntries.verbSense: learn from a teacher, take lessons in
newEntries.trap: English 'learn' leads to benkyou suru, but piano o benkyou shita sounds like studying it as a subject. Lessons with a teacher are narau: piano naratteta. oboeru is memorising or picking something up yourself (shigoto oboeta = I've learned the job).

example.ja: 小さい頃、ピアノ習ってた。
example.english: I took piano lessons when I was little.

examplePolite.romaji: chiisai koro, piano o narattemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 小さい頃、ピアノを習ってました。
examplePolite.english: I took piano lessons when I was little.

newEntries.freqNote: 習い事 (naraigoto, lessons taken as a hobby) #15541. 弾く (hiku, play the piano) is #5832.
newEntries.notes: The teacher's side is oshieru (piano o oshiete iru); after-school lessons like this are called naraigoto.

newEntries.english: go out for fun; go visit
newEntries.use: Covers a fun day or night out and a visit to someone's home: shuumatsu shibuya ni asobi ni itta, tomodachi no uchi ni asobi ni iku. Casual speech often drops ni (asobi iku?). The mirror image, kondo asobi ni kite, is the standard 'come over sometime'.
newEntries.verbSense: go (asobi is the noun of asobu, have fun, hang out)
newEntries.trap: English 'play' makes asobu sound childish, but adults say asobi ni iku all the time for a fun outing or a visit to a friend's place. And 'I'll come and visit' is asobi ni iku, not asobi ni kuru: as with mukae ni iku, you are the one going.
partners: omimai (visiting someone sick: omimai ni iku)
aisatsu (dropping by to say hello: aisatsu ni iku)

example.ja: 今度、遊びに行くね！
example.english: I'll come and visit sometime!

examplePolite.romaji: kondo, asobi ni ikimasu ne!
examplePolite.ja: 今度、遊びに行きますね！
examplePolite.english: I'll come and visit sometime!

newEntries.freqNote: The whole phrase 遊びに行く has its own entry at #4009 and 遊びに来る (come over) at #3038; the verb 遊ぶ is #674. The tokenizer tags 遊び as a verb stem, so the pair count is only 11, but the written form 遊びに行 counts 47, and 遊びに来 outnumbers it at 64 (asobi ni kite alone 33).
newEntries.notes: Among friends kondo asobou (let's hang out sometime) is the plain invitation, often a friendly maybe rather than a fixed plan.

newEntries.use: Said when popping out for a walk, often as chotto sanpo itte kuru (I'm off for a little walk). Casual speech drops ni. sanpo suru puts the focus on the walk itself and takes the place you walk through with o: kouen o sanpo shita.
newEntries.verbSense: go; with an activity noun + ni, go out to do it
newEntries.trap: Not sanpo o toru, copied from 'take a walk': you go on one (sanpo ni iku) or just do one (sanpo suru). With a dog it is inu no sanpo ni iku, never inu o aruku.

example.ja: ちょっと散歩行ってくるね。
example.english: I'm just popping out for a walk.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto sanpo ni itte kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと散歩に行ってきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'm just going out for a walk.

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. The pair count is 52 (ni 46). The written form 散歩に行 counts 43 against 133 for all forms of sanpo suru, which is the more frequent verb but a plain noun + suru; ni iku is the set built on the noun.
newEntries.notes: Walking the dog is inu no sanpo (ni iku); aimless wandering about town is burabura suru.

newEntries.use: The spring outing everyone talks about: ohanami ikou, ohanami itta? Casual speech drops ni. It is mostly a picnic under the cherry trees with food and drinks, not just looking. Plain hanami is heard mostly in compounds like hanami kyaku (blossom-viewing crowds).
newEntries.verbSense: go (hanami = hana 'flowers' + mi 'viewing', here with polite o-)

example.romaji: raishuu, minna de ohanami ikou yo.
example.ja: 来週、みんなでお花見行こうよ。
example.english: Let's all go see the cherry blossoms next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu, minna de ohanami ni ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 来週、みんなでお花見に行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's all go cherry-blossom viewing next week.

newEntries.freqNote: 花見 #10548; お花見, the form you hear most, has no entry of its own. Films barely mention it (7 lines, 4 of them お花見), but it is a fixture of every Japanese spring.
newEntries.notes: The blossoms coming out is sakura ga saku, and full bloom is mankai.

newEntries.use: Usually a plan or an invitation (karaoke ikanai?), often as the second stop after dinner. Casual speech drops ni: karaoke iku.
newEntries.verbSense: go; with an activity noun + ni, go out to do it
newEntries.trap: karaoke is where you sing, so the usual phrasing is karaoke de utau, karaoke suru, or just karaoke iku. karaoke o utau, copied from 'sing karaoke', is heard but sounds off to many speakers.

example.ja: 昨日カラオケ行って、声枯れた。
example.english: Went to karaoke yesterday and lost my voice.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou karaoke ni itte, koe ga karemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日カラオケに行って、声が枯れました。
examplePolite.english: I went to karaoke yesterday and lost my voice.

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. Films mention karaoke only 39 times, so the pair count (4) says little; in Japan it is an everyday night out.
newEntries.notes: At a work do, karaoke is the classic nijikai (second stop); going alone is hitori karaoke, or the slang hitokara.

newEntries.kana: きぶんてんかんになる
newEntries.english: be a nice change of pace, do someone good
newEntries.use: Said to encourage someone or about something that helped: ii kibun tenkan ni naru yo (it'll do you good), ii kibun tenkan ni natta. It often comes with ii. kibun tenkan ni alone means 'for a change': kibun tenkan ni sanpo shite kuru.
newEntries.verbSense: become, turn into
partners: kibarashi (taking your mind off something: ii kibarashi ni natta)

example.romaji: issho ni ikou yo, ii kibun tenkan ni naru yo.
example.ja: 一緒に行こうよ、いい気分転換になるよ。
example.english: Come with us, it'll be a nice change of pace.

examplePolite.romaji: issho ni ikimashou yo, ii kibun tenkan ni narimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きましょうよ、いい気分転換になりますよ。
examplePolite.english: Do come along, it'll be a nice change of pace.

newEntries.freqNote: 気分転換 #5393 ranks above 気晴らし #8089 in the drama list. The tokenizer splits 気分転換, so there is no pair count; in the subtitles the written forms are 気分転換 85 and 気晴らし 120, with 気分転換になる and 気晴らしになる 9 each.
newEntries.notes: kibarashi works the same way and is about as common in films; it leans to taking your mind off something bad: ii kibarashi ni natta, kibarashi ni sanpo suru. iya na koto o wasureru (forget your troubles) is another natural way to say it.

newEntries.use: Said about camping trips, often family or summer ones. Casual speech drops ni (kyanpu iku?), and being at the campsite is kyanpu shiteru.
newEntries.verbSense: go; with an activity noun + ni, go out to do it
newEntries.trap: Not kyanpingu ni iku: the activity is kyanpu, and kyanpingu turns up mainly in compounds like kyanpingu kaa (camper van).

example.romaji: natsuyasumi, kazoku de kyanpu ni itta.
example.ja: 夏休み、家族でキャンプに行った。
example.english: We went camping as a family over the summer break.

examplePolite.romaji: natsuyasumi, kazoku de kyanpu ni ikimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 夏休み、家族でキャンプに行きました。
examplePolite.english: We went camping as a family over the summer break.

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. In the subtitles キャンプ is often a military or summer camp, so the count (53) mixes senses.

newEntries.use: Said about going to the cinema, usually as a plan or an invitation: eiga ikanai? Casual speech drops ni. eiga mi ni iku says the same with the watching spelled out; at home it is just eiga o miru.
newEntries.verbSense: go; with an event noun + ni, go out to see it

example.ja: 週末、映画行かない？
example.english: Want to go to a movie this weekend?

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu, eiga ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末、映画に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go to a movie this weekend?

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. In the subtitles 映画に行 (24) is more common than 映画を見に (14).
newEntries.notes: eigakan is the building: eigakan de mita (I saw it at the cinema).

newEntries.english: make the year's first shrine visit
newEntries.use: Asked by everyone in early January: hatsumoude itta? It means the year's first visit to a shrine or temple, usually in the first few days of the year. Casual speech drops ni.
newEntries.verbSense: go (hatsumoude = hatsu 'first' + moude 'visit to a shrine')
newEntries.trap: 'Visit' pulls toward houmon suru, which is a formal call on a person or company. Visiting a shrine is just going: hatsumoude ni iku, or on other days jinja ni omairi ni iku. hatsumoude suru (hatsumoude shita?) is also fine.

example.ja: 初詣、もう行った？
example.english: Been to the shrine for New Year yet?

examplePolite.romaji: hatsumoude ni wa mou ikimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 初詣にはもう行きましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you made your New Year shrine visit yet?

newEntries.freqNote: 初詣 #22266 never appears in the film subtitles, yet hatsumoude itta? is one of the most-asked questions of early January.
newEntries.notes: At the shrine most people also draw a fortune: omikuji o hiku.

newEntries.use: Said at shrine and temple visits, especially at New Year: omikuji hiita? and then what you got (daikichi datta!). Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: pull; also draw lots, a card or a raffle
newEntries.trap: English 'draw' leads to kaku, which is drawing a picture. Drawing lots, a card or a fortune is hiku (pull): omikuji o hiku, kuji o hiku. It is the hiku of kaze o hiku, not the one in piano o hiku.

example.ja: おみくじ引いたら、大吉だった！
example.english: I drew a fortune slip and got great luck!

examplePolite.romaji: omikuji o hiitara, daikichi deshita!
examplePolite.ja: おみくじを引いたら、大吉でした！
examplePolite.english: I drew a fortune slip and got great luck!

newEntries.freqNote: 引く #1039 covers every 'pull' sense, including kaze o hiku. 大吉 (daikichi, great luck) is #15710. Films use おみくじ only 6 times.
newEntries.notes: Fortunes run from daikichi (great luck) down to kyou or even daikyou (bad, very bad luck), and a bad one is tied to a rack at the shrine and left behind.

newEntries.english: hear a voice; (on a call) can hear someone
newEntries.use: The voice that reaches you is the subject: tonari no heya kara koe ga kikoeru. On calls and video meetings it's the check koe kikoeteru? (can you hear me?), or just kikoeru?, and the reply chotto kikoenai (I can't really hear you).
newEntries.verbSense: can be heard, reach your ears; also 'sound like' (X ni kikoeru)
newEntries.trap: For 'I can hear a voice' or 'can you hear me?', learners use kiku, but kiku is listening on purpose: kiiteru? means 'are you listening?'. A sound reaching you is kikoeru, with the voice as subject: koe kikoeru?

example.ja: もしもし、声聞こえてる？
example.english: Hello? Can you hear me?

examplePolite.romaji: moshimoshi, koe kikoemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: もしもし、声聞こえますか？
examplePolite.english: Hello? Can you hear me?

newEntries.freqNote: 声+聞こえる 242 in the subtitles (ga 212), a strong pairing. The list has no entry for the whole phrase, so the noun and verb are ranked separately. The bare call check is frequent too: 聞こえる？ 286, 聞こえますか 212.
newEntries.notes: X ni kikoeru means 'sounds like X': iiwake ni kikoeru (that sounds like an excuse). koe ga suru (there's a voice) says a voice is there; kikoeru is whether it reaches you, which is why calls use kikoeru. On a bad line, koe ga tooi (you sound far away) is the other stock complaint.

newEntries.use: Heard as often in the negative as the positive, with ga dropped: jishin nai (I'm not sure I can) before a test, an interview or a date. What you're confident in takes ni: ryouri ni wa jishin aru (I'm good at cooking and I know it).
newEntries.verbSense: there is, exist; here you have it (confidence)
newEntries.trap: 'Confident' is an adjective in English, but Japanese has confidence: jishin aru / jishin nai, and a confident person is jishin aru hito. For 'I'm not sure I can do it', a bare wakaranai sounds like 'I don't know'; say jishin nai, or dekiru ka wakaranai, which is also fine.

example.romaji: ashita no mensetsu, anmari jishin nai na.
example.ja: 明日の面接、あんまり自信ないな。
example.english: I'm not too confident about tomorrow's interview.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no mensetsu, amari jishin ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の面接、あまり自信がないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm not very confident about tomorrow's interview.

newEntries.freqNote: 自信 #839 is its own entry, apart from 自身 'oneself' #1355 and 地震 'earthquake' #7156. No phrase entry. Subtitle pairs: 自信+ある 143, 自信+ない 118, 自信+持つ 112. 自信満々 is #10967.
newEntries.notes: To encourage someone it's motto jishin motte (yo), with motsu, not aru. jishin manman (full of confidence) can sound teasing; the same sound jishin also means earthquake.

newEntries.english: be in a bad mood, grumpy
newEntries.use: Said mostly about someone whose mood shows, with ga often dropped: kyou kachou kigen warui. It's also the word for a fussy, cranky baby or child (nemukute kigen warui); for yourself, iraira shiteru (I'm irritable) is more usual.
newEntries.verbSense: bad; here someone's mood is bad and it shows
newEntries.trap: For 'in a bad mood', learners say kibun ga warui, which means feeling sick or put off. A mood others can see is kigen ga warui: kare kyou kigen warui.
partners: kibun (kibun ga warui: feel sick, not grumpy)

example.ja: 今日課長機嫌悪いね。
example.english: The boss is in a bad mood today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kachou, kigen ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は課長、機嫌が悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: The boss is in a bad mood today, isn't he.

newEntries.freqNote: Phrase entries 機嫌が悪い #12058 and 機嫌がいい #23070; ご機嫌 #4177 and 不機嫌 #8467 rank higher. 期限 'deadline' #4825 shares the sound.
newEntries.notes: fukigen (sulky, grumpy) is common too, and kigen naoshite asks someone to stop sulking. For a good mood, kigen ii (kyou kigen ii ne) and gokigen (gokigen da ne) both work.

newEntries.use: Mostly negative, after tasting or comparing two things: zenzen chigai wakannai (I can't tell the difference at all), with ga dropped. The things compared take no: kono futatsu no chigai.
newEntries.verbSense: understand, be clear; here you can make out the difference
newEntries.trap: Learners put o on it (chigai o wakaranai), but wakaru takes ga, or drops it in speech: chigai wakannai. 'Tell' isn't iu or oshieru here either: chigai o oshiete asks someone to explain the difference. kubetsu tsukanai (can't tell them apart) also works.
partners: aji (aji ga wakaru: have a palate)
yosa (yosa ga wakaru: see what's good about it)

example.ja: 正直、全然違い分かんない。
example.english: Honestly, I can't tell the difference at all.

examplePolite.romaji: shoujiki, zenzen chigai ga wakarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 正直、全然違いが分かりません。
examplePolite.english: Honestly, I can't tell the difference at all.

newEntries.freqNote: The list has no entry for the whole phrase, so the noun and verb are ranked separately; the verb 違う chigau (#94) carries most talk about differences. Subtitle pair count 53 (ga 40).
newEntries.notes: The verb chigau does much of this work too: nani ga chigau no? (what's the difference?). In the positive it praises a discerning palate: chigai ga wakaru hito (someone who can tell good from ordinary).

newEntries.use: Tears that come on their own, mostly past: namida deta after a yawn, onions, laughing too hard or a moving film, with ga often dropped. namida dete kita is welling up as it happens, and namida desou (I'm going to cry) comes at a moving scene; crying outright is naku.
newEntries.verbSense: come out, appear
newEntries.trap: Learners use naku (cry) for any tears, but naku is crying from emotion. Watery eyes from a yawn, onions, hay fever or laughing are namida ga deru: akubi shitara namida deta. At a moving film both work: naita, or the softer namida deta (I teared up).

example.ja: 笑いすぎて涙出た。
example.english: I laughed so hard I teared up.

examplePolite.romaji: waraisugite namida ga demashita.
examplePolite.ja: 笑いすぎて涙が出ました。
examplePolite.english: I laughed so hard I teared up.

newEntries.freqNote: The phrase has its own entry, 涙が出る #6982; 泣く naku is #407. Subtitle pair count 25 (ga 22).
newEntries.notes: namida ga tomaranai means the tears won't stop, from a sad film or from hay fever.

newEntries.use: Mostly past as a reaction, with ga dropped: torihada tatta! after a great song, a scary story or a cold blast of air. mite, torihada tatteru (look, I've got goosebumps) shows them as they happen.
newEntries.verbSense: stand, rise; here the bumps on your skin stand up
newEntries.trap: 'Get goosebumps' pulls learners toward morau or dekiru, but goosebumps 'stand up': torihada ga tatsu. It's the plain word for all goosebumps: cold, fear or being moved.

example.ja: 今の歌、鳥肌立った！
example.english: That song just gave me goosebumps!

examplePolite.romaji: ima no uta, torihada ga tachimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今の歌、鳥肌が立ちました。
examplePolite.english: That song just gave me goosebumps.

newEntries.freqNote: 鳥肌 #19017; phrase entries 鳥肌が立つ #23053 and the ga-less 鳥肌立つ #25477. Subtitle pair count 9, plus 4 kana たつ hits the tokenizer filed under 経つ. As a reaction to songs and live shows it is likely more common in life than in scripts (a judgement, not data).
newEntries.notes: Once only for cold, fear or disgust; for being moved it's now standard. torihada mono (goosebump-worthy) is the casual compliment.

newEntries.use: Mostly past, about what gave you a lift, with ga often dropped: amai mono tabetara genki deta, or arigatou, genki deta after a kind word. The negative genki denai means you can't shake a low mood.
newEntries.verbSense: come out, appear; here energy wells up in you
newEntries.trap: English 'cheer up' is both 'I cheered up' and 'cheer up!', but Japanese splits it: genki deta about yourself, genki dashite to someone else. genki dete! isn't a request, though genki dete kita (I'm perking up) is fine.

example.ja: ありがとう、なんか元気出た。
example.english: Thanks, that cheered me up.

examplePolite.romaji: arigatou gozaimasu. okage de genki ga demashita.
examplePolite.ja: ありがとうございます。おかげで元気が出ました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you. That cheered me up.

newEntries.freqNote: The phrase has its own entry, 元気が出る #8964, near the request genki dashite (元気出して #7639, the kept genki o dasu). 33 subtitle hits (ga 29).
newEntries.notes: genki moratta (it gave me a boost) is a common way to credit a song, a person or a message.

newEntries.use: Mostly negative, after big news like passing an exam, a new job, a wedding or a baby: mada jikkan wakanai (it hasn't sunk in yet). jikkan nai says the same, and the polite mada jikkan ga wakanai desu is a stock line in interviews. Once it does sink in: yatto jikkan waite kita.
newEntries.verbSense: well up, spring up (water, feelings)
newEntries.trap: Learners reach for mada wakaranai or rikai shite nai, which sound like you don't understand the news. Japanese says the real feeling hasn't welled up: mada jikkan wakanai. mada shinjirarenai (I still can't believe it) also works.
partners: imeeji (imeeji ga wakanai: can't picture it)

example.ja: まだ全然実感湧かない。
example.english: It still hasn't sunk in at all.

examplePolite.romaji: mada zenzen jikkan ga wakanai desu.
examplePolite.ja: まだ全然実感が湧かないです。
examplePolite.english: It still hasn't sunk in at all.

newEntries.freqNote: Phrase entries 実感が湧く #28148 and 実感がわく #51487; 湧く #3148. The subtitle pair count is 9, filed under 沸く 'boil' because the tokenizer lemmatises わく that way (the subtitles mostly write 湧く); film dialogue likely under-counts the interview line.
newEntries.notes: Don't mix up wakanai (doesn't well up, from waku) with wakannai (don't get it): one n apart.

newEntries.use: Said about a book, show, talk or piece of advice you come away from knowing more: ano bangumi, tame ni naru yo. Ni is kept, and before a noun it's tame ni naru hanashi (a talk worth hearing). With a person, X no tame ni naranai means it does X no good.
newEntries.verbSense: naru: become; here, turn out to be of benefit
partners: sankou (sankou ni naru: useful as a reference)
kusuri (ii kusuri ni naru: a setback that teaches you a lesson)

example.romaji: ano hon, honto ni tame ni naru yo.
example.ja: あの本、ほんとにためになるよ。
example.english: That book's really worth reading.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hon wa hontou ni tame ni narimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの本は本当にためになりますよ。
examplePolite.english: That book is really worthwhile.

newEntries.freqNote: ため #203 is mostly the grammar word (-tame ni, 'in order to'). The phrase ためになる has its own entry at #4007, just above 勉強になる #4175. なる #29.
newEntries.notes: Not the grammar -tame ni (in order to): here the phrase ends in naru, and tame means benefit. benkyou ni narimashita is the thank-you said on the spot; tame ni naru judges a book, show or advice as good for you; yaku ni tatsu says it was of practical use (a tool, a tip that helped).

newEntries.english: have a loud voice, be loud
newEntries.use: Said about someone who talks loudly (ano hito, koe ookii yo ne) or to quieten someone: chotto, koe ookii! Casual speech drops ga, and friends often say koe dekai (dekai is blunter and more slangy than ookii). The opposite, koe ga chiisai, means quiet or soft-spoken (koe chiisai yo = speak up, I can't hear you).
newEntries.verbSense: ookii: big; for sounds and voices, loud
newEntries.trap: Not koe ga takai, which in everyday speech means high-pitched. urusai also works for 'you're being noisy', but it sounds annoyed (urusai! = shut up) and calls the person noisy or nagging, not their voice loud. To describe a loud voice, say koe ga ookii (casually koe dekai).

example.ja: ちょっと、声大きいよ！
example.english: Hey, you're being loud!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, chotto koe ga ookii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと声が大きいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, you're being a bit loud.

newEntries.freqNote: 声 #327; 大きい #536 (大きな #538); でかい #1836; 大声 oogoe #5023; うるさい #517. The film count (67) includes ookii koe before a noun (ADJ:19).
newEntries.notes: 'Speak up' is motto ookii koe de, and 'in a loud voice' is ookina koe de. In older speech and period dramas, shh, koe ga takai! means 'keep your voice down'.

newEntries.use: Said about cafes, restaurants, shops and towns: kono mise, ii fun'iki da ne, or with the noun first and ga dropped, fun'iki ii ne. About a person, fun'iki is their air: ano hito, fun'iki ii yo ne (he/she has a nice vibe), or yasashii fun'iki no hito (someone with a gentle air). About two people, ii fun'iki means they seem into each other.
newEntries.verbSense: ii: good, nice
newEntries.trap: 'Atmosphere' isn't kuuki here: ii kuuki or kuuki ga ii means fresh air, and kuuki as a mood is mostly kuuki o yomu or kuuki ga omoi (an awkward mood). A place's nice feel is ii fun'iki.

example.romaji: kono kafe, ii fun'iki da ne.
example.ja: このカフェ、いい雰囲気だね。
example.english: This café has a nice vibe.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kafe wa ii fun'iki desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このカフェはいい雰囲気ですね。
examplePolite.english: This café has a lovely atmosphere.

newEntries.freqNote: 雰囲気 #1448; いい #24. Neither いい雰囲気 nor 雰囲気いい has its own entry. The film count (32) is mostly ii fun'iki before the noun (ADJ:27).
newEntries.notes: fun'iki kawatta ne (you look different) is the usual remark on a new hairstyle; many natives say fuinki.

newEntries.use: Said about kids, classmates and athletes: ano ko, ashi hayai ne, often with ga dropped. Japanese puts the speed in the legs, ashi ga hayai; hashiru no ga hayai also works. The opposite is ashi ga osoi (a slow runner).
newEntries.verbSense: hayai: fast; the same word also means early
partners: shigoto (shigoto ga hayai: a fast worker)
henji (henji ga hayai: quick to reply)

example.romaji: ano ko, kurasu de ichiban ashi hayai n da.
example.ja: あの子、クラスで一番足速いんだ。
example.english: That kid's the fastest runner in the class.

examplePolite.romaji: ano ko wa kurasu de ichiban ashi ga hayai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの子はクラスで一番足が速いんです。
examplePolite.english: That child is the fastest runner in the class.

newEntries.freqNote: 足 #707; 速い #2346 (speed). The kana はやい also covers 早い #396 (early), so the kana rank overstates this sense. The phrase itself is listed under the other spelling, 足が早い #89256, and the opposite as 足が遅い #58166 (足速い #37273 is ashibayai, 'brisk-paced', a different word). The film count (22) is filed under 早い too, pooling both spellings.
newEntries.notes: ashi ga hayai also means food spoils fast (namamono wa ashi ga hayai).

newEntries.use: Describes someone's hair in the person wa kami ga nagai frame: imouto, kami nagai yo, with ga dropped. Before a noun ga becomes no (kami no nagai hito), and 'your hair's got long' is kami nobita ne.
newEntries.verbSense: nagai: long (length or time)
newEntries.trap: Not nagai kami o motte iru ('has long hair'): Japanese doesn't 'have' hair. Say kami ga nagai, the same frame as se ga takai, or nagai kami o shite iru, nagai kami no hito.

example.romaji: imouto, kami nagai n da yo.
example.ja: 妹、髪長いんだよ。
example.english: My little sister's got long hair.

examplePolite.romaji: imouto wa kami ga nagai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 妹は髪が長いんですよ。
examplePolite.english: My younger sister has long hair.

newEntries.freqNote: 髪 #1752 (髪の毛 kami no ke #3658); 長い #467; 短い #1621. The kana かみ is shared with 神 #1988 and 紙 #2672. The film count (20) is mostly nagai kami before the noun (ADJ:14); the kami ga nagai frame is judged.
newEntries.notes: Short hair is kami ga mijikai, but people often just say shooto (shooto ni shita = I went short).

newEntries.kana: うんどうしんけいがいい
newEntries.use: The everyday 'athletic, coordinated': ano hito, undou shinkei ii yo ne, with ga dropped. The opposite, undou shinkei ga nai, is common self-deprecation, and so is undou onchi (uncoordinated).
newEntries.verbSense: ii: good
newEntries.trap: Not asurechikku (in Japanese that's an obstacle-course playground): say undou shinkei ga ii. supootsu ga tokui and undou ga dekiru (good at sports) are also natural.

example.romaji: undou shinkei ii ne! nanka supootsu yatteta?
example.ja: 運動神経いいね！なんかスポーツやってた？
example.english: You're athletic! Did you use to play a sport?

newEntries.freqNote: 運動神経 #12050 as a whole compound. It occurs almost only in this phrase and in undou shinkei ga nai / warui, so the phrase is more common than the rank suggests. 運動音痴 undou onchi #37364.
newEntries.notes: Literally 'motor nerves are good'.

newEntries.use: The everyday comment on a crowded place: kyou, hito ooi ne, usually with ga dropped. Said of stations, festivals, shops and tourist spots; for a place packed right now, konderu is just as common. The opposite is hito ga sukunai, or suiteru (not crowded).
newEntries.verbSense: ooi: many, a lot (used as a predicate)
newEntries.trap: Not ooi hito ga iru: ooi rarely goes before a noun, so 'there are lots of people' is hito ga ooi (or hito ga ippai), and before a noun it's takusan no hito.

example.romaji: shuumatsu wa hito ooi kara, heijitsu ni ikou.
example.ja: 週末は人多いから、平日に行こう。
example.english: Weekends are crowded, so let's go on a weekday.

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa hito ga ooi node, heijitsu ni ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 週末は人が多いので、平日に行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: Weekends are crowded, so let's go on a weekday.

newEntries.freqNote: 人 (ひと) #60; 多い #360; 少ない #1076. No phrase entry. 混む #5984; 人混み hitogomi #18818.
newEntries.notes: hitogomi (a crowd) is the noun: hitogomi nigate (I can't stand crowds).

newEntries.use: The compliment every learner hears, often after a single sentence: nihongo jouzu desu ne! Casual speech drops ga, and friends also say nihongo umai ne. The usual reply is iie, mada mada desu or sonna koto nai desu.
newEntries.verbSense: jouzu: skilful, good at (praise for someone else's skill)
newEntries.trap: Jouzu is for praising others: watashi wa nihongo ga jouzu desu sounds like boasting. About yourself, say nihongo ga sukoshi dekimasu, or mada mada desu when complimented.

example.ja: 日本語上手になったね！
example.english: Your Japanese has got really good!

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo ga jouzu ni narimashita ne!
examplePolite.ja: 日本語が上手になりましたね！
examplePolite.english: Your Japanese has improved!

newEntries.freqNote: 日本語 #3651; 上手 #1309, お上手 #5903; うまい #246 also covers 'tasty'. Films rarely compliment anyone's Japanese (3 hits), so commonness is judged.
newEntries.notes: It's said after a single konnichiwa, so it's politeness more than a verdict.

newEntries.use: Said when recommending a shop, restaurant, doctor or teacher: ano mise, hyouban ii yo, with ga dropped. Before a noun ga becomes no (hyouban no ii mise), and the opposite is hyouban ga warui.
newEntries.verbSense: ii: good
newEntries.trap: Not ii hyouban o motte iru ('has a good reputation'): the reputation is the subject, hyouban ga ii (hyouban no ii mise). yuumei only says famous, not that people speak well of it.
partners: uke (uke ga ii: go down well)

example.ja: あの歯医者さん、評判いいよ。
example.english: That dentist's got a good reputation.

examplePolite.romaji: ano haisha-san wa hyouban ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの歯医者さんは評判がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: That dentist has a good reputation.

newEntries.freqNote: 評判 #1932; いい #24. No phrase entry; 口コミ kuchikomi #16520. Film count 23, with hyouban ga warui at 14.
newEntries.notes: For online reviews, kuchikomi is the word: kuchikomi mo ii yo.

newEntries.use: Said while carrying shopping or luggage, often before an offer to help: nimotsu omoi desho, motou ka? Casual speech drops ga, and before a noun it's omoi nimotsu (heavy bags).
newEntries.verbSense: omoi: heavy; also serious, weighing on you

example.ja: 荷物重いでしょ？持とうか？
example.english: Your bags must be heavy. Want me to carry them?

examplePolite.romaji: onimotsu, omoi desu yo ne. mochimashou ka?
examplePolite.ja: お荷物、重いですよね。持ちましょうか？
examplePolite.english: Your bags must be heavy. Shall I carry them for you?

newEntries.freqNote: 荷物 #1140; 重い #1004 (the kana おもい is mostly 思い #616); 重たい omotai #5482; 軽い #1175. The film count (17) is mostly omoi nimotsu before the noun (ADJ:12), some of it figurative ('a heavy burden'); the everyday remark is judged.
newEntries.notes: omotai is a spoken variant that stresses how heavy it feels: kono kaban, omotai. Shop staff and juniors offer with the humble omochi shimashou ka.

newEntries.use: Gossip about someone mean or spiteful, almost always with ga dropped: ano hito, seikaku warui yo ne. It judges who a person is, so it's said about people far more than to them; before a noun it's seikaku no warui hito.
newEntries.verbSense: warui: bad
newEntries.trap: Not warui hito, which judges someone as a bad person in the moral sense (warui hito ja nai kedo... = he's not a bad guy, but...): mean or nasty by nature is seikaku ga warui. ijiwaru (mean, spiteful) works for a person or an act: ijiwaru shinaide = don't be mean.

example.romaji: ano senpai, honto seikaku warui n da yo.
example.ja: あの先輩、ほんと性格悪いんだよ。
example.english: That senior is seriously mean.

examplePolite.romaji: ano senpai wa hontou ni seikaku ga warui n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの先輩は本当に性格が悪いんですよ。
examplePolite.english: That senior is really mean.

newEntries.freqNote: 性格 #1670; 悪い #139. The phrase has its own entries, 性格悪い #14102 and 性格が悪い #30468, both above 性格がいい #47898. 意地悪 ijiwaru #4005.
newEntries.notes: Among friends, the clipped seikaku waru! is a playful 'that's so mean!'.

newEntries.use: Heard most in the negative, about age or being out of shape: mou tairyoku nai (I've got no stamina left), with ga dropped. Tairyoku aru ne praises someone who keeps going, and a drop in stamina is tairyoku ga ochita.
newEntries.verbSense: aru: there is; have (things, qualities)
newEntries.trap: 'Fit' isn't fitto (in Japanese that's how clothes fit). genki covers 'well, healthy' (mada genki = still going strong), but for stamina and being in shape use tairyoku: tairyoku aru / tairyoku nai.

example.romaji: saikin undou shitenai kara, tairyoku nai n da.
example.ja: 最近運動してないから、体力ないんだ。
example.english: I haven't been exercising lately, so I've got no stamina.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin undou shite inai node, tairyoku ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近運動していないので、体力がないんです。
examplePolite.english: I haven't been exercising lately, so I have no stamina.

newEntries.freqNote: 体力 #3077; ある #21, ない #43. The film count (6) is too low to use, so commonness is judged. 体力的 tairyokuteki #20161; スタミナ #13386; 運動不足 undou busoku #19482.
newEntries.notes: tairyoku o tsukeru (build up stamina) is the usual resolution: tairyoku tsukenakya.

newEntries.use: A common compliment on someone's figure, usually meaning slim and well-proportioned: sutairu ii ne, with ga dropped. It's said of men and women alike, and an amazing figure is sutairu batsugun.
newEntries.verbSense: ii: good
newEntries.trap: False friend: sutairu ga ii is about the body, not fashion. To praise how someone dresses, say oshare or fuku no sensu ga ii.

example.ja: スタイルいいね！モデルみたい。
example.english: You've got a great figure! Like a model.

examplePolite.romaji: sutairu ga ii desu ne! moderu mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: スタイルがいいですね！モデルみたいです。
examplePolite.english: You have a great figure! You look like a model.

newEntries.freqNote: スタイル #3954 covers both senses of the loanword, so it is not a count of this phrase. いい #24; おしゃれ #3483; 体型 taikei #19649.
newEntries.notes: For a toned build, kitaeteru ne (you work out, don't you) is the usual compliment.

blocks.label: Rain and snow
blocks.rationale: What rain and snow do and what you do about it: it's coming down, it has stopped, the umbrella's own verb, and getting rained on.
blocks.interference: ame ga furu and yuki ga furu share furu, so drill them in one frame (soto, ___ futteru yo), and set ame ni furareta (it rained on me) against plain ame futta. Keep ame ga yamu (it stops by itself) apart from yameru (a person quits), and kasa o sasu (have it up) apart from kasa motsu (carry it).

blocks.label: Weather and wind
blocks.rationale: The remarks people trade about conditions outside: nice weather, a strong wind, heavy rain, a breeze, and stepping out for some air.
blocks.interference: kaze ga tsuyoi and ame ga tsuyoi both use tsuyoi where English says 'windy' and 'heavy', so learn them in one frame (kyou ___ tsuyoi ne). kaze (wind) sounds exactly like kaze (a cold) and only the verb tells them apart: kaze ga fuku and kaze ni ataru are the wind, kaze o hiku is catching a cold.

blocks.label: Storms and quakes
blocks.rationale: The big events people warn each other about, and the forecast that got it wrong: a typhoon on the way, an earthquake, thunder, a missed forecast.
blocks.interference: English 'hit' fits none of them: a typhoon kuru (comes), an earthquake okiru (happens; jishin kita as it shakes) and thunder naru (sounds), so drill the three verbs side by side. kaminari ga naru is 鳴る 'sound', not naru 'become', and a forecast hazureru (misses) or ataru (is right), never machigaeru.

blocks.label: Sun and moon
blocks.rationale: What the sky does through the day: it gets dark, the sun comes up and goes down, the moon comes out.
blocks.interference: hi ga shizumu (the sun sinks) and hi ga kureru (the day closes) both mean evening: shizumu is the sun itself, kureru is the light going, and it isn't kureru 'give'. The sun noboru (climbs) but the moon usually deru (comes out), like a person going out.

blocks.label: Seasons
blocks.rationale: Sets that mark the year in daily talk: blossoms out in spring, summer heat and cicadas, snow lying in winter.
blocks.interference: semi ga naku uses naku (鳴く, an animal's call), not naku 'cry' (泣く), and pairs with kaminari ga naru: animals naku, things naru. atsusa ni yowai is the osake ga yowai idea with ni (samusa ni yowai for cold), and snow furu as it falls but tsumoru once it lies.

textFixes.value: kaze is both 'wind' and 'a cold', and only the verb tells you which: kaze ga fuku is the wind blowing, kaze o hiku is catching a cold. kaze ni ataru (get some air) is the wind too.

Classic autumn remark: hi ga kureru no hayaku natta ne (it's getting dark earlier). Joking 'this'll take forever': sonna no yattetara hi ga kurechau yo. Days getting longer: hi ga nobita ne. The sun itself going down is hi ga shizumu; kureru is the light going with it.

value: jishin (earthquake: jishin kita! as it shakes; the usual set is jishin ga okiru)

blocks.label: Hungry, full, thirsty
blocks.rationale: Everyday appetite signals: hungry (two ways), full and thirsty.
blocks.interference: onaka suita and onaka hetta mean the same, but hetta sounds blunter, so learn suita first and hetta as its casual twin. Both use the past tense for hunger you feel now, and so does nodo kawaita. onaka ippai has no verb of its own (add ni natta for the past).

blocks.label: Washing and grooming
blocks.rationale: Looking after your body day to day: washing your hands, face and hair, and cutting your hair and nails.
blocks.interference: arau covers every kind of washing, from hands to hair, so there's no separate shampoo verb. The kiru in kami o kiru and tsume o kiru means cut (kitta), not wear (fuku o kiru, kita), and kami kitta is said even when a stylist cut it.

blocks.label: Aches and pains
blocks.rationale: Saying what hurts: body part + ga itai for any pain, plus stiff shoulders.
blocks.interference: X ga itai covers every pain (atama itai, nodo itai), and koshi is the lower back, which English just calls 'my back'. kata ga koru is stiffness and takes the verb koru, never itai.

blocks.label: Feeling unwell
blocks.rationale: Saying you feel off, from the general guai ga warui and the work-safe taichou ga warui to being in or out of form.
blocks.interference: guai ga warui and taichou ga warui both mean 'I don't feel well', and taichou is the safer word at work. choushi ga warui / ii is being off or on form, and also a device acting up. kibun ga warui is feeling sick or faint right now. kimochi warui (in senses) is queasy or gross.

blocks.label: Getting sick
blocks.rationale: Coming down with something: catching a cold, catching one from someone, a real illness, getting run down and an upset stomach.
blocks.interference: kaze o hiku is getting a cold; kaze ga utsuru is catching it from someone. byouki ni naru sounds like a real illness, so for a rough few days say taichou kuzushita. kuzusu and kowasu both mean break: taichou o kuzusu for your health in general, onaka o kowasu for your stomach. kaze 'cold' sounds like kaze 'wind'.

blocks.label: Cold symptoms
blocks.rationale: Describing a cold or flu: a fever, a cough, a runny nose and that heavy, run-down feeling.
blocks.interference: Symptoms 'come out' with deru (netsu deta, seki ga deru, hanamizu ga deru); netsu ga aru is having a fever right now, never motsu. karada ga darui uses the adjective darui, and darui on its own also means 'can't be bothered'.

blocks.label: Doctor and medicine
blocks.rationale: Getting treated: going to the doctor, taking medicine and the medicine working.
blocks.interference: English 'see' and 'take' pull toward miru and toru, but a doctor visit is byouin ni iku and medicine is drunk, kusuri o nomu. The kiku in kusuri ga kiku (it works) sounds the same as kiku 'hear, ask'.

blocks.label: Rest and recovery
blocks.rationale: Lying down and getting better: the fever drops, the cold clears up, the tiredness goes.
blocks.interference: sagaru, naoru and toreru say the thing goes away by itself, so they take ga; their o twins mean someone does it (netsu o sageru, kaze o naosu). yoko ni naru is lying down to rest, not neru (sleep).

blocks.label: Long-term health
blocks.rationale: Health beyond today's symptoms: what's good for you, getting older, quitting smoking and allergies.
blocks.interference: karada ni ii keeps its ni even in casual talk. Getting older is toshi o toru, not furuku naru. tabako o yameru uses the same yameru as quitting a job (kaisha o yameru). An allergy is something you have: ebi no arerugii ga aru.

blocks.label: Visible signs
blocks.rationale: What shows on your body or someone else's: an injury, blood, sweat, a pale or flushed face. These are often followed by daijoubu?
blocks.interference: An injury takes suru (kega o suru), and blood comes out just like a fever does (chi ga deru, chi deteru yo). Sweat takes kaku (ase o kaku), which is not kaku 'write'. A pale face is kaoiro ga warui (bad colour), while a red face is just kao ga akai.

blocks.label: Moving your body
blocks.rationale: Body instructions heard in class, at the doctor or at a massage: raise your hand, close your eyes, relax.
blocks.interference: Eyes take tojiru, not shimeru (which is for doors and windows). chikara o nuku pulls the strength out and is the opposite of chikara o ireru. te o ageru can also mean raising a hand to someone (hitting them).

textFixes.value: The sets next to it split the job. Taichou ga warui means the same in a more careful word, and it's the safe phrase for calling in sick at work. Choushi ga warui is being off form, and also a machine acting up (pasokon no choushi ga warui). Kibun ga warui is feeling sick or faint right now (in a car, in a crowd). Kimochi warui (in the senses list) is queasy, but also 'gross, creepy'.
An upset stomach from something you ate is onaka o kowasu (onaka kowashita). Onaka no choushi ga warui is the discreet way to mention it.
Japanese complain of stiff shoulders where English speakers often say neck or back. Lower-back pain is koshi ga itai.

blocks.label: Clothes and shoes
blocks.rationale: The everyday on/off pairs for what you're dressed in: clothes go on with kiru, shoes with haku, and both come off with nugu.
blocks.interference: kiru vs haku: kiru for the torso or whole body, haku for anything you step into; nugu takes both off, so drill kiru/haku against the one nugu (fuku kite / kutsu haite / kutsu nuide).

blocks.label: Trying clothes on
blocks.rationale: Dressing past plain on/off, the mirror and fitting-room talk: trousers take haku, getting changed is kigaeru, then whether it suits you (niau) and whether it fits (saizu ga au).
blocks.interference: zubon takes haku like shoes, not kiru; niau (looks good on you) vs saizu ga au (right size), which English both calls 'fit' or 'suit', and this au also sounds like au 'meet'; changing clothes is kigaeru, not fuku o kaeru.

blocks.label: Masks and glasses
blocks.rationale: Two on/off pairs for the face: a mask goes on with suru, glasses with kakeru, and both come off with hazusu.
blocks.interference: suru vs kakeru for putting on, one shared hazusu for taking off; never nugu, which is for clothes and shoes.

blocks.label: Hats and accessories
blocks.rationale: The rest of what you wear, each with its own verb: a hat is pulled on with kaburu, a ring and a tie just take suru, perfume goes on with tsukeru.
blocks.interference: kaburu for anything over the head, suru for small worn items (as in masuku o suru), tsukeru for things put onto the body; a hat comes off with toru or nugu, a ring or tie with hazusu.

textFixes.value: Off: fuku o nugu. Changing into other clothes is fuku o kigaeru; looking good in them is fuku ga niau (niau ne).

Off: masuku o hazusu or toru. The same suru goes with a ring or a tie (yubiwa o suru, nekutai o suru). tsukeru is the catch-all for things put on the body: nekkuresu / piasu / kousui o tsukeru (necklace, earrings, perfume). A scarf is also mafuraa o maku (wrap it).

changelog.change: Trap rewritten (natural, traps, nuance): the claim that English 'fit' has no one-word match was backwards, since au alone can mean fit. The difference is the subject (the size, not the garment). The trap still warns off niau and fitto suru.

Partners glossed (natural/traps): kutsu now shows au with the item as subject (kono kutsu, ashi ni awanai). megane became megane no do (prescription) and makura is marked as 'isn't right for me', so neither reads as a size set.
commonness 3 -> 4 (natural): it's the standard fitting-room and online-order line, which film subtitles under-count.
verbSense: dropped the 'au:' prefix (nuance, form). Notes: added that this au sounds exactly like au 'meet' (nuance).

Trap trimmed to the kiru/suru point (form, nuance). hameru, hameteru = has one on (traps), tsukeru and hazusu moved into notes, so they no longer repeat the trap. Notes now also cover the finger taking ni (kusuriyubi ni yubiwa shiteru) (natural).
Partner nekutai replaced with buresuretto, because nekutai o suru is now its own entry (traps, nuance).

Trap corrected (major, natural; also traps, nuance). fuku o kaeru isn't wrong: it's about switching outfits (are, fuku kaeta?). kigaeru is the everyday verb for getting changed, and 'change into' takes ni.
Notes: added the variant reading kikaeru (traps).

The warning against making the person the subject is gone. anata/kimi in model phrases were replaced (nuance). blocks.label: Out and back
blocks.rationale: Leaving the house, stepping outside, running errands and getting home (late or not): the trip that starts and ends every day.
blocks.interference: The particle shows direction: o for the place you leave (uchi o deru), ni for where you end up or what you go to do (soto ni deru, uchi ni kaeru, kaimono ni iku). 'Go home' is kaeru, because uchi ni iku means visiting someone's house.

blocks.label: Bathroom
blocks.rationale: The washroom routine people mention morning and night: the toilet, a shower, a bath, teeth, a shave.
blocks.interference: shawaa o abiru and ofuro ni hairu are both 'take a ___' in English, but a shower is poured over you (o abiru) and a bath is gone into (ni hairu); drill them in one frame, saki ni ___ kuru ne. Teeth are polished (migaku), and a shave names what comes off (hige o soru).

blocks.label: Doors and locks
blocks.rationale: The front door both ways, opening and shutting, plus locking up: each act paired with the state it leaves.
blocks.interference: Each act with o has a ga partner for what the door does or how it is now: akeru/aku, shimeru/shimaru, kakeru/kakaru. Keep doa akete (open it) apart from doa aiteru (it's open), and kagi kakete (lock it) apart from kagi kakatteru (it's locked).

blocks.label: Windows and curtains
blocks.rationale: The same open/close pair on windows and curtains: airing the room, shutting out rain or cold, closing up for the night.
blocks.interference: English 'draw the curtains' hides the direction; Japanese names it: kaaten o shimeru (close) or kaaten o akeru (open). Windows take the same akeru/shimeru as doors, with mado aiteru for the open state.

blocks.label: Lights and buttons
blocks.rationale: Switching things on and off and pressing a button: the on/off pair, the light's own state, then the press.
blocks.interference: Don't carry akeru and shimeru over from doors: lights go on with tsukeru and off with kesu (not shimeru or tomeru). Drill the pair in one frame: denki ___te.

blocks.label: Bed and waking
blocks.rationale: Bedtime to morning: dreaming, waking, getting under the covers and setting the alarm, plus the kotatsu people crawl under on winter evenings.
blocks.interference: okiru from the versatility list gets mixed up with me ga sameru: okiru can mean getting out of bed, but me ga sameru never does. Getting into bed is going in, futon ni hairu, the same ni hairu as kotatsu ni hairu and ofuro ni hairu.

blocks.label: Trash and tidying
blocks.rationale: Keeping the place in order: binning things, trash day, the messy room and putting things back.
blocks.interference: gomi o suteru is throwing something away; gomi o dasu is putting the bags out for collection. A messy room is chirakatteru, not kitanai (dirty), and the fix is katazukeru (put away), not souji (scrub).

blocks.label: Kitchen
blocks.rationale: Round a meal at home: washing up, boiling the kettle, wiping the table.
blocks.interference: Each job has its own verb where English says 'wash' or 'boil': arau is with water, fuku is with a cloth, and the water you boil is already oyu (hot water) and takes wakasu, not niru, which is for cooking food.

blocks.label: Housework and laundry
blocks.rationale: The chores beyond the kitchen: housework as a whole, laundry from the line to the drawer, and vacuuming.
blocks.interference: hosu is you hanging the washing out, kawaku is it drying (sentakumono kawaita?), and folding is tatamu, not oru (paper). 'Vacuum' is a verb in English, but Japanese runs the machine with kakeru: soujiki o kakeru, like mezamashi o kakeru.

blocks.label: Your place
blocks.rationale: Talking about where you live: renting, a cramped room, keeping a pet, parcels arriving.
blocks.interference: Renting uses kariru, the 'borrow' verb, and a cramped room is usually semai (narrow) rather than chiisai. The kau of keeping a pet sounds like kau 'buy', and parcels todoku (reach you) rather than tsuku (arrive) like people.

textFixes.value: Once it's dry (sentakumono ga kawaku: kawaita?), bringing it in is torikomu (sentakumono torikonde!) and folding it is tatamu (fuku o tatamu).

Putting things back where they belong (moto ni modosu), as in the parent's nag heya katazukenasai. Casual speech drops o; cleaning is souji suru (vacuuming is soujiki o kakeru), and heya o kirei ni suru covers both.

blocks.label: Drinks
blocks.rationale: Water, coffee, alcohol and tea all take nomu. These are the four drinks people offer and ask about every day.
blocks.interference: All four take nomu, so drill them in one frame (mizu nomu? koohii nomu?); medicine and soup take nomu too. Making the tea or coffee is ocha o ireru (in Breakfast), never ocha o tsukuru.

blocks.label: Meals at home
blocks.rationale: A meal at home from start to finish: cooking it, calling out that it's ready, eating it, and letting it go cold.
blocks.interference: gohan means the meal here, not only rice: gohan tsukuru is cooking dinner and gohan dekita yo means it's ready. Hot food cooling off is sameru (samechau yo), not samuku naru, which is for weather and people.

blocks.label: Eating out
blocks.rationale: A meal out: suggesting it, finding the place packed, saying it's your treat, and remarking on a big portion.
blocks.interference: gohan ni iku needs no taberu. mise ga komu is said as konderu and is not mise ga aiteru (open). Treating someone is ogoru (kyou wa ogoru yo); being treated is gochisou ni naru (in People). A big portion is ryou ga ooi, not ookii.

blocks.label: Drinking out
blocks.rationale: A night out drinking: the invitation, asking about smoking, and whether you can hold your drink.
blocks.interference: nomi ni iku is the drinking version of gohan ni iku, and nomi means alcohol without saying osake. osake ga tsuyoi and osake ga yowai describe the drinker, while kono osake tsuyoi means the drink is strong. Tobacco takes suu, not nomu.

blocks.label: How it tastes
blocks.rationale: The everyday comments on flavour: what it tastes like, and seasoning that is too light or too strong.
blocks.interference: A taste you notice uses suru (hen na aji suru), not aru. Seasoning is usui (light) or koi (strong), never yowai or tsuyoi, which are kept for osake.

blocks.label: Breakfast
blocks.rationale: The morning kitchen: making a cup of tea or coffee, putting sugar in it, making toast, or skipping breakfast.
blocks.interference: ireru works two ways here: ocha o ireru is brewing the cup, and satou o ireru is literally putting sugar in. Neither is tsukuru. Toast is pan o yaku (yaku covers bake, grill and toast), and skipping a meal is nuku, not tobasu.

blocks.label: Fridge and microwave
blocks.rationale: Putting food away and getting it out again: into the fridge, a lid on, heating it up, and checking whether it's past its date.
blocks.interference: reizouko ni ireru takes ni for where the food goes, unlike satou o ireru. Heating food up is atatameru (obentou atatamemasu ka? at the konbini), not atsuku suru. A lid goes on with futa o suru; a screw cap is futa o shimeru. Expiry has no verb of its own: the date runs out with kireru, like juuden ga kireru.

textFixes.value: koohii o ireru works the same way. Serving tea to a guest is ocha o dasu; ireru is the brewing. Sugar or milk going into the cup uses ireru in its plain 'put in' sense: satou ireru? (do you take sugar?).
meshi kuu (meshi kutta?) is the rough, mostly male version. Skipping a meal, by choice or habit, is nuku: asagohan nuita (I skipped breakfast).

blocks.label: TV and music
blocks.rationale: Watching and listening at home: TV and the news, music you listen to or put on, and switching channels.
blocks.interference: ongaku o kiku (you listen) vs ongaku o kakeru (you put it on): same noun, different verb. TV and the news both take miru, English 'play' is never asobu here, and channeru o kaeru uses kaeru 'change', not kaeru 'go home'.

blocks.label: Photos and your phone
blocks.rationale: The phone as camera and album: taking photos, looking at them, sending them, and idle time on the phone in between.
blocks.interference: Three verbs on shashin: toru (take), miru (look at), okuru (send). Idle phone use is ijiru, not asobu or tsukau, and shashin o okuru shares okuru with meeru o okuru.

blocks.label: Phone calls
blocks.rationale: One phone call on the noun denwa: calling, picking up and hanging up, then the phone ringing and calls that came in for you.
blocks.interference: The o/ni sets are things you do (kakeru, deru, kiru) and the ga sets happen to you (naru, aru, kakaru): denwa o kakeru vs denwa ga kakaru differ only in o/ga, with kara for the caller. This naru is 'ring', not naru 'become', and kiru ends the call.

blocks.label: Numbers and messages
blocks.rationale: Keeping in touch in writing: swapping numbers, then a message's round trip of send, receive and reply.
blocks.interference: meeru o okuru (you send, o) vs meeru ga kuru (it comes to you, ga) is the same out/in split as the phone calls. 'Give me your number' is bangou oshiete, not kudasai, and kaesu 'send back' sounds like kaeru 'go home'.

blocks.label: Power, battery, sound
blocks.rationale: Switching a device on and off, and the times it stops working: a dead battery or no sound.
blocks.interference: dengen o ireru / kiru (you switch it on or off) vs juuden ga kireru (it runs out on its own) is transitive kiru vs intransitive kireru, as in denwa o kiru / denwa ga kireta. Lights and the TV take tsukeru / kesu, and oto ga deru (sound comes out of a device) is not oto ga suru (you hear a noise).

blocks.label: Internet and apps
blocks.rationale: Getting online and what you do there: looking things up, connection and signal trouble, and putting apps on your phone.
blocks.interference: netto de shiraberu (look things up, de for the means) vs netto ga tsunagaru (the net connects, ga). Phone signal is denpa, not shingou, and apuri o ireru uses the same 'put in' ireru as dengen o ireru.

textFixes.value: denwa kita is the short everyday version. Passing on a call that came while someone was out is denwa ga aru: tanaka-san kara denwa ga arimashita. This -te kuru means 'toward me', not the 'go and do' sense of -te kuru. The partners take kakaru in its 'running' sense.

blocks.label: Getting on and off
blocks.rationale: The ride itself: one frame, X ni noru, for train, bus, car and bike, and oriru for getting off.
blocks.interference: Getting on takes ni and getting off takes o (densha ni noru, densha o oriru), so drill them as a pair. You never take a bus or ride a bike with toru or o noru, and how you travel takes de: jitensha de iku.

blocks.label: Catching the train
blocks.rationale: Train timing: a late train, making it, when it leaves, missing it, and the last train gone.
blocks.interference: densha ga okureru (the train runs late) and densha ni okureru (you're late for it, so you miss it) differ only in ga or ni. 'Miss' is never misu suru: say nogashita, or make the train the subject, shuuden nakunatta (the last train's gone).

blocks.label: On the way
blocks.rationale: Updates from the journey: I'm at the station, the roads are jammed, a seat's come free, I rode past my stop.
blocks.interference: Crowded is konderu and a free seat is aiteru, while a whole empty train or road is suiteru, never isogashii or hima. Arriving takes ni (eki ni tsuku), but the stop you ride past takes o (eki o norisugosu).

blocks.label: On a trip
blocks.rationale: Going away: the trip, the flight, the hotel, the gifts you bring back and the hot spring.
blocks.interference: Each place takes ni with its own verb: noru for the plane (English 'fly' is not tobu), tomaru for staying the night (not iru, and not yoru, which is dropping in), hairu for the hot spring.

blocks.label: Picking someone up
blocks.rationale: Collecting someone and driving them: going to get them, taking their bags, giving them a lift, parking, and stopping at the konbini on the way.
blocks.interference: For mukae ni iku Japanese says iku where English says 'I'll come'. noseru (give a lift) is the transitive of noru. tomeru (park) gets mixed up with yoru (drop in) and with tomaru (a car pulling up, or staying the night).

blocks.label: Finding the way
blocks.rationale: Directions and losing your way: turning left at the corner, getting lost, going the wrong way, getting separated.
blocks.interference: The corner takes o and the side takes ni (tsugi no kado o hidari ni magaru), and turning is magaru, not mawaru. mayou means you don't know where you are, machigaeru means you took the wrong road, and maigo means you got separated, like a lost child.

textFixes.value: Mostly heard as a check or a result: maniau? (will we make it?), maniatta (made it), maniawanai (we won't make it). The noun drops once the train is clear. Once it has gone, say densha ni okureta, or more casually nogashita or noriokureta (I missed it). For the last train people usually say shuuden nakunatta (the last train's gone) or shuuden nogashita.

The place you got lost in takes de: eki no naka de mayotta. Taking the wrong road on a route you know is michi o machigaeru (michi machigaeta). Getting separated from the people you're with, like a child in a shop, is maigo ni naru. Asking the way is michi o kiku: sumimasen, chotto michi o kikitai n desu kedo.
Missing your stop is eki o norisugosu: nete te norisugoshita (I fell asleep and missed my stop). The same verb goes down stairs: kaidan o oriru.
