blocks.label: No time, no money
blocks.rationale: Being busy or broke in one frame: no time, no free time, no money, not enough money, nothing to spare.
blocks.interference: All take ga nai, never o mottenai. jikan nai is no time now or for this, hima nai is no free time at all; okane nai is broke, okane tarinai is short for one thing; yoyuu nai covers money, time or headspace and alone means 'I'm swamped'.

blocks.label: Ready and how long
blocks.rationale: Getting things done: are you ready, it takes a while, time's gone by, it's a hassle.
blocks.interference: kakaru vs tatsu: ichinen kakatta = it took a year, ichinen tatta = a year has gone by; tema ga kakaru is effort, not minutes. Readiness is asked in the past (junbi dekita?), never junbi dekiru?.

blocks.label: Costs and paying
blocks.rationale: Money at the till and the table: what it costs overall, one item's price, pricey, paying, and splitting the bill.
blocks.interference: No single verb for 'cost': okane ga kakaru is the overall cost (kekkou kakatta), ikura suru is an item's price (ikura shita?), nedan ga takai says the price is high. okane o harau is you handing it over, and warikan ni suru is splitting evenly, not wakeru.

blocks.label: Are you free?
blocks.rationale: Setting a time: are you free, have you got plans, and whether a time suits.
blocks.interference: aiteru (got a gap) vs yotei aru (got plans) is the yes/no; tsugou ii / warui is the tactful pair for whether a time suits, not benri / fuben.

blocks.label: Can't make it
blocks.rationale: The stock reasons for saying no or heading off: something on, an early start, already booked, a prior engagement.
blocks.interference: All use aru or hairu, never motsu. youji ga atte is the vague errand excuse, yotei haitteru says the day is taken, senyaku ga atte is the politer 'prior engagement'; asa hayai kara makes the morning the subject. Something 'comes up' as youji ga dekita or yotei ga haitta, not okita.

blocks.label: Spending and saving
blocks.rationale: Two verb pairs for money going out and piling up: spend money, pay by card, save up, collect points.
blocks.interference: Spending money is tsukau (use), never sugosu, which is only for time; the same tsukau asks about cards (kaado tsukaemasu ka?). tameru is saving money and collecting points alike, not hozon suru or setsuyaku.

blocks.label: Out on errands
blocks.rationale: Running errands: grab some cash, is the shop open yet, has it closed, wait your turn.
blocks.interference: A shop's aiteru means 'open', not 'free' as in ashita aiteru?; shimatteru is 'closed'. orosu is cash from the ATM, not toru. junban o matsu is waiting your turn, while standing in the queue itself is narabu.

blocks.label: Plans and promises
blocks.rationale: How plans go: wait and see, called off, keep your word, plan it out.
blocks.interference: English verbs mislead in all four: 'wait and see' is yousu o miru, not matsu; events are called off with chuushi ni naru rather than kyanseru sareru; promises are mamoru (protect), not motsu; plans stand up with tateru, not tsukuru.

blocks.label: Using your time
blocks.rationale: The jikan o verbs for what you do with time: put it into something, set it aside, make it, kill it.
blocks.interference: English spend, take, make and kill map to kakeru, toru, tsukuru and tsubusu (crush), never korosu; how long something takes stays jikan ga kakaru, and spending time with people is sugosu.

textFixes.value: jikan aru? (got a minute?) is the question it answers; jikan ga aku (aiteru) is having a free slot. hima ga nai is the wider 'no free time these days', while jikan nai is about now or this one thing. 'No time to cook' puts the verb first: ryouri suru jikan ga nai.
jikan o kakeru = spend time on something on purpose (jikan kakete tsukutta). tema ga kakaru is the same frame for effort: it's a hassle.

Intransitive partner: okane ga tamaru (the money builds up). Points work the same way: pointo o tameru. The same sound also means letting things pile up through neglect: shigoto o tameru, sutoresu ga tamaru (溜める).

A booked plan is yotei haitteru, and the politer excuse is senyaku ga atte (a prior engagement). Drawing up a schedule (a trip, a study plan) is yotei o tateru, like keikaku o tateru; fixing a day with friends is hi o kimeru, and arranging to meet is yakusoku suru.

blocks.label: School and work days
blocks.rationale: The daily round, guessable sets first: going to school, going to work, getting off work, being busy with it.
blocks.interference: gakkou ni itteru and shigoto ni itteru mean you attend or are there now, not that you're on the way; owaru and isogashii make the work the subject with ga, where English says 'I'.

blocks.label: Questions and learning
blocks.rationale: Class talk: having a question, answering one, speaking English, then the thanks phrase benkyou ni naru.
blocks.interference: shitsumon ga aru (have one) takes ga and shitsumon ni kotaeru (answer it) takes ni, never o; benkyou ni natta (I learned from it) is not benkyou shita (I studied).

blocks.label: What's on
blocks.rationale: The timetable: a class, meeting or exam you have (all ga aru), then plans shifting: work coming up, something postponed.
blocks.interference: jugyou, kaigi and shiken all take ga aru, never motsu; shigoto ga hairu and enki ni naru say what happened to the plan, with no 'I' or 'they' doing it.

blocks.label: Breaks and time off
blocks.rationale: Stepping away from work, commonest first: missing a day, booking leave, a short break, quitting for good.
blocks.interference: yasumu (stay off) and yameru (quit) sound alike; yasumi o toru is days off, while a few minutes' rest is kyuukei o toru.

blocks.label: Homework and grades
blocks.rationale: Schoolwork from the desk to the report card: doing homework, handing it in, working problems, good grades.
blocks.interference: shukudai o suru is doing it and shukudai o dasu is handing it in (or setting it, when a teacher says it); a problem you work out is toku, not kotaeru.

blocks.label: Exams and results
blocks.rationale: An exam from start to finish: you sit it, get your score, the results come out, you pass or fail.
blocks.interference: The exam is ukeru but the score is toru (never shiken o toru); ukeru (take, with o) and ukaru (pass, with ni) sound alike, and ochiru is ukaru's opposite.

blocks.label: University and jobs
blocks.rationale: Getting in somewhere: looking for work, finding it, entering a university or company, the experience you bring.
blocks.interference: Looking is shigoto o sagasu (o) but finding is shigoto ga mitsukaru (ga); daigaku and kaisha both take ni hairu, and keiken takes ga aru, not motsu.

blocks.label: Getting work done
blocks.rationale: The work itself: using your head, delivering results, taking notes, ideas coming to you, stamping papers.
blocks.interference: kekka o dasu (you deliver results) is not kekka ga deru (results come out); ideas come to you with ga ukabu, while notes are taken with o toru.

textFixes.value: 'Take' leads to shiken o toru, but toru is for the score you get (ten o toru), a licence, or signing up for a class (jugyou o toru). Exams, tests and interviews are 'undergone': shiken o ukeru.
To check before asking: shitsumon ii? (can I ask something?). Answering one is shitsumon ni kotaeru.

blocks.label: Talking to people
blocks.rationale: The four everyday hanashi sets: talking, listening, opening a serious talk, and someone who goes on and on.
blocks.interference: All four share hanashi, so drill them together: hanashi o suru (you talk), hanashi o kiku (you listen, or do what someone says), hanashi ga aru (I need to talk to you) and hanashi ga nagai (they go on forever), which is not nagai hanashi (a long story: nagai hanashi ni naru kedo...).

blocks.label: Making friends
blocks.rationale: Meeting someone new: making friends, becoming friends with one person, swapping names, going up to someone, and chances to meet people.
blocks.interference: tomodachi ga dekiru is gaining friends in general (tomodachi dekita), while one person is X to tomodachi ni naru; neither is tomodachi o tsukuru. 'Tell me your name' is namae oshiete, not iu, and going up to someone is koe o kakeru, not hanasu.

blocks.label: Kids and growing up
blocks.rationale: Family life: having kids, a baby arriving, growing up, raising children and looking after someone.
blocks.interference: kodomo iru? (got kids?) is having them and kodomo umareta (the baby came) is the birth, with the child as subject in both, not kodomo o motsu. sodateru is raising (sodatsu is being raised), otona ni naru is growing up, and mendou o miru (look after) is not mendokusai (what a hassle).

blocks.label: Close and in touch
blocks.rationale: How things stand with people: close or on bad terms, staying in touch, and hearing from them.
blocks.interference: naka ga ii and naka ga warui say the relationship is good or bad, where English uses a verb (get along). renraku o toru is getting or staying in touch; renraku ga kuru (renraku kita?) is them getting in touch with you, like meeru ga kuru.

blocks.label: Lies, jokes and complaints
blocks.rationale: What friends say to each other: lies, jokes, complaints, venting and secrets.
blocks.interference: Lying takes tsuku (uso tsuita), but joking, complaining and venting take iu. monku o iu is complaining at someone or about something wrong, while guchi o iu is grumbling to let off steam. naisho takes ni suru, not mamoru.

blocks.label: Seeing people
blocks.rationale: Getting together: meeting up with a friend, seeing someone home, going back to your parents', and birthdays.
blocks.interference: au takes ni (tomodachi ni au), not o. Seeing someone home is okuru (okutte iku yo), not tsurete iku. jikka ni kaeru is going back to your parents' place, while uchi ni kaeru is just going home.

blocks.label: Favours, sorry, cheer up
blocks.rationale: Asking a favour, apologising for the trouble or worry you caused, and cheering someone up.
blocks.interference: onegai ga aru is asking a favour and onegai o kiku is granting one. meiwaku o kakeru and shinpai o kakeru put trouble or worry on someone else, while shinpai suru means you are the one worrying. genki dashite (cheer up) is not ganbatte (hang in there).

blocks.label: Manners and thanks
blocks.rationale: Being polite and grateful: saying thanks, speaking politely, not making a fuss, and the guest's thanks for care and meals.
blocks.interference: keigo o tsukau (speak politely) and ki o tsukau (fuss over others) share tsukau, and ki o tsukau is not ki o tsukeru (be careful). In osewa ni naru and gochisou ni naru, ni naru puts you on the receiving end; the giver says mendou o miru or ogoru.

blocks.label: Pride and teasing
blocks.rationale: Looking foolish or cool: being made fun of, embarrassing yourself, and showing off.
blocks.interference: Making fun of someone is baka ni suru (baka ni shinaide), not warau. haji o kaku uses the same kaku as ase o kaku. kakko tsukeru is acting cool, while kakko ii is being cool.

blocks.label: Worries and advice
blocks.rationale: Talking a problem through: having something on your mind, asking for advice, hearing someone out, and saying what you really think.
blocks.interference: soudan ga aru (can I ask your advice?) is the side with the problem and soudan ni noru (I'll hear you out) is the friend's side; neither uses adobaisu. honne o iu is saying what you really feel, where shoujiki ni iu is just being frank.

textFixes.value: Wanting friends is usually tomodachi hoshii or tomodachi tsukuritai. Having them takes ga iru, as in kodomo ga iru: dekita is the moment it happens, iru is having them (tomodachi iru?). Becoming friends with one person is X to tomodachi ni naru.
kodomo dekita = we're having a baby, or we've had kids (kekkon shite kodomo mo dekita). The birth itself is kodomo ga umareru: kodomo umareta (the baby's here).
gochisou ni naru (be treated to a meal) is built the same way: with ni naru, you are the one receiving. The one doing the looking after says mendou o miru (or sewa o suru).
hanashi ga aru n da kedo = I need to talk to you; soudan ga aru n da kedo = can I ask your advice?
X no iu koto o kiku = do what X says (oya no iu koto kikinasai). Listening to a friend's problem and helping them think it through is soudan ni noru.

blocks.label: Read, watch, sing, draw
blocks.rationale: The everyday pastimes whose English verb carries straight across: a book is read, a film watched, a song sung, a picture drawn or painted.
blocks.interference: Little between them. e o kaku uses the same sound as kaku (write) and covers painting too, never hiku as in sen o hiku (draw a line). miru is 'watch' for films and TV alike (eiga mita, terebi miteru).

blocks.label: Going out for fun
blocks.rationale: Everyday plans to go out and do something, all built the same way: the activity noun goes straight before ni iku.
blocks.interference: English 'go for a walk' or 'go to karaoke' tempts a verb before ni iku, but the noun goes straight in: sanpo ni iku, karaoke ni iku. eiga ni iku is the outing and eiga o miru the watching. asobi ni iku also means dropping by someone's place (asobi ni kite ne).

blocks.label: Play and lessons
blocks.rationale: English 'play' splits in two: games and sports take suru (casually yaru) and instruments take hiku. Taking lessons in any of them is narau.
blocks.interference: asobu tempts for all of them. suru/yaru names the activity or hobby (piano yatteru), hiku is actually playing (piano hikeru?), and narau is lessons with a teacher (piano naratteta), never benkyou suru. Keep this hiku apart from kaze o hiku and omikuji o hiku, which sound the same.

blocks.label: Hooked, tickets, winning
blocks.rationale: What comes up once a hobby takes hold: being into something right now, managing to get tickets for a concert or game, and a match won or lost.
blocks.interference: geemu ni hamaru and shiai ni katsu both take ni where English uses 'into' or a direct object, never o. chiketto o toru keeps o, and its toru means securing them (toreta! = I got them), not buying (katta) or being given them (moratta).

blocks.label: Exercise and outdoors
blocks.rationale: Getting your body moving and getting out into nature at the weekend, plus what people say it does for them: a nice change of pace.
blocks.interference: yama ni noboru takes ni, not the bare object of English 'climb a mountain'. tsuri ni iku and kyanpu ni iku put the activity straight before ni iku. kibun tenkan ni naru (with naru) means something did you good, while kibun tenkan suru is taking the break yourself.

blocks.label: Seasonal outings
blocks.rationale: The two big outings of the Japanese year: cherry-blossom viewing in spring, and the first shrine visit at New Year, where you draw a fortune slip.
blocks.interference: In speech hanami is nearly always ohanami. omikuji o hiku uses hiku 'pull, draw', as in kuji o hiku (draw lots), not toru. It sounds the same as piano o hiku but is a different verb.

textFixes.value: Going to the cinema is its own set, eiga ni iku. The invitation is eiga ikanai? or eiga mi ni ikanai?, which mean the same.

Not piano o asobu, and not piano o suru carried over from sakkaa o suru: playing the instrument is hiku (piano hiiteru, piano hikeru?). piano yatteru ('I do piano') names it as a hobby, and lessons with a teacher are piano o narau (piano naratteta); neither means playing it right now.

blocks.label: Feels good or bad
blocks.rationale: How something feels to you (kimochi), your mood (kibun), someone's temper (kigen) and a place you like being in (igokochi).
blocks.interference: English 'feel good/bad' covers all of these: kimochi ii is a physical sensation, kibun ii is your mood, igokochi ii is a place you're at ease in. kimochi warui is queasy or gross, while a grumpy mood others can see is kigen ga warui, not kibun ga warui (feel sick).

blocks.label: Noticing
blocks.rationale: A smell, a sound or a voice reaches you, and you notice something.
blocks.interference: The smell, sound or voice is the subject (nioi suru, oto shita, koe ga kikoeru), so you don't use kagu or kiku; kikoeru? (can you hear me?) is not kiiteru? (are you listening?). ki ga tsuku (notice) sounds almost like ki o tsukeru (be careful).

blocks.label: Understanding
blocks.rationale: The wakaru family: you get what something means, how someone feels, or the difference between two things.
blocks.interference: All three take ga + wakaru, never shitteru, which is knowing a fact; 'tell the difference' is wakaru, not iu. imi nai (it's pointless) is not imi wakannai (it makes no sense).

blocks.label: Likes, interest, confidence
blocks.rationale: How you feel about a thing or a plan: you like it, you're into it, you can't wait, you're sure you can do it.
blocks.interference: English 'interested' and 'confident' are adjectives, but here they are nouns that exist: kyoumi aru, jishin aru (or nai). ki ni itta (I love it) sounds like ki ni natta (it bugged me).

blocks.label: Motivation and mood
blocks.rationale: Your energy and mood: no motivation, getting yourself going, perking up, getting hyped, stress piling up.
blocks.interference: yaruki and genki both 'come out' (deru): yaruki denai is can't get going, genki deta is it gave me a lift, and genki dashite is what you say to someone else. Mood goes up (tenshon agaru) while stress piles up (tamaru); tenshon means hype, not tension.

blocks.label: When it hits you
blocks.rationale: Reactions to a big moment like a concert, a sad film or big news: tears come, goosebumps rise, it hasn't sunk in yet.
blocks.interference: Each reaction is the subject with its own verb: namida ga deru (not naku, which is crying outright), torihada ga tatsu (stand, not deru). jikkan wakanai (it hasn't sunk in) sounds close to wakannai (I don't get it).

textFixes.value: Often comes with a sound word: gatan tte oto shita (there was a thud). For 'can hear', the verb is kikoeru: oto ga kikoeru, and koe ga kikoeru for voices and calls.

value: chikara (strength: chikara ga denai, can't muster the strength)

blocks.label: Looks and voice
blocks.rationale: Describing what someone looks and sounds like: tall, short, loud, long hair, a good figure.
blocks.interference: Each noun picks its own size word: height is takai/hikui (never ookii or mijikai), hair is nagai, and a loud voice is ookii, since koe ga takai means high-pitched. sutairu ga ii is a good figure, not fashion (that's oshare).

blocks.label: Smart and skilled
blocks.rationale: Praise for what someone is good at: brains, Japanese, their job, taste.
blocks.interference: Each noun takes its own word for 'good': atama ga ii (never jouzu), nihongo ga jouzu (a skill done well), shigoto ga dekiru (capable, not jouzu), sensu ga ii. nihongo ga dekiru only says you can speak it; jouzu says you speak it well.

blocks.label: Luck and help
blocks.rationale: Quick verdicts on how something went: lucky, unlucky, that helped, that did me good.
blocks.interference: un ga ii and un ga warui are one pair, so drill them in one frame (un ii ne! / un warui na). yaku ni tatsu is practical help with a task (not benri, handy); tame ni naru is something that does you good over time, like a talk, a book or an experience.

blocks.label: Personality and mood
blocks.rationale: What someone is like and how they seem: nice, mean, pleasant to deal with, down today.
blocks.interference: seikaku is who someone is underneath, kanji is the impression their manner gives, and genki ga nai is how they seem right now. seikaku ga warui means mean or nasty, far stronger than 'not nice', and genki ga nai is low and flat, not kibun ga warui (feel sick).

blocks.label: Out and about
blocks.rationale: Remarks about a shop, a place or a day out: crowded, popular, a nice vibe, well reviewed, heavy bags.
blocks.interference: ninki ga aru means lots of people like it, hyouban ga ii means people speak well of it (reviews, word of mouth). Crowded is hito ga ooi or konderu, never isogashii. ii fun'iki puts ii first, though fun'iki ga ii is just as natural.

blocks.label: Body and fitness
blocks.rationale: What someone's body can do: see, run, play sport, keep going; often said about yourself in the negative (me warui, tairyoku nai).
blocks.interference: English adjectives (short-sighted, fast, athletic, fit) all become noun + ga + word: the eyes are bad, the legs are fast, the motor nerves are good, the stamina is there. Speed is hayai, coordination is ii, and stamina takes aru/nai, not ii.

textFixes.value: tasukatta (you saved me) is the warmer thanks when someone helps you. To offer help: nanika yaku ni tateru koto attara itte ne. A talk, book or experience that does you good in the longer run is tame ni naru (tame ni naru hanashi), and to thank a senior for a talk, say benkyou ni narimashita.

In the reverse order, ii kanji (いい感じ) means 'going well, looking good': ii kanji da ne! For the mood of a café or a room, the usual set is ii fun'iki. Kanji (感じ, feeling) sounds the same as kanji (Chinese characters).

value: inshou (inshou ga ii: make a good impression)
taido (taido ga warui: have a bad attitude)
tsukiai (tsukiai ga ii: sociable, always up for things)

textFixes.value: Not shigoto ga jouzu. Jouzu praises how skilfully something is done (nihongo ga jouzu, ryouri ga jouzu), while dekiru says someone is capable. Being good at your job is shigoto ga dekiru, usually as shigoto ga dekiru hito.
Popular with the opposite sex is the single verb moteru. Hyouban ga ii is different: people speak well of it (reviews, word of mouth), while ninki ga aru means lots of people like it or go there.

Shumi ga ii also means good taste, but shumi mostly means 'hobby', and ii shumi shiteru ne is often sarcastic. Keep it apart from sutairu ga ii, which means a good figure, not style; someone who dresses well is oshare.

fixes.value: The polite way to turn down an invitation for a particular day: sumimasen, sono hi wa sen'yaku ga atte..., left trailing, since a flat ...kara sounds like an excuse. Friends say it too (gomen, sen'yaku aru n da) when the plan is with someone else; yotei aru is vaguer.

Used about parenting as a whole: hitori de kodomo o sodateta (she raised her kids alone), kodomo sodateru no tte taihen da yo. Everyday talk often uses the noun kosodate (parenting) instead: ima kosodate-chuu (I'm busy raising kids).
Kin'en-chuu (I'm off cigarettes for now) is the other everyday phrase; kin'en on a sign means no smoking.

consistency.notes:
The list has 405 sets: 208 old and 197 new. Every old id is placed exactly once. I checked against the full new entries in scratchpad/new_full.json and against the chunk-step groups in chunks.json. merge.py applies the chunk-step groups first and these fixes after them.

(1) Duplicates: none, so nothing is dropped. These look close but are different sets, and all are common:
- denwa ga aru / denwa ga kakaru: their notes already separate "a call happened, passed on" from "a call comes in to you".
- hima ga nai / jikan ga nai
- jikan o toru / jikan o tsukuru
- soto ni deru / uchi o deru
- tomodachi ni naru / tomodachi ga dekiru
- taichou ga warui / guai ga warui
- hi ga shizumu / hi ga kureru
- gohan o ogoru / gochisou ni naru: the two sides of being treated.

(2) Spelling:
- Every new headword's romaji was converted from its kana and compared. Every romaji token in the headwords, polite forms and examples, old and new, was checked for variant spellings. The only headword miss is senyaku ga aru. This list writes n' (fun'iki, ten'in, kin'en, tan'i), so it is fixed to sen'yaku in romaji, polite and use.
- The schema cannot touch examples. Both example romaji of c-senyaku-ga-aru still say "senyaku" and need the same change at merge.
- Suffix -chuu is hyphenated everywhere (kaigi-chuu, shigoto-chuu, denwa-chuu in the versatility list). "kosodate chuu" and "Kin'en chuu" are aligned to that.
- honto/hontou and bakkari/bakari are casual versus polite on purpose and are left alone.
- Outside this list: 20-list-versatile.json writes zenin (item B-zenin), konya and panya-san with no apostrophe. Kotoba's convention on n' is therefore not settled across the two lists.

(3) Contrast groups:
- Four groups had a single member after chunking: kireru-run-out, todoku-tsuku, tabako and yowai-tolerance. Each now has its natural partner, and the entries' own text names that partner:
  - juuden ga kireru joins kigen ga kireru.
  - eki ni tsuku joins nimotsu ga todoku, whose trap is tsuku versus todoku.
  - tabako o suu joins tabako o yameru. The group is renamed tabako-pair to match shitsumon-pair, shukudai-pair and the others.
  - atsusa ni yowai joins osake ga yowai / tsuyoi, whose notes already contrast it. All three are renamed tsuyoi-yowai.
- Three new pairs, each set naming the other in its use or trap:
  - chuushi ni naru / enki ni naru (chuushi-enki)
  - bangou o oshieru / namae o oshieru (oshieru-tell)
  - kami o kiru / tsume o kiru (kiru-cut, same block)
- Three sets join existing groups:
  - oto ga deru joins sense-perception. Its notes contrast it with oto ga suru.
  - kaimono ni iku joins outing-ni-iku. Its trap is the same noun + ni iku pattern.
  - onsen ni hairu joins take-verbs. Its trap is abiru versus ofuro ni hairu.
- Left as they are:
  - jikan o toru stays in take-verbs, because its trap is toru versus kakaru.
  - nihongo ga jouzu keeps the chunker's jouzu-dekiru.

(4) englishVerb: I kept the last pass's reading, which bans parentheticals but allows phrasal verbs ("take off", "turn on"). Values that include the noun are cut to the word the trap names:
- make friends → make (same as tomodachi ga dekiru)
- go home → go (same as uchi ni kaeru)
- ask advice → ask (same as onegai ga aru)
- give advice → advise

Ids that can't change but no longer match their romaji:
- c-kibarashi-ni-naru is now kibun tenkan ni naru. kibarashi only appears as a partner.
- c-kakkou-o-tsukeru is kakko tsukeru.
- c-uchi-made-okuru is ie made okuru.
- c-hanami-ni-iku and c-bentou-o-atatameru carry the o- prefix in romaji.
Of these, only kibarashi names a different noun. Rename it at merge if ids may still change.

stages.name: Stage 1
stages.summary: Talk about the weather, being hungry or in pain, going out and coming home, the bathroom, catching a train, school and work days, chatting and making friends, simple hobbies, how you feel, and what people look like and are good at.

stages.name: Stage 2
stages.summary: Talk about meals and drinks, catching a cold and getting better, doors, lights and bedtime, TV and photos, what you're wearing, family and friends, noticing and understanding things, and what you like.

stages.name: Stage 3
stages.summary: Make plans and say when you're free, pay and spend, phone and message people, go out to drink, take trips and pick people up, find your way, tidy up, take time off, and handle favours, apologies and thanks.

stages.name: Stage 4
stages.summary: Talk about breakfast and the fridge, housework, gadgets and apps, glasses and accessories, exams, job hunting and getting work done, long-term health and injuries, errands and promises, moods and worries, and outings through the seasons.
